Sports.title: Usyk Camp Rejects Tyson Fury’s Backup Plan
Sports.content:
Usyk’s manager, Sergey Lapin, was unimpressed by the public offer.

“Usyk is not Tyson’s backup plan,” Lapin told Sky Sports. “If Fury needs an opponent, he should visit the Ready to Fight platform. They can help him find a worthy opponent there. Oleksandr is always open to big challenges. But serious intentions are backed by a concrete offer, not statements in the press.”

The Joshua negotiations have not stalled because neither boxer has formally refused to fight. Both men signed individual contracts, but their teams remain divided over the venue.

Joshua and Matchroom want Wembley Stadium, which they believe was included in the agreement. The organizers and broadcast partners favor Madison Square Garden in New York, where the event can be staged at a more convenient hour for Netflix’s American audience.

A Wembley event designed around United States viewing hours may require an early morning ring walk in London. That creates transportation, licensing, and logistical issues while asking British ticket buyers to attend a fight at an unreasonable hour.

Declaring the fight dead and naming Usyk gives Fury a way to pressure Joshua into accepting New York without admitting that the original contest remains under negotiation.

It is unclear how serious Fury is about pursuing the trilogy. Calling out Usyk gives him another famous name to mention while the Joshua event remains tied up over its venue.

Actually fighting Usyk would be a far greater risk. Fury lost both previous meetings on points and came close to being stopped in the ninth round of their first contest. A third defeat would make the Joshua event an even harder sell. The contest is already based largely on nostalgia. Both men are former champions in the later stages of their careers, and each has suffered damaging defeats.

If Fury lost to Usyk again, he and Joshua would hold a combined record of zero wins and five losses against the Ukrainian. Promoters would then be selling a meeting between two aging British heavyweights who repeatedly failed against the same opponent.

Having vacated his remaining heavyweight belts, Usyk can now select the final fights of his career without mandatory obligations controlling his schedule. He has no sporting reason to rescue Fury’s November date through a hastily arranged trilogy.

A pair of victories already settled matters in Usyk’s mind. Stepping in again calls for massive purses, extensive camp preparations, plus contract clauses honoring the undisputed winner of their first two bouts. Lapin’s reaction guards those advantages. The champion keeps possibilities open without letting Fury treat him like an easy backup while Joshua talks stall.

Ultimatums, false retirement vows, and substitute names constantly pop up whenever Fury sits at the bargaining table. This callout fits the usual routine: fabricate panic, point fingers, then pretend another blockbuster remains ready to sign. A trilogy could still materialize eventually. Yet a social media challenge hardly counts as an actual contract talk.

The real threat facing Fury and Joshua is letting this matchup disappear altogether. Without championship belts between them, another setback for either man would instantly erode their commercial draw. Every prolonged holdout simply turns the contest into a nostalgic showcase of past glories rather than a fight that matters in the present.

Until Fury’s team sends Usyk a concrete proposal, the trilogy callout is best understood as leverage in the Joshua venue dispute.

Sports.title: Andy Cruz Gets Second IBF Title Chance
Sports.content:
Raymond Muratalla surrendered the belt after struggling to make 135 pounds for his recent defense against Robson Conceição. He plans to continue his career at light welterweight, creating an opening for the IBF’s two highest-ranked available contenders.

Cruz (7-1, 4 KOs) lost a majority decision to Muratalla in January after challenging for the championship in only his seventh professional appearance. Muratalla’s pressure and activity became increasingly effective during the later rounds, showing that Cruz’s extensive amateur background had not fully prepared him for the physical demands of a hard professional fight.

The 31-year-old Cuban returned in July and stopped late replacement Abraham Montoya in three rounds. His brief comeback gave no clear indication that he had corrected the weaknesses exposed by Muratalla.

An exceptional counterpuncher with world-class reflexes, Cruz often depends on distance, quick reactions, and single clean shots. Those tools can control shorter amateur bouts. Over 12 rounds, repeatedly changing direction and escaping exchanges can drain a fighter who is not comfortable holding his ground or working inside.

Subkhankulov (12-0, 6 KOs) will try to force that type of contest. The 34-year-old Russian southpaw earned his position by stopping Bakhodur Usmonov in the 12th round of their April eliminator. Usmonov went down four times across the final three rounds before the referee ended the action.

His southpaw position will also test Cruz’s lead foot placement and ability to land the right hand without remaining in range for counters. Subkhankulov is unlikely to be discouraged by feints or a difficult opening six rounds. His best chance is to attack the body, keep Cruz working, and turn the final third into another test of stamina.

There is history between them. Cruz defeated Subkhankulov by split decision when they met in the semifinals of the Ústí nad Labem Grand Prix in May 2019. The three-round amateur result offers Cruz some familiarity, but it says little about how their styles will interact over a professional championship distance.

The October 7 deadline may determine more than the fighters’ pay. Cruz has spent his professional career fighting in the United States, while Subkhankulov has done much of his work in Russia and on IBA-promoted cards. If negotiations fail and Subkhankulov’s side wins the purse bid, Cruz may have to pursue the championship far from his usual surroundings.

This is still a favorable route back for Cruz. He avoids another meeting with Muratalla and faces someone he has already beaten. However, two championship appearances within his first nine professional outings show how aggressively his career is being pushed.

At 31, Cruz does not have years to spend developing against mid-level opposition. Winning the vacant belt against Subkhankulov may be the calculated shortcut his team needs. Losing would show that the rush from decorated amateur to professional champion asked too much of him too quickly.

Sports.title: Jack Dempsey Escapes Without A Verdict Against Miske
Sports.content:
At 22 years of age, Dempsey was tearing through the heavyweight division with his aggressive style and crushing left hook. Miske, 24, had the benefit of fighting before his hometown supporters, but he was far more than a protected local attraction.

Dempsey weighed 187½ pounds, while Miske came in at 182.

Known as the “St. Paul Thunderbolt,” Miske was a fast, clever boxer who understood how to block punches, smother attacks, and work at close range. Those skills gave Dempsey one of his hardest tests during his climb toward Jess Willard’s heavyweight championship.

The local favorite supplied a tactical lesson for smaller fighters facing dangerous punchers. Instead of continually backing away, he stepped into Dempsey’s punching range and crowded him. Retreating would have given Dempsey space to drive forward, build speed, and launch his leaping left hook. Miske took away that leverage by getting close, controlling Dempsey’s arms and preventing him from completing his punches.

The rolling movement associated with Dempsey’s attacks depended upon momentum. He bobbed his upper body from side to side, shifted his weight, and sprang forward with hooks from changing angles. An opponent who backed away gave that attack time to gather force.

Meeting Dempsey chest to chest changed the exchanges into an arm wrestle. His long swings lost much of their force as Miske blocked the hook, jammed the punching arm, and answered with short shots before tying him up.

Quick punches inside prevented the younger man from finding a steady rhythm. Dempsey had productive stretches in the second and third rounds, but Miske answered with a hard right cross in the third.

Years later, Dempsey admitted that Miske was landing more punches and building what looked like a lead. He also recalled being hurt during one exchange and struggling to remain upright until the bell.

“Miske had landed more telling blows than I had,” Dempsey recalled. “He suddenly came at me with a volley that nearly put me out.”

It was a revealing admission from a fighter remembered for overwhelming opponents. Raw aggression had run into a boxer who understood distance, timing and leverage. The visiting fighter finally produced his strongest attack in the seventh. A heavy left to the body followed by a right to the jaw troubled Miske and helped Dempsey recover ground. Neither man scored a knockdown, leaving the newspapers to decide which work they valued more.

Miske’s approach was almost the opposite of the one Jess Willard used against Dempsey in Toledo the following year. The 6’6″ champion tried to control the challenger from long range but remained too upright and stationary.

That distance allowed Dempsey to leap forward with hooks and overhand punches. Willard became an easy target once the challenger closed the distance, leading to seven knockdowns during the savage opening round.

Such a runway was never available against Miske. He moved toward the danger, shortened the punches, and forced Dempsey to work without full leverage. Willard waited at the end of Dempsey’s forward rush, while Miske intercepted it before the punches reached full speed.

The St. Paul fight showed that smothering Dempsey was safer than surrendering the ring and waiting for him to attack. Gene Tunney receives credit for solving Dempsey in 1926 and repeating the result one year later. Miske had exposed several of the same weaknesses eight years earlier. Their tactics were not identical. Tunney relied more heavily on footwork, his jab, and movement at long range. Miske was more willing to hold his position, work inside, and smother Dempsey physically.

Both remained composed when Dempsey attacked. They refused to become stationary targets at his preferred distance and punished him when his forward movement became predictable.

Before their first fight, Tunney studied films of Dempsey and brought former opponents and sparring partners into camp. There is no firm evidence that Miske personally supplied Tunney’s plan, but the St. Paul contest had established the central principle: Dempsey became less effective when an opponent denied him momentum and forced him to restart his attacks.

Miske supplied the early evidence that denying Dempsey momentum made him less effective, and Tunney later produced the polished championship version.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press surveyed eight writers at ringside. Four favored Dempsey, one selected Miske and three scored the fight even. The newspaper published the bout as a draw, although other reports awarded Dempsey a narrow newspaper decision based on his aggression and heavier punches.

A later collection drawing upon additional newspaper sources produced seven verdicts for Dempsey, four draws and one for Miske. That broader tally included reports beyond the eight writers questioned in St. Paul.

Such disagreement exposed the weakness of the no decision era. A boxer’s official record remained untouched after a distance fight, even when most observers believed he had lost. Local sports editors became unofficial judges without a uniform scoring system or any requirement to agree.

Reports from St. Paul do not support the claim that hometown writers simply protected Miske. Four of the eight surveyed writers favored the visiting Dempsey, while only one selected Miske. Regional loyalty may have influenced individual accounts, but the split also reflected a genuinely close fight.

Miske landed more often and controlled long portions of the contest, while Dempsey delivered the harder individual blows. Some writers valued activity and craft; others favored aggression and damage.

Promoters benefited from the uncertainty. Dempsey survived a difficult night without receiving an official loss, allowing his handlers to continue selling him as the next threat to Willard. Miske also avoided a formal defeat and remained a leading heavyweight attraction in Minnesota. Jack Kearns wanted knockouts that would sell Dempsey to a national audience. Taking him into Miske’s hometown against a fast, experienced boxer was a serious gamble.

The no decision format reduced the danger because only a knockout placed an official loss on the record. It did not remove the promotional risk. A decisive beating reported across the country still would have damaged Dempsey’s growing reputation.

Kearns learned that clever defensive fighters presented a different challenge from the large, slower heavyweights Dempsey destroyed. His fighter continued facing dangerous opposition, including Fred Fulton, Battling Levinsky, Bill Brennan and Miske himself, but the first fight supplied a warning. Dempsey’s power did not automatically solve every style.

The pair met again in Philadelphia on November 28, 1918, with most newspapers favoring Dempsey after six rounds. By then, the future champion had gained more experience against Miske’s troublesome methods.

Their third fight came on September 6, 1920, after Dempsey had taken the heavyweight championship from Willard. Miske was suffering from Bright’s disease and was knocked out in the third round of Dempsey’s first title defense.

His illness was not common public knowledge, so there is no basis for claiming Kearns selected Miske because he knew the challenger was dying. In hindsight, the physical decline made the title fight far less dangerous than their first meeting had been.

That knockout became the lasting image of their rivalry. Miske is now remembered primarily as the sick challenger who needed money, while Dempsey remains one of boxing’s most recognizable champions.

The familiar family story belongs mainly to the end of Miske’s life, not the 1920 title fight. A gravely ill Miske returned against Bill Brennan in November 1923, scored a fourth-round knockout, and used the money to give his family a memorable Christmas. He died on January 1, 1924.

Remembering only the tragedy reduces Miske to a sympathetic opponent in Dempsey’s championship story. Reports from 1918 present the fuller picture.

At that time, the St. Paul Thunderbolt was one of the sharpest technical boxers in the heavyweight division, possessing the timing, defense, and composure to frustrate Dempsey near his physical peak. He survived 10 rounds and forced the future champion to abandon many of his preferred attacks. The press left St. Paul unable to agree on a winner.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Claims Benn Overlooks His Ring Intelligence
Sports.content:
The less flattering side is his habit of retreating in straight lines until his back reaches the ropes. He often relies on a high guard, clinch, or awkward turn instead of circling into open space. Benn will attempt to close those exits, making Ryan’s footwork an immediate test of the boxing depth he is advertising.

Aggression also creates danger for the challenger. Benn was dropped twice by Cedrick Peynaud early in his career, and he can still rush inside without setting up his attacks. Those entries give Ryan opportunities to land his fastest counter.

Charging forward carelessly during the opening three rounds would leave Benn exposed. Ryan is at his most dangerous when an opponent supplies the movement and gives him a stationary target. One poorly timed leap may be all the champion needs.

The body offers Benn his clearest route to slowing Ryan. Gervonta Davis stopped him with a liver shot in 2023, and Benn throws heavy hooks downstairs when he gets within punching range. Sustained body work could reduce Ryan’s movement and take some of the speed from his counters.

Reaching that distance is the difficult part. Ryan owns the faster hands and is more dangerous from the outside, leaving his challenger dependent on close-quarters exchanges and a punishing pace.

Returning to 147 pounds raises another question for Benn. He added size for two fights with Chris Eubank Jr., and camp footage shows a noticeably leaner fighter coming back down to welterweight. If the cut weakens his legs or stamina, trapping Ryan will become increasingly difficult.

This is Ryan’s opportunity to support his claim. Knocking Benn out with another hook would confirm the power everyone already recognizes. Escaping the ropes, controlling distance, working inside, and adjusting to the body attack would demonstrate the boxing IQ he believes Benn has failed to appreciate.

Sports.title: Fury Calls Itauma A Billion-Dollar Loss
Sports.content:
A few soft opponents will not cause supporters to abandon Itauma. The real difficulty is finding fighters who can extend him without beating him.

To support his warning, Fury used his own career as the example Itauma should have followed.

“I did it the traditional route, and it’s done like that for a reason,” Fury said. “I was 27 years old when I fought Wladimir Klitschko; I was a 10-1 underdog [but] I was ready. If I’d have fought him at 21, I’d have got knocked out, too.”

There is some truth in that. Fury spent years fighting domestic and European opposition before receiving his first world title opportunity. He entered the Klitschko fight with a 24-0 record, making the November 2015 contest his 25th professional bout.

What his version leaves out is Klitschko’s condition at the time. The champion was 39 and nearing the end of his career. His reactions, punch output, and willingness to exchange had declined. Fury did not complete a traditional apprenticeship and then defeat a heavyweight champion at his physical peak.

With only 35 professional rounds behind him, Itauma was given a much more dangerous test. Hrgovic was experienced, durable, and able to force a hard pace after absorbing Itauma’s best punches.

The promotional obsession with Itauma breaking Mike Tyson’s record as the youngest heavyweight champion also helped accelerate his development. That age window had already closed by the time he fought Hrgovic, but the rush had shaped his career. Opponents were selected to produce quick knockouts and keep him moving toward a marketing milestone.

Those victories established Itauma’s destructive image without preparing him for the moment a world-class heavyweight refused to disappear.

Stories about Itauma handling leading heavyweights in sparring helped create confidence in his readiness. Fabio Wardley also confirmed that Itauma had completed 12-round sparring sessions despite an earlier interview clip suggesting otherwise.

Completing 12 rounds in a gym is not the same as fighting nine hard rounds under championship pressure. Sparring partners can reduce the pace and stop when instructed. There are no judges, title stakes, or thousands of spectators reacting to every punch.

Once the fight began, Hrgovic presented a psychological test that closed gym sessions could not reproduce. Itauma hit him hard, dropped him in the second round, and continued attacking, yet the older man kept coming. Every unsuccessful attempt to finish Hrgovic increased the physical and mental cost.

Nothing in Itauma’s professional experience had prepared him for an opponent absorbing that much punishment and returning with greater pressure after six rounds.

It would be too simple to blame roadwork or poor cardiovascular conditioning. Itauma exhausted himself through the way he fought.

Nearly every combination was thrown with maximum torque. He remained tense at close range and repeatedly searched for a damaging finish. He lacked a controlling jab that would allow him to maintain distance, score without spending heavily, and recover while remaining offensively active.

After Hrgovic survived the early assault, Itauma had no economical gear. His legs weakened, his punches lost their shape, and he no longer had the energy to defend himself or slow Hrgovic’s advance.

The jump in opposition was considerable, but the matchmaking alone did not cause the defeat. Itauma’s approach made an already difficult test even harder.

Proof that a young heavyweight can recover from a defeat is already available within Queensberry. Frank Warren continued working with Daniel Dubois after losses to Joe Joyce and Oleksandr Usyk.

After both fights, Dubois faced criticism, particularly when he took a knee and allowed the referee to count him out. Those defeats did not destroy his commercial value or end his title ambitions. Queensberry lowered the pressure, found suitable fights, and gave him another opportunity to develop.

Rather than watching a “billion-dollar” future disappear, Itauma may be following a rougher version of the Dubois route. The difference is that Queensberry must use the rebuilding period to correct an identifiable weakness instead of merely restoring his knockout streak.

“I just think that knocking out a low-level man is different to knocking out a world-class man; different power, toughness, everything,” Fury said. “It is totally different. “It’s about getting the balance right. Get him in with somebody who is durable, not that dangerous, who can take punishment and give him the rounds. He needs to get used to getting the rounds in.”

Here, Fury makes his strongest point. Queensberry needs durable opponents who can survive Itauma’s opening attacks, make him think, and force him to regulate his output. He must learn to vary the speed of his punches, take quiet periods, and stop treating every opening as a chance to produce a knockout.

Until he does, the Hrgovic blueprint will remain available. A mobile heavyweight can stay away during the early rounds, while a durable pressure fighter can absorb his power and wait for him to slow down.

Careful matchmaking can restore Itauma’s popularity, but it cannot disguise his stamina forever. If his engine remains suited to six rounds, the same ending will remain possible whenever an opponent lasts long enough to test it.

Sports.title: Hearn Says TKO Gave Joshua 90 Minutes for America
Sports.content:
“Yesterday, TKO went around the back again to try and offer Joshua money to do the fight in America,” Hearn told DAZN. “It’s a dirty, dirty game, mate, to be honest with you. It’s made it even harder for them because Josh just ain’t about that. You’ve got an hour and a half to make your decision. Mate, what don’t you understand? I signed to fight in Britain. I want the fight in Britain.”

The 90-minute demand is the major addition to Hearn’s story. A deadline that short would leave Joshua little time to study revised terms, consult his lawyers, or calculate the financial consequences of moving the event from Britain.

It sounds like an attempt to place a large number in front of AJ and force an immediate decision. No amount has been disclosed, but TKO presumably understood that a modest increase would not persuade him to surrender Wembley Stadium, his home support, and the protection Hearn says was written into the signed agreement.

“You can’t buy everybody,” Hearn continued. “Especially the ones who it means something to.”

Hearn said the approach strengthened Joshua’s determination to keep the Fury fight in Britain. The growing public support has also changed the tone of the venue negotiations. A week earlier, Hearn said there was “zero interest” in London and that New York was being treated as the only destination. He now claims Sela has asked him about contacting London Mayor Sadiq Khan to help make the British event possible.

The conflict with TKO has not ended. When asked if Matchroom would take action over the direct approach, Hearn said his team had already written to the company.

“What are you doing?” Hearn said. “You guys are on the New York Stock Exchange. What is this? Just coming around the back trying to bung someone a few quid. Come on. It doesn’t have to be like that. But it’s pushing the fight further away because of their behavior.”

That is the danger behind TKO’s alleged tactic. The company may have believed a quick financial offer would settle the American venue, but Hearn says it produced the opposite response. Joshua is now more committed to Britain, Matchroom has contacted TKO in writing, and the relationship between the parties has deteriorated.

Hearn placed the likelihood of Fury and Joshua fighting in Britain at 64%. That oddly precise estimate still leaves New York in contention, but it is more optimistic than his position a week ago.

The missing financial figure remains fascinating. If TKO wanted Joshua’s answer within 90 minutes, it must have believed the offer was large enough to make him reconsider everything he had signed for.

Sports.title: Muhammad Ali, Richard Dunn, And The AccuPunch
Sports.content:
Both stood 6’3″, but nearly everything else separated them. Ali traveled with an international promotional circus and commanded million-dollar purses. Dunn was a former paratrooper and working scaffolder who balanced his trade with professional boxing. Their meeting was not part of the original plan.

German promoters anticipated that Bernd August would win the vacant European championship and provide Ali with a German challenger. Dunn ruined the arrangement by stopping August in the third round at London’s Royal Albert Hall seven weeks before the Munich date.

That victory sent Bradford’s working-class champion into a fight with the most famous athlete in the world.

Dunn was Ali’s third championship opponent in barely three months. Ali stopped Jean Pierre Coopman in February, struggled through 15 rounds with Jimmy Young in April, and returned against Dunn only 24 days later.

The champion traveled between Puerto Rico, Maryland, and West Germany while completing three training camps and fulfilling three promotional commitments. Money helped drive the pace. His large entourage, expensive lifestyle, and business obligations required a steady supply of purses.

Ali’s performance against Young showed what the schedule was costing him. He looked slow, poorly conditioned, and frustrated as Young made him miss before leaning through the ropes to escape exchanges.

The judges awarded Ali a unanimous decision, but the scores did not erase the criticism. Young had exposed how much of the champion’s timing and movement had disappeared since his physical peak.

Munich gave Ali an opportunity to look dominant again. Dunn held three respected championships, but his direct, aggressive style offered fewer complications than Young’s movement and defensive tricks.

The promotion struggled before either boxer reached the ring. A dispute involving $225,000 from Ali’s purse and German taxes placed the event in danger only days before the fight.

A late compromise kept the card alive. Ali’s purse was reported at approximately $1.6 million after adjustments, while Dunn received about $100,000, easily the largest payday of his career. Ali also helped cover a shortage in the challenger’s money.

The champion spent another $100,000 purchasing 2,000 tickets for American servicemen stationed near Munich. Even that gesture did not rescue the live gate.

The main event began around 3 a.m. local time to place it on NBC during American primetime. That decision served the television audience but punished German ticket buyers. High prices and the brutal starting hour helped leave thousands of seats unsold.

Roughly 11,000 people were inside the 12,700-seat Olympiahalle, but about 4,000 reportedly attended with complimentary tickets. Estimates placed the promoters’ losses between $300,000 and $500,000. Ali and Dunn received their money. The local backers were left with the bill.

Ali frequently described southpaws as awkward opponents. Karl Mildenberger had given him uncomfortable moments from the left-handed stance during their 1966 championship fight, creating the belief that the alignment itself caused Ali trouble. Dunn demonstrated the limits of that theory. A southpaw stance changes punching angles, but it does not automatically provide timing or defense. Dunn approached Ali upright, followed him instead of cutting off the ring, and often began his attacks with looping punches.

Those wide shots gave Ali time to recognize what was coming. Dunn also advanced without consistent head movement, leaving a direct lane for the champion’s right hand.

A quicker and more deceptive southpaw might have punished Ali’s low left hand and tendency to pull away from punches. Dunn lacked the speed and disguise required to take advantage. His stance altered the angles, but his technical flaws gave Ali the solution.

Ali waited for Dunn to square himself and drove short rights through the opening. The fight showed that his difficulties were not caused by southpaws alone. They came against opponents who knew how to use the stance.

Dunn pressed forward from the opening bell and tried to force a physical contest. His activity kept Ali from treating the bout as an exhibition, but much of his work struck gloves, arms, or empty space.

The challenger’s bravery soon worked against him. He continued marching forward after Ali established his advantages in speed, timing, and power. Instead of changing his approach, Dunn kept presenting the same openings.

Ali was more than 10 pounds lighter than he had been against Young. He remained heavier and less mobile than the dazzling fighter of the 1960s, but the lower weight helped him look sharper.

The champion stayed patient during the early rounds, studied Dunn’s attacks, and gradually began sitting down on his punches. Once he committed to the right hand, Dunn lacked the defensive reactions to protect himself.

Ali dropped him three times in the fourth round. Each knockdown exposed the difference between determination and defensive ability at championship level.

Dunn rose from another knockdown in the fifth, but a short right sent him to the canvas again. Referee Herbert Tomser stopped the fight at 2:05 as Ali theatrically wound up his right arm from a neutral corner.

Ali later credited taekwondo instructor Jhoon Rhee for teaching him the short right used in the finish. Rhee called it the “AccuPunch” and said its quick delivery was based on a technique Bruce Lee had shown him.

The punch was designed to remove the physical warnings that normally precede a power shot. Instead of drawing back the hand or first rotating the shoulder, the boxer sent the fist directly toward the target and brought the rest of the body behind it.

That approach suited the opening against Dunn. The challenger was advancing with his head high and his guard separated. Ali released the right from close range before Dunn recognized the attack.

The exaggerated arm motion came afterward, when Ali knew the contest was finished and began performing for the crowd.

It gave him the 37th knockout of his professional career. Ali never stopped or officially knocked down another opponent.

The Dunn victory was the last time Ali increased the pressure, repeatedly floored an opponent, and ended a fight before the final bell.

His later victories depended more heavily on endurance, clinching, defense, and carefully rationed attacks. Ken Norton forced him through another punishing 15 rounds. Earnie Shavers hurt him badly before Ali rallied in the final round. Leon Spinks outworked him in their first fight and pushed him through 15 more rounds in the rematch.

Ali retained the ability to produce combinations and fight through exhaustion, but he was no longer an offensive finisher. His legs moved less, his punches carried less force, and too many rounds were spent on the ropes while opponents worked.

Dunn became the final opponent Ali was able to erase once he decided to attack.

Ali had little time to recover. Just 33 days after beating Dunn, he faced Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in a mixed rules exhibition at Tokyo’s Nippon Budokan.

Inoki spent much of the 15-round contest on the canvas, repeatedly kicking Ali’s legs while remaining outside punching range. Ali absorbed more than 100 kicks and left with severe swelling, bleeding, an infection, and two blood clots.

Three months later, he defended his championship against Norton at Yankee Stadium and escaped with a disputed decision after another exhausting 15 rounds.

The sequence captured the reckless pace of Ali’s career. He fought Young in April, Dunn in May, Inoki in June, and Norton in September. His body received little opportunity to recover between major events.

Thousands of people lined the streets of Bradford to welcome Dunn home. They honored a working scaffolder who had risen to challenge the most famous boxer in the world.

His championship run ended five months later when Joe Bugner stopped him in the first round. Dunn retired after a 1977 knockout loss to Kallie Knoetze.

The Munich promotion lost money, but the fight gained historical importance. Dunn became the final opponent Ali stopped, permanently linking the Bradford heavyweight to The Greatest.

Sports.title: Dave Allen’s 40 Fight Plan Gets Bizarre Twist
Sports.content:
Officials had several possible outcomes to consider after watching the replay. Allen could not receive a stoppage victory because the punch was ruled an accidental foul rather than a legal blow. A disqualification would have required the referee to treat the foul as intentional.

Trainer Jamie Moore accepted the no contest despite Allen’s visible unhappiness inside the ring. “He’s gone to hit him in the side of the head. He’s turned his head, he’s hit him in the back of the head, and he’s fallen out of the ring,” Moore told IFL TV. “Dave can’t win on an unintentional foul, but he can’t lose either. So it’s got to be a no contest. By the rules, they’ve done the right thing.”

Under the unified rules commonly used in professional boxing, a fighter knocked out of the ring receives 20 seconds to return without assistance. An injury caused by an accidental foul before four completed rounds generally produces a no contest or technical draw, depending on the governing commission. There were no completed rounds available for a technical decision.

Consequently, neither boxer could be awarded a win from such an unusual sequence. The brief fight was erased competitively, leaving both men without a satisfactory result after completing full training camps.

Falling outside the ring also carried more danger than an ordinary knockdown. Carty dropped from the elevated platform into an area containing chairs and other ringside equipment. Medical personnel therefore had to consider the impact outside the ropes rather than judging his condition solely by the punch.

Before the ending, Carty had used his southpaw jab and attempted to press Allen. Moore was encouraged by how quickly his fighter closed the distance. Allen reached Carty at close range earlier than anticipated and forced the type of physical exchanges that suited him.

“I thought he hurt him a couple of times,” Moore said. “I was over the moon with the way it was going up until that point. It was just over way too quickly to tell anything.” Allen now has one appearance remaining under his 40-fight limit. The Carty contest counts as his 39th professional bout even though it ended without a winner.

A rematch would settle the unfinished business, but it would also require Allen to use his intended last appearance on another meeting with a tricky southpaw. He could instead pursue a larger domestic payday and leave Carty as one of the strangest opponents listed on his record.

Ghana News.title: Chance for Childhood, GJA call for increased funding to strengthen inclusive education
Ghana News.content:
The Country Representative and Safeguarding Lead at Chance for Childhood, Richard Opoku, and the Vice President of the Ghana Journalists Association (GJA), Rebecca Ekpe, have called for increased investment in inclusive education to remove barriers preventing children with disabilities and special educational needs from fully participating in mainstream schools.

Mr Opoku said inadequate funding remained a major challenge to the implementation of Ghana’s Inclusive Education Policy, introduced in 2015 by the Ministry of Education and the Ghana Education Service (GES).

He made the call when he spoke to journalists on the sidelines of a Media Workshop on Disability and Inclusive Education held at the British Council on Tuesday, September 8.

According to him, although the policy provides an important framework for promoting inclusive education, its success depends on adequate resources to translate its provisions into meaningful support for children.

“The main challenge is with the implementation of the policy because of largely inadequate funding,” he said.

Mr Opoku said funding for inclusive education had consistently remained below one per cent of the overall education budget, limiting the provision of essential support for children with disabilities.

He therefore appealed to the government to increase the allocation to at least two per cent, particularly to fund teacher training and appropriate teaching and learning materials.

“We will want to make a special appeal to the government that it should consider the budget allocation for the implementation of inclusive education,” he said.

He said increased investment would help ensure that children with different disabilities and special educational needs could learn alongside their peers in mainstream schools.

“This will ensure that all children, regardless of their disabilities and special educational needs, are able to participate and learn in the mainstream schools,” he added.

Mr Opoku also stressed the need for continuous capacity building for teachers working with children with disabilities.

He said regular training was necessary to equip teachers with the knowledge and skills required to respond to the varying needs of learners.

He further called for greater recognition and motivation for teachers who had devoted their careers to supporting children with disabilities.

According to him, motivation should not be limited to financial incentives, although additional funding would be beneficial.

“There are other ways that we can motivate teachers who have devoted their time to teaching children who have disabilities,” he said.

Madam Ekpe also called for increased government funding, saying inadequate resources, poorly trained teachers and infrastructure deficits continued to undermine inclusive education.

She said the current allocation of less than one per cent should be increased to at least two per cent to support teaching and learning materials, particularly assistive technology that could help remove barriers faced by children with disabilities.

“Without money, we all know that the policy remains [unfulfilled],” she said.

She cited statistics indicating that more than 80 per cent of teachers lacked the necessary training to effectively support inclusive education.

“If you do not have the teachers to teach, I think we are going nowhere,” she said.

Madam Ekpe also urged journalists to expose infrastructure gaps in schools, noting that about 80 per cent of schools reportedly lack essential accessible facilities, including laboratories, toilet facilities and suitable furniture.

She further cited statistics indicating that about 1,700 children with severe communication impairments were out of school, saying the situation required sustained public and media attention.

The two speakers stressed the important role of the media in changing public perceptions about disability.

Mr Opoku said the language, images and voices used in news reports could either reinforce stigma and discrimination or promote a society that respected the rights, dignity and potential of persons with disabilities.

He urged journalists to report disability-related issues responsibly and sensitively, while giving affected persons greater space to tell their own stories.

Madam Ekpe similarly urged journalists to use their platforms to amplify the concerns of persons with disabilities and investigate exclusion within their own communities.

“Our responsibility is to amplify the voices of those who do not have a voice,” she said.

She encouraged journalists to move beyond national statistics and identify disability-related challenges within their immediate communities, arguing that local reporting could expose barriers that might otherwise remain unnoticed.

Mr Opoku said achieving meaningful inclusion required a collective effort involving government, schools, civil society organisations, NGOs, corporate institutions, the media and the wider public.

He said the media workshop was intended to strengthen journalists’ understanding of disability and inclusive education and equip them to use their platforms to promote a more inclusive society.

“The main reason why we organised this event is to ensure that, collectively, we strengthen our understanding about disability and inclusive education, so that we can use our various media platforms to ensure that we build a more inclusive Ghana,” he said.

He urged stakeholders to support and motivate teachers working to prevent children with disabilities from being excluded from the education system.

Madam Ekpe, meanwhile, called on journalists to leave the engagement committed to making society “less disabling and more disability-friendly”, stressing that sustained media attention could help influence policy, challenge stigma and promote equal access to education for all children.

Ghana News.title: TUC’s resistance to ECG privatisation reflects lessons from past – NPP MP
Ghana News.content:
The Member of Parliament for Afigya Kwabre North and a member of Parliament’s Energy Committee, Collins Adomako-Mensah, says the Trades Union Congress (TUC) has legitimate reasons to be cautious about proposed private sector participation in the operations of the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG).

His comments come after the TUC rejected the World Bank’s push for private sector participation (PSP) in the operations of ECG and the Northern Electricity Distribution Company (NEDCo).

The union has accused the World Bank of being “disingenuous” in its description of the proposed arrangement and warned that it would resist what it considers an attempt to privatise Ghana’s electricity distribution sector.

Speaking on JoyNews' The Pulse on Tuesday, September 9, Mr Adomako-Mensah stressed that there is an important distinction between privatisation and private sector participation.

According to him, his political party is not opposed to private participation in the energy sector, provided such an arrangement improves efficiency and reliability.

“Fundamentally, the party I belong to, we are not against private participation, and I use the word private participation for a reason, because there’s a fundamental difference between privatisation and private participation.”

He said the party’s manifesto makes clear that it has no major objection to private sector involvement if it can make ECG more efficient and reliable.

“Our [Minority] view is that, and our manifesto was quite clear on that, that we do not have too much problem with private participation, if only it’s going to bring about more efficiency and reliability,” he said.

However, Mr Adomako-Mensah acknowledged the concerns being raised by organised labour, arguing that Ghana’s experience with previous private collaborations in the energy sector makes caution necessary.

He said the TUC’s position should therefore not necessarily be interpreted as opposition to private participation but as a call for the government to carefully scrutinise the proposed arrangement.

“I must also say that it’s against private players within the energy space, because of the history that it has,” he noted.

According to him, the concerns should serve as a reminder to policymakers to ensure that the proposed arrangement is properly designed and does not repeat challenges associated with previous private sector collaborations.

“I’m sure they are cautioning that we should be careful, and that we should make sure we dot every i and cross every t, so we don’t experience what we experienced with other private collaborations,” he said.

The TUC has maintained that the proposed PSP arrangement goes beyond the World Bank’s description of “only revenue collection.”

The union has argued that the model proposed by the Transaction Advisor appointed at the instance of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) raises broader concerns about private control and participation in electricity distribution.

The debate is therefore expected to centre on whether the proposed arrangement constitutes genuine private sector participation aimed at improving ECG’s performance or amounts to a form of privatisation that could have long-term implications for Ghana’s electricity distribution system.

Ghana News.title: Dorothy’s Hope Foundation to host women’s health forum, gala in New York
Ghana News.content:
Screenshot

Dorothy’s Hope Foundation will host two major women’s health and breast cancer advocacy events in New York in September and October 2026.

Dorothy’s Hope Foundation, a non-profit dedicated to the advocacy of breast cancer awareness, women’s health, and empowerment across Ghana, is strengthening its Africa-Diaspora engagement with two major events in New York this year: the Health is Wealth Forum on 24 September and the Brushes of Strength Fundraising Gala on 23 October 2026.

For over a decade, Dorothy’s Hope Foundation (DHF) has championed breast cancer advocacy, with a focus on advancing research and translating awareness into meaningful access to quality cancer care.

Through its research initiatives, DHF has gathered and analysed data from the Greater Accra, Ashanti, Western, and Volta regions to better understand the challenges and critical gaps within Ghana’s cancer care landscape.

Drawing on research findings, DHF has advocated for strengthened healthcare infrastructure, structural and policy reforms, improved cancer care facilities and services, robust data collection and management systems, and stronger partnerships among key stakeholders, all aimed at building a more responsive, equitable, and sustainable cancer care system that improves outcomes for patients across Ghana.

Growing beyond borders

Building on this work, DHF is strengthening its Africa-Diaspora engagement through the “Health is Wealth Forum”, a high-level global women’s health, leadership, and impact forum held as a side event of the 81st United Nations General Assembly on 24 September 2026 from 11am to 2pm EST.

Under the theme “Empowering Women through Leadership and Global Impact”, the Forum will convene influential women leaders, healthcare professionals, policymakers, entrepreneurs, philanthropists, creatives, and diaspora leaders from Africa, the United States, and beyond to foster strategic partnerships, shared learning, and collective action for women’s health, economic empowerment, and holistic well-being.

On 23 October 2026 at 6pm EST, DHF will host the Brushes of Strength Fundraising Gala, a distinguished black-tie event bringing together eminent dignitaries, celebrated personalities, influential leaders, philanthropists, and organisations to honour the courage and resilience of breast cancer survivors while championing a shared commitment to moving beyond awareness towards meaningful access, action, support, and improved outcomes.

Both events represent DHF’s continued commitment to mobilising strategic partnerships and translating advocacy and evidence into meaningful action that advances women’s health and well-being.

DHF welcomes media organisations in Ghana, New York, and across the Diaspora to join in amplifying these important conversations and extending the reach and impact of the initiatives to communities on both sides of the Atlantic.

Ghana News.title: Mahama appoints Dr Aziz-Bamba as Acting Director-General of Value for Money Office
Ghana News.content:
President John Mahama has appointed Dr Abdul-Baasit Aziz-Bamba as Acting Director-General of the Value for Money Office.

According to a statement issued by the Presidency on Tuesday, September 8, 2026, the appointment was made in accordance with Article 195(1) of the 1992 Constitution and Section 14(1) of the Value for Money Office Act, 2026 (Act 1172).

Dr Aziz-Bamba will serve in an acting capacity pending the receipt of the constitutionally required advice of the Governing Board, given in consultation with the Public Services Commission.

Until his appointment, Dr Aziz-Bamba served as a Senior Lecturer at the University of Ghana School of Law.

He is also a Harvard-trained lawyer.

The Value for Money Office is mandated to ensure that public expenditure delivers value and serves the public good.

Ghana News.title: State closes case against Kwabena Adu-Boahene and two others
Ghana News.content:
The State has closed its case against Kwabena Adu-Boahene and two others in the trial involving an alleged GH¢49.1 million loss to the state.

Deputy Attorney General Justice Srem-Sai announced the development in a Facebook post on Tuesday, September 8, 2026.

According to him, the prosecution’s case is that Mr Adu-Boahene allegedly used “clever means” to take the money from a state agency and, with the assistance of his wife and their company, spent the funds.

The accused persons have been charged with stealing, money laundering and causing financial loss to the Republic.

Justice Srem-Sai said Mr Adu-Boahene’s main response was that the money was not used for himself, his family or friends, but to purchase a cyber defence system for the state agency.

Prosecution calls four witnesses

The Republic called four witnesses to support its case.

The first witness, identified as the family driver of Mr Adu-Boahene and his wife, testified that he ran money errands for them and transported large sums of money from banks to the couple and their friends, family and associates.

The second witness, the Head of Finance of the state agency whose money was allegedly taken, testified about the agency’s financial procedures and the process for procuring cyber defence systems.

Justice Srem-Sai said the witness told the court that the names on the three cheques did not correspond with the bank account into which the money was eventually deposited.

The witness also testified that no such cyber defence system had been ordered for the agency.

According to the Deputy Attorney General, the invoice number Mr Adu-Boahene allegedly relied on was linked to a different piece of equipment that the agency had officially purchased on another occasion.

The witness further told the court that the account into which the three cheques were deposited was not the agency’s account and that the agency had no knowledge of the company or the account.

The third witness, an employee who handled the personal financial and business affairs of Mr Adu-Boahene and his wife, testified about how the money was allegedly spent through their company and other companies, family members and associates.

Justice Srem-Sai said the witness also explained how Mr Adu-Boahene dealt with banks and how one bank filed a suspicious transaction report concerning his activities, after which he closed the account.

The witness also testified about the couple’s investments in real estate and other financial instruments and tendered cheques allegedly pre-signed by them.

Some of the cheques, according to the post, were used to pay builders working on properties in Accra and Asokore Mampong.

The fourth witness was an EOCO investigator, who tendered the three cheques and deposit slips allegedly used to transfer the GH¢49.1 million from the state agency’s account into a private company’s account.

The investigator also presented incorporation and bank account-opening documents for companies linked to the accused persons, bank statements showing how the money was allegedly spent, and purchase documents for landed properties.

Other evidence included Mr Adu-Boahene’s salary as a civil servant over approximately two decades and information on companies and assets associated with him.

Case adjourned to November 5

The court has given the accused persons until September 25 to file their submissions of no case to answer.

The Republic is expected to respond within 14 days after being served.

The case has been adjourned to November 5, 2026.

Ghana News.title: Afrodancehall prodigy TMBwoy debuts new album “Chapter one”
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian Afrodancehall artiste TMBwoy has released his debut album, ‘’Chapter One,” marking a significant milestone in his growing career.

Now available in all stores, the project arrives as TMBwoy’s first full-length body of work, following a string of singles and collaborations that have gradually introduced his voice, energy and ambition to Ghana’s music audience.

‘’Chapter One” is rooted in the Afrodancehall sound. The album blends the bass-heavy drive and rhythmic bounce of dancehall with African percussion, reggae influences and contemporary Afrobeats melodies. Its sound is lively and youthful, balancing club-ready grooves with a melodic approach that makes the songs easy to connect with.

The project gives TMBwoy room to present more than the short, immediate impact of a standalone single. His vocal delivery remains direct and energetic, carrying the confidence associated with dancehall, while the melodies add a softer and more accessible layer to the music. The album’s production draws from familiar African dancefloor rhythms, but keeps the tempo and attitude of Jamaican-rooted dancehall in focus.

“Chapter One” offers a colourful mix of movement, melody and street-inspired expression, with Afrodancehall serving as the album’s central musical foundation. The project draws strength from the genre’s fusion of African rhythm and dancehall energy, while also carrying the vibrancy of Afrobeats and the warmth of reggae-inflected music. That combination reflects the direction of a new generation of Ghanaian artistes using Afrodancehall to create music with a distinct local identity and wider African appeal.

The 9-track album includes collaborations with two of Ghana’s exciting contemporary voices, Beeztrap KOTM and OlivetheBoy, on “Cover” and “Touch,” respectively.

The release also represents the next step in TMBwoy’s steady rise in the Ghanaian music industry. Rather than arriving with one viral moment, the artiste has built his profile gradually, releasing singles, growing a community of listeners and taking opportunities to place his name before new audiences. ‘’Chapter One” serves as the clearest statement yet of that progress.

TMBwoy came to wider public attention after Ghanaian dancehall star Stonebwoy gave him a platform to showcase his talent. That exposure helped introduce the emerging artiste to a broader audience and opened the door for further industry recognition. Before releasing his debut album, TMBwoy also featured on Stonebwoy’s BNNG 16-track project, ‘’Tribes and Tongues,” a credit that strengthened his visibility within the dancehall space.

Born Einstein Boakye and hailing from Dunkwa-On-Offin in Ghana’s Central Region, TMBwoy is one of the emerging voices shaping Ghana’s Afrodancehall movement. His music is primarily defined by a fusion of African rhythms, dancehall energy and reggae

influences. With “Chapter One”, he takes a decisive step from releasing individual songs to presenting a complete artistic statement, as he continues to chart his path in the Ghanaian and African music scene.

Ghana News.title: Chance for Childhood calls for increased funding for inclusive education in Ghana
Ghana News.content:
The Country Representative and Safeguarding Lead at Chance for Childhood, Richard Opoku, has called on the government to increase funding for the implementation of Ghana’s Inclusive Education Policy to ensure that children with disabilities and special educational needs can fully participate in mainstream education.

According to him, inadequate funding remains one of the major obstacles to the effective implementation of the policy, despite its introduction by the government in 2015 as a framework for promoting inclusive education in the country.

Mr Opoku made the call when he spoke to journalists on the sidelines of a Media Workshop on Disability and Inclusive Education held at the British Council on Tuesday, September 8.

He said Chance for Childhood, a disability inclusion organisation, was committed to ensuring that every child, regardless of their abilities or educational needs, had the opportunity to learn, participate and achieve.

“Chance for Childhood, as a disability inclusion organisation, recognises that every child is different and every child learns differently,” he said.

He explained that the organisation's work was centred on creating an educational environment in which children, particularly those with special educational needs and disabilities, could access learning opportunities and participate meaningfully in school and society.

Mr Opoku said although Ghana had taken an important step by introducing the Inclusive Education Policy in 2015 through the Ministry of Education and the Ghana Education Service (GES), the success of the policy depended largely on adequate resources for its implementation.

“The main challenge is with the implementation of the policy because of largely inadequate funding,” he said.

He therefore appealed to the government to review upwards the allocation for inclusive education in the national education budget.

According to him, the funding allocated to inclusive education has consistently remained below one per cent of the overall education budget, a situation he believes limits the ability of relevant institutions to provide the necessary support for children with disabilities.

“We will want to make a special appeal to the government that it should consider the budget allocation for the implementation of inclusive education,” Mr Opoku said.

He proposed that the allocation should be increased to at least two per cent to support critical interventions, particularly teacher training and the provision of appropriate teaching and learning materials.

He said adequate investment would help create conditions in which children with different forms of disabilities and special educational needs could learn alongside their peers in mainstream schools.

“This will ensure that all children, regardless of their disabilities and special educational needs, are able to participate and learn in the mainstream schools,” he added.

Mr Opoku also stressed the need for greater support for teachers who work with children with disabilities and other learners requiring special educational assistance.

He said continuous capacity building was essential because teachers needed to regularly update their knowledge and skills to respond effectively to the diverse needs of learners.

“For teachers who are teaching children with disabilities and others who are making provision for those special educational needs, the main support that they will need is continuous capacity building so that they will be equipped all the time to provide the needed support,” he said.

Beyond professional training, he said teachers also needed to be adequately motivated and recognised for the work they were doing.

He noted that motivation should not necessarily be limited to financial incentives, although additional funding and financial support would be welcome.

According to him, institutions and organisations could explore other ways of recognising and encouraging teachers who had dedicated their careers to supporting children with disabilities.

“But again, they also require motivation,” he said.

“When you talk about motivation, not necessarily in terms of funding — although funding would be great — there are other ways that we can motivate teachers who have devoted their time to teaching children who have disabilities.”

A major focus of the media workshop was the role of journalists and media organisations in shaping public understanding of disability and inclusive education.

Mr Opoku said the media had significant influence over how persons with disabilities were perceived, adding that the manner in which disability-related issues were reported could either reinforce negative stereotypes or contribute to a more inclusive society.

He said the images used in news reports, the language employed by journalists and the voices given prominence in stories could have lasting effects on public attitudes towards disability.

“We know that the media tell stories about disabilities and inclusive education. The images that they share on disabilities and the voices that they choose to amplify can either strengthen the stigma and discrimination against disabilities, or they can help to build an inclusive society that respects the rights, dignity and potential of children and persons with disabilities,” he said.

He urged journalists to approach disability-related reporting with greater sensitivity and a stronger understanding of the issues affecting persons with disabilities.

According to him, responsible reporting could help challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma and ensure that the concerns and experiences of persons with disabilities received appropriate attention in national discourse.

Mr Opoku further emphasised that achieving inclusive education could not be left to schools or government institutions alone.

He said government, schools, civil society organisations, non-governmental organisations, corporate institutions, the media and the wider public all had important roles to play.

“When you talk about inclusive education, we also acknowledge that it is the responsibility of everyone, including schools, government and the media,” he said.

He explained that the media engagement was organised specifically to strengthen journalists' understanding of disability and inclusive education and equip them to use their respective platforms to promote inclusion.

“The main reason why we organised this event is to ensure that, collectively, we strengthen our understanding about disability and inclusive education, so that we can use our various media platforms to ensure that we build a more inclusive Ghana,” he said.

He also called for broader recognition and support for teachers who were making deliberate efforts to ensure that children with disabilities were not excluded from the education system.

“All of us — I mean the government, NGOs, civil society, corporate bodies, the media and everyone — have a role to play in making sure that teachers who are making efforts to promote the learning of children with disabilities are motivated to continue the work that they do,” he added.

Ghana News.title: Twelve girls participate in Egli Studios’ maiden Besties Camp
Ghana News.content:
What started as a children's podcast is evolving into something bigger: a thriving community of girls finding friendship, discovering themselves, and creating memories that matter.

Egli Studios officially launched Besties, a groundbreaking community initiative extending beyond digital content, with the inaugural Besties Summer Camp this September.

Over three days, from September 2-4. twelve girls, including the four original Best Girlfriends hosts, participated in an immersive 60-hour residential experience designed to blend entertainment with meaningful learning and authentic connection.

The camp is a major milestone for the production company, showing it's expanding from podcast and TV into live experiences and community building.

"When we started Best Girlfriends, we knew we were creating more than a podcast," said Aggor Yorm, Founder of Egli Studios and Camp Director. "We wanted girls to have a space where they could see themselves, hear their voices reflected and know that they belonged. Besties is the next step in that vision."

The three-day camp kicked off with a welcome party featuring music from DJ Galdem, games, food, karaoke and informal bonding sessions that helped the girls settle into their shared living space and begin forming friendships.

From there, the itinerary balanced creativity with skill-building. Girls participated in pottery workshops where they worked with clay, attended a beading and fashion masterclass with renowned designer Kofi Akotua, and competed in cooking challenges, including a spirited Indomie cook-off where teams worked under pressure to create their best dishes.

Fitness sessions, outdoor games, and team competitions provided movement and friendly rivalry throughout the experience. But the camp's organizers were intentional about including substance alongside the fun.

One standout moment came during a candid session with Lady, a former Miss Malaika Ghana winner, who facilitated an age-appropriate discussion on menstrual hygiene. The session included practical lessons on proper use and positioning of sanitary pads, a topic many girls never receive formal education about.

"Besties isn't just about entertainment," Yorm explained. "It's about creating a space where girls can learn about themselves, ask questions that might feel uncomfortable elsewhere, and have meaningful conversations while still enjoying the magic of being young."

This philosophy guided every aspect of the camp's design, from the activities chosen to the people invited to facilitate them.

Throughout the 60-hour experience, professional cameras captured every moment, the laughter, the challenges, the conflicts and resolutions. The girls had access to a diary room where they could reflect privately and share individual perspectives, bringing an authentic reality television element to the proceedings.

That footage is currently in post-production and will be presented as a Besties reality television experience, with the programme set to air on television platforms soon. The reality format adds another layer to Egli Studios' content strategy, transforming the camp experience into shareable, watchable content for a broader audience.

The ambition behind Besties extends far beyond this inaugural camp. Egli Studios envisions a comprehensive ecosystem combining content, experiences, events, creative workshops, mentorship opportunities and community engagement.

"The first camp was a beginning," Yorm said. "Besties is being built as a place where girls can find their people, try something new, discover their interests, have important conversations, laugh together and leave with stories of their own."

According to the studio, future iterations of the camp will expand in scope and scale, with plans to reach more girls across different regions and potentially create year-round programming beyond the summer experience.

Best Girlfriends, which launched as a podcast featuring four young female hosts discussing friendship, culture, dreams and personal development, has grown into a multi-platform phenomenon with a strong following across television, YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram.

The transition to Besties represents Egli Studios' recognition that modern audiences, particularly young people, crave authentic connection and real-world experiences, not just digital content.

"Best Girlfriends started the conversation. Besties is building the community," Yorm reflected. "And after 60 hours, 12 girls and one house, that community has officially begun."

Egli Studios has confirmed that the Besties reality television programme will debut soon on Egli Studios YouTube channel.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
