The poll was released after the address the president gave to the nation on Thursday, in which he said the islands “are Argentine by history and by right, there is no discussion about it” and announced he would speed up sanctions against oil companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation. Nine in ten respondents were aware of that address.

The figures distinguish between support for the position and the credibility of the shift. The sovereignty claim enjoys majority backing in Argentine society, but Milei's call for unity inspired confidence in 41% of those consulted and distrust in 56%. On the content of the speech, 44.6% considered he had announced concrete measures and 44.2% that he had confined himself to general statements, a tie within the margin of error.

The position marks a change from his earlier statements. Milei has repeatedly declared his admiration for Margaret Thatcher, British prime minister during the 1982 conflict, and had acknowledged the islanders' right to self-determination, arguing that Argentina should persuade them to prefer being Argentine. That possibility was ruled out in Thursday's message.

After the speech, the Office of the President circulated the results of an open poll run by the newspaper Clarín on its social media accounts, according to which 81.3% of those who responded supported the announced measures. Such polls are not representative samples and are not comparable with probability-based surveys.

The government is drafting a national sovereignty defence bill to send to Congress, along with the terms of the National Security Council the president announced. Officials calculate the opposition will find it difficult to reject legislation strengthening the defence of national interests.

The issue emerged at an adverse moment for the government's economic agenda, little more than a year before the 2027 presidential elections. Unemployment tops Argentines' concerns at 36%, ahead of corruption and inflation; arrears on credit to individuals reached 17.5% in June, and 60% of respondents in another survey expect their personal situation to worsen in coming months. Peronist lawmakers are preparing a session in the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday on maintaining treatment for people with disabilities and relief measures for indebted households.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and Argentina maintains a sovereignty claim. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed retaining British overseas territory status, with three votes against. Milei's speech followed remarks by Donald Trump, who said he reviews “every position” when asked about sovereignty over the islands, without committing to any decision.

World.title: Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination
World.content:
Falklands: Lords confirm UK’s unwavering support for Islanders right to self-determination

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 10:00 UTC Full article

Baroness Winterton, “we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands”.

The issue of President Javier Milei’s speech last week with its threats to the Falkland Islands, Islanders right to self-determination and the Islands’ right to develop its resource, was addressed by the House of Lords on Monday.

Lord Callanan made a question on the matter to Baroness Winterton, who repeatedly replied on UK’s unwavering support for the Islanders and the Islands.

Lord Callanan, C, said, “my Lords I beg leave to ask a question of which I have given prior notice, the question is as follows, ‘To ask her Majesty’s government what recent discussions they have had, if any, with one, the government of Argentina and two, the government of the United States pertaining to the future of the Falkland Islands and what steps they are taking to ensure the security of those Islands.

Baroness Winterton of Doncaster, and Under Secretary of State for the Indo-Pacific, FCDO replied, My Lords, the UK remains steadfast in its support for the Islanders right to self-determination. This is not the first time Argentina has made economic threats against the Falklands.

These threats have not prevented the community’s remarkable economic development and we have made clear to Argentina that the measures announced by president Milei will not change the UK’s unwavering commitment to the Islands.

The United States is our closest ally, they can have no doubt about our unwavering support for the Islanders.

World.title: Germany: why AfD won in Saxony Anhalt, and what happens next
World.content:
Germany: why AfD won in Saxony Anhalt, and what happens next

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 09:21 UTC Full article

The polarized nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects

By Ed Turner (*)



The results of Germany’s Saxony-Anhalt state election on September 6 were far worse than feared for the country’s mainstream political parties. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) came close to winning a majority of votes, with 43.8%. This was about 4% higher than polls had suggested.

Support for the centre-right Christian Democratic Union of Germany (CDU), on the other hand, imploded. It won 17.2% of the vote, down from 37.1% in 2021, performing substantially worse than predicted.

At nearly 78%, turnout was up substantially compared with 2021 – in a way that helped the AfD. Analysis suggests the growth in its support came mostly from former non-voters, joined by a substantial number of erstwhile CDU supporters.

The polarized nature of the election, with 41% of voters surveyed beforehand wanting an AfD-led government but 46% favouring one led by the CDU, had some surprising effects. One was that it flattered the social democratic SPD and the Greens.

Both the SPD and Greens received tactical support from CDU and Left Party voters to make sure they reached the 5% of votes required to win seats in the state parliament.

The AfD, which has sais it would only seek to govern if it had a majority, now has several paths to seeing its candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, elected as Saxony-Anhalt’s minister president. Most likely is a deal with the Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), a party that combines left-wing economic policies with conservative ones on topics such as migration.

On election night, the BSW made clear it had “overlaps” with AfD positions in some areas and that it would be “completely undemocratic” for the AfD to be excluded entirely from government.

If this failed, some support from the CDU would be a further route. The election of minister president is a secret ballot, and several CDU MPs reelected on Sunday have a long history of suggesting there should be more openness to working with the AfD.

Support across society



The AfD did best in Saxony-Anhalt among working-class voters (59%), as well as those with a lower level of education (57%) and those who perceived their economic situation as bad (65%). But even among graduates (30%) and voters who saw themselves in a good economic situation (37%), the AfD performed respectably.

It also secured over 40% of support among all age groups apart from the over 70s (31%). So the AfD can really claim to be a Volkspartei or “people’s party”, with support from across society, across the state.

By no means was this a single-issue election. Exit polls revealed immigration was one motivating factor for AfD voters, with 91% of them agreeing with the statement that they “were very worried too many foreign people live in Germany”. But so too was concern with security and the economy.

There was also real dissatisfaction (66% of all voters) at the state government, which had been led by the CDU since 2002. But the standing of Friedrich Merz’ government in Berlin was worse, with 83% taking the view it was insufficiently concerned with the problems of ordinary people. Just 20% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt trust it to improve the country substantially in the coming years.

Accompanying these sentiments, which can be found across Germany albeit more strongly in Saxony-Anhalt and other eastern states, there is a strand of dissatisfaction particular to the east. Seventy-three percent of all voters in Saxony-Anhalt believed easterners were still second-class citizens in many situations.

This view is taken by 83% of AfD voters. The AfD has been rather successful in mobilising grievances about reunification and some nostalgia about the days of the communist East Germany.

Assuming the AfD does form a government, there will be close scrutiny of the extent to which it can implement its hard-right manifesto – and, indeed, whether it confirms the view of German intelligence that the party is demonstrably “right wing extremist” in the state.

In fields such as education, culture, law and order and public broadcasting it will go on the front foot, though there may well be persistent legal challenges to more radical measures. These include attempts to force teachers to represent particular ideological positions in schools.

The AfD will also use its position for further publicity, and of course each time it is blocked from realising its aims by courts or other parties, it can claim to be a victim of establishment stitch-ups. This is a common populist tactic.

Wider political consequences



The results make Merz’s position even harder. Already as unpopular as any German chancellor has ever been, he stands no prospect of any boost from the state election in Mecklenburg West Pomerania on September 21. That election is set to be a clear battle between the AfD and SPD.

On the same day, the state of Berlin, with its highly fragmented politics, might offer the chance of a first-place finish for Merz’s CDU on a low vote-share. But that would not be a game-changer.

Crucially, many of his MPs will demand changes. Most will push for a rightward shift to close down an open flank the AfD can exploit. But that can hardly be achieved in coalition with its current coalition partner, the SPD.

Others will push for reopen major reform packages, such as pensions, slated for decision in the Autumn, noting the loss of ground among working-class voters. However, that would rub up against Merz’s analysis of what Germany needs to do to get its faltering economy back on track.

Saxony-Anhalt may be asking a very hard question not just of Merz, but of German society: is the country now so fragmented politically that it is becoming almost ungovernable?

Coalitions of easy bedfellows (Christian Democrats with Liberals or Social Democrats with Greens) would barely get 25% of the vote at a federal election. So mainstream parties are forced to form governments with parties with whom they fundamentally disagree simply in order to keep the AfD out.

These governments quarrel, they put off decisions as they cannot agree, and they collapse. And from this negative dynamic, the AfD is able to profit.

World.title: Jaguar-Land Rover will cut 4.000 jobs to compete with Chinese electric carmakers
World.content:
Jaguar-Land Rover will cut 4.000 jobs to compete with Chinese electric carmakers

8th Tuesday, September 2026 - 04:29 UTC Full article

Falkland Islands are considered the land of the ‘Landy’ Rover

Jaguar Land Rover announced on Monday it will cut 4,000 jobs across its global workforce as it tries to cut costs and compete with Chinese electric carmakers. Britain’s biggest automaker said the job cuts will take place over the next two years as it targets 1.7 billion pounds (US$2.3 billion) in savings to make it more competitive as the industry transitions to electrification.

“The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty,” chief executive PB Balaji said in a statement.

The job cuts and savings will help the company invest 15 to 18 billion pounds (US$ 20-24 billion) over the next five years in electrification, digital technologies and other areas, he added.

Jaguar Land Rover, which makes the Range Rover, Discovery and other luxury SUVs, has faced pressure amid intense competition from cheaper Chinese EVs, soaring costs and the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Its sales were also hit last year when a cyberattack forced it to halt production for a month.

The company, owned by India’s Tata Motors, makes most of its cars in factories across the U.K. It employs around 34,000 people in the country and the majority of the job cuts are expected to affect its U.K. operations.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said Monday that while market conditions are challenging for the automotive sector globally, Britain’s government will not consider a bailout for Jaguar Land Rover.

World.title: The Falklands pay tribute in London to the merchant seafarers who served in 1982
World.content:
The Falklands pay tribute in London to the merchant seafarers who served in 1982

7th Monday, September 2026 - 19:26 UTC Full article

Hyslop with Lord West of Spithead (central) and Chris Locke (right), former Royal Fleet Auxiliary (RFA) Chief Officer, Marine Officer, alongside other attendees at the Navy Day Memorial

The Falkland Islands Government Representative to the United Kingdom and Europe, Richard Hyslop, laid a wreath on Sunday on behalf of the people and Government of the islands during the annual Merchant Navy Day service held at Trinity Square Gardens in London.

The ceremony took place at the Falkland Islands Memorial, within the grounds of the Merchant Navy Memorial. Hyslop was joined by veterans of the South Atlantic Medal Association, which brings together those who served in the 1982 conflict, and by Lord West of Spithead, patron of the Merchant Navy Association, a former First Sea Lord and himself a veteran of that campaign. Also present was Chris Locke, a former Royal Fleet Auxiliary chief officer who served as Falkland Islands Marine Officer and Harbour Master.

“Each year, we pause to remember the service and sacrifice of merchant seafarers who served during the Falklands War to defend the freedom and right to self-determination of Islanders,” Hyslop said. “We remain hugely grateful to the Merchant Navy, both past and present, for their invaluable role in supporting the Falklands and allowing our modern Islands to prosper.”

The commemoration falls each year on September 3, the date on which the SS Athenia was sunk in 1939, the first British merchant vessel lost in the Second World War. The Red Ensign, the merchant navy's flag, is flown in recognition of a sector that carries more than 90% of the United Kingdom's trade.

During the 1982 conflict, the British Ministry of Defence requisitioned or chartered dozens of civilian vessels under the arrangement known as Ships Taken Up From Trade, among them the liners Canberra and Queen Elizabeth 2, used as troop transports. The costliest episode was the loss of the Atlantic Conveyor, a converted container ship struck by a missile on May 25, 1982, which sank with the loss of twelve lives, including that of its master, Ian North. Heavy-lift helicopters intended for the land campaign went down with her.

Maritime transport remains central to the archipelago, which depends on shipping for its supplies and for the export of its fisheries production, the main source of income for its economy.

World.title: A port dispute in Montevideo blocks a second ferry operator on the Buenos Aires route
World.content:
A port dispute in Montevideo blocks a second ferry operator on the Buenos Aires route

7th Monday, September 2026 - 19:20 UTC Full article

Port of Montevideo

Uruguayan ferry company Colonia Express obtained authorisation from the Ministry of Transport and Public Works at the end of July to operate the passenger and vehicle route between Montevideo and Buenos Aires, but cannot begin the service because the only ramp at the Montevideo port suitable for unloading cars belongs to Buquebus, the company that currently runs the crossing alone.

A pontoon of this kind is the floating platform that allows vehicles carried in ships' holds to be loaded and unloaded. The one at the Maciel pier was built by Buquebus after it obtained the passenger terminal concession in 1996, and ceased to form part of public infrastructure in 2016, when the National Ports Administration terminated that concession. Colonia Express is asking the authorities to establish shared use; Buquebus opposes it.

Sources at the National Ports Administration told the Montevideo newspaper El País the matter is one “between private parties” and that the body has received no formal documentation on the authorisation. They said any ferry operation may use public berths or be agreed privately, but that the pontoon is not part of the authority's pier, so the decision on its use rests with its owner. Ministry officials said the file is within its review period and that administrative appeals are under way.

Colonia Express director Sebastián Planas announced the company will go to court seeking an injunction against both the ministry and the ports authority. “The ministry must respond to us and give us a solution, but on the other hand it is the ports authority that should require Buquebus to share the pontoon or remove it,” he told the outlet El Observador. The company also argues the state of the Maciel pier does not allow a second platform to be installed, and it aims to operate during the coming summer season.

The pier, 380 metres long with a five-metre draught, has dredging problems and maintenance shortfalls that cause periods of inactivity. A tender for its reconstruction is under way, with specifications still being drawn up. In March, the National Ports Administration declared of interest a private initiative submitted by Buquebus to rebuild the pier and modernise the terminal, valued at between 66 and 100 million dollars with a concession estimated at fifty years. That declaration gives the company preference in the tender process.

Between January and July, more than 500,000 passengers and 57,000 vehicles crossed the River Plate on this route. Buquebus, owned by Argentine businessman Juan Carlos López Mena, recorded 70,000 more boarding and disembarking movements than in the same period last year. Colonia Express has operated since 2007. The company has made no public statement on the pontoon.

World.title: The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide
World.content:
The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide

7th Monday, September 2026 - 09:10 UTC Full article

President Javier Milei addressed the nation on Thursday following Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of US neutrality

The sovereignty claim over the Falklands is one of the few points of consensus that cuts across Argentina's political fracture, known locally as “la grieta”, a polarisation that splits the country into two opposing camps on almost every public question. That cross-cutting quality explains both its constant presence in popular culture and its recurrence in political discourse.

Political scientist Mariana Altieri, author of a comparative study of the archipelago and Gibraltar, links that centrality to Argentina's founding narrative. “When Argentina became independent from Spain, the islands were part of it and then they were taken from us, and that is associated with Argentina's trauma, with what could have been and is not,” she says. Anthropologist Rosana Guber, a researcher at Conicet and a specialist on the 1982 conflict, suggests understanding it as a symbol comparable to the flag or the anthem: “They speak to people who may hold different positions on everything else.”

The attachment is strongest in the far south. In Río Grande, less than 600 kilometres from the islands and almost 12,800 from British shores, the outline of the archipelago appears on school uniforms, sports kit and numerous murals. The anthem of Tierra del Fuego province is the March of the Malvinas, and the vigil held every April 1 draws up to 20,000 people, according to historian Esteban Rodríguez.

Concrete knowledge of the territory, by contrast, is limited. Journalist Nicolás Cassese, who has travelled to the archipelago three times, estimates that fewer than 1% of Argentines have visited it. “Of Messi and Maradona we have an enormous amount of information, and of the islands we know almost nothing,” he says. He recounts that when he published a novel set in Stanley some readers did not recognise the place name, and notes the settlement was founded in 1845, when the British already administered the islands, and that Argentines themselves used that name for decades.

That consensus has made political use easier. President Javier Milei addressed the nation on Thursday following Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of US neutrality, announcing sanctions on companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation and the construction of a military base in the south. The opposition noted that a 2011 law already provides for such sanctions and that construction of the base had begun before his own government halted it. The La Plata veterans' centre criticised his use of the claim as a “lifebelt”. In 2025 Milei had argued that islanders should decide: “We hope the islanders choose to vote for us with their feet.” Altieri describes Thursday's speech as “a 180-degree turn”.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and maintains that its status depends on the wishes of its inhabitants. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to remain a British overseas territory, with three votes against.

World.title: An Argentine court returns an 18th-century work to the heirs of a Jewish art dealer
World.content:
An Argentine court returns an 18th-century work to the heirs of a Jewish art dealer

7th Monday, September 2026 - 09:01 UTC Full article

An Argentine federal court on Friday ordered the return of the painting Portrait of a Lady to the family of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, almost 90 years after the Nazi regime looted his collection in Amsterdam. The work surfaced last year at a house in Mar del Plata, 400 kilometres from Buenos Aires.

The ruling was issued at a hearing chaired by federal judge Santiago Inchausti, attended by prosecutors, the heir's lawyers and the defendants. Patricia Kadgien and her husband, Juan Carlos Cortegoso, had been accused of possessing and concealing a work of art stolen in the context of a genocide. After initially arguing they were the legitimate owners by inheritance, they accepted an agreement with prosecutors to avoid trial and irrevocably renounced any right over the painting. The deal includes a donation of 4.8 million pesos, around 3,200 dollars, to the support association of a maternal and child hospital. Prosecutor Carlos Martínez said the outcome amounts to “a reparation of a historic character for the victims”.

Patricia Kadgien is the daughter of Friedrich Kadgien, an SS member and financial expert for the National Socialist regime from 1938, with a prominent role in currency purchases and in the plunder of occupied territories. A 1945 US report described him as “a snake of the worst kind”. He fled to Switzerland, then Brazil and finally Argentina, where he established himself as a businessman and died in 1978 without ever facing trial.

The discovery came through a property listing. In August 2025, marking eighty years since the end of the Second World War, the Dutch newspaper Algemeen Dagblad sent correspondent Peter Schouten to Mar del Plata to try to contact Kadgien's daughters. No one answered, but he noticed a for-sale sign on the front of the house. Searching for the listing on the estate agency's website, he found among the interior photographs the painting hanging in the living room. The couple were held for 72 hours until they handed the work over.

The piece is an oil on canvas measuring 119.5 by 89 centimetres. Goudstikker's records attributed it to Giuseppe Ghislandi, but analysis by Argentina's National Academy of Fine Arts confirmed it is by Giacomo Ceruti, the 18th-century Italian painter known as Il Pitocchetto. Its market value is estimated at around 250,000 euros.

The painting will be handed to Marei von Saher, the dealer's daughter-in-law, who has spent decades tracing pieces from the collection of more than 1,100 works. Through her lawyers she said she does not accept “86 years of plunder” but is not seeking revenge or compensation. Her intention is for the painting to be exhibited on loan at a museum in Buenos Aires before its return. It remains in the custody of Argentina's Supreme Court.

World.title: Rodolfo ‘Baby’ Casanova and the golden age of Mexican boxing
World.content:
Sometime in early 1867, a group of wealthy young men of possibly dubious habits gathered at a gymnasium in Mexico City. Frenchman Nicolas Poupard had run a fencing school in the city for some time but had recently lost much of his trade to a new arrival, Thomas Hoyer Monstery. In a showdown to demonstrate who was the master of combat sports, they staged a series of contests ranging from sword fighting to boxing. Whether these were exhibitions or duels is uncertain, but the truth probably lies somewhere in between.

Monstery was quite a character and is worth a mention in passing. Born in Denmark, he traveled the world with the Danish navy, then became a master fencer and a talented boxer. He spent a spell in Russia as a fencing instructor and was forced to flee Copenhagen after killing a man in a sword duel. By 1867, Monstery was in Mexico, where he and Poupard fought the first recorded boxing match in the country. Yet, while this makes a good story, it did not inspire any great interest in boxing, and the Mexican origins of the sport lie elsewhere.

From gentlemen’s clubs to the circus

President Porfirio Diaz saw sport as a symbol of the modern Mexico he sought to build, with activities centered on sports clubs open to the upper and middle classes. Cricket, soccer, tennis and golf were all popular, but there were also boxing lessons. The noble art was seen as a fine way for a gentleman to exercise and defend himself if needed. The sport, however, also had some less refined roots, and the man who might be considered the father of both Mexican wrestling and boxing was Enrique Ugartechea.

Although Ugartechea came from a middle-class background, he acquired his interest in boxing from a grittier source. In 1903, while still a teenager, he watched the Italian wrestler Romulus at a circus and challenged the performer to a wrestling match in the local bullring. This was the first step toward young Ugartechea becoming “El Hombre Mas Fuerte de Mexico” (“The Strongest Man in Mexico”). Over the next few years, Ugartechea and his fellow bodybuilders regularly promoted boxing and wrestling matches in bullrings, theaters and carnivals throughout the country. This might be considered the birth of boxing in Mexico, while their wrestling tournaments were an early — though not direct — ancestor of lucha libre.

Revolution and port city rings

The revolution in 1910 set sport back, and whatever fights took place were hidden away in neighborhood boxing gyms or parks. The sport was in its infancy in Mexico, and when Jack London wrote “The Mexican,” fiction mirrored real life in that his young hero had to move to Los Angeles to pursue a boxing career. Notably, the most famous boxer of this period, Miguel Ángel Febles, “The Lion of Veracruz,” learned his art in Cuba. Febles was another colorful character whose resume included serving as a cavalry captain during the Mexican Revolution and a boxing instructor to the police. It was a tough way to make a living, and Febles performed at carnivals, fairs and circuses up and down the country, once fighting bouts in Puebla, Pachuca and Guadalajara in the same week.

The port cities along the Gulf of Mexico were another center of boxing, with visiting seamen using a rope and four chairs to set up a ring in a shady nightclub. Hats would be passed among the spectators to collect drinking money for the fighters, and one of the images boxing had to contend with was that it was a violent sport for drunken foreigners. Boxing had lost much of its early respectability, but the men coming through this age of small neighborhood fights would shape the golden age of the sport that followed.

International stars reignite the sport

Boxing was given a boost in 1919 when world champion Jack Johnson arrived in Mexico City. Johnson had broken U.S. segregation laws by marrying a white woman, and his exile in Mexico created considerable excitement. Hundreds turned up to watch him train; there was an exhibition match in a bullring and a confrontation with armed police who came to seize his car. As the country became more peaceful, sports centers once again became popular, and the excitement generated by Johnson helped boxing in Mexico City reemerge from the shadows. The sport received another boost in 1923 with the historic boxing match between Jack Dempsey and Luis Ángel Firpo at the Polo Grounds in New York. The prospect of a Latin American boxer fighting the great Dempsey for a world title captured the Mexican imagination and was widely covered by the media, including newspapers and radio.

Moving to the barrio

At the same time boxing was breaking into the news, the Mexican economy was starting to prosper, and there was a migration of people from the countryside into the big cities. In Mexico City, many found lodgings in the working-class neighborhood of Colonia Guerrero, where boxing joined jai alai and wrestling as cheap street entertainment that could draw an enthusiastic local crowd. With this, the center of boxing moved from the rich sports club to the barrio gym. At one point, parliament considered banning the sport, but it slowly won the approval of the authorities.

Both government and church were concerned over the vices the young were being exposed to in the expanding slums, and boxing was seen as a way of offering the city’s poor discipline and purpose. With boxers coming from the growing population of the slums, the middle class was largely excluded from participation, but many rich and influential men could be seen at the ringside for big fights. They introduced organization to the sport, including founding the Mexico City Boxing Commission in 1923. With this, championship titles became official, and boxers could be enticed down from the United States, reasonably certain they would collect the promised purse at the end of the fight.

The rise of Baby Casanova

One of the men promoting the sport was Jimmy Fitten. Born in San Francisco, he had a long professional career of 59 recorded bouts spanning from 1909 to 1924. Coming to Mexico in 1925, he turned promoter just in time to benefit from boxing’s new popularity. He was ambitious, gritty, understood the art of promotion and had a web of connections in a sport he had given his life to. Fitten is particularly linked with one of the most beloved fighters of this age, Rodolfo “Baby” Casanova.

Casanova’s father died during the civil war, after which his mother moved the family to Mexico City. He grew up in the slums of La Lagunilla and entered the ring in 1932 as a 16-year-old. He had 15 fights that year, and when he was put into the ring against Speedy Dado, he was expected to be a tough opponent but not a real danger to a man in line for a world title. Casanova, however, beat Dado in Mexico City, earning him big-money fights in Los Angeles.

Fighting in LA

At the time, L.A. was a growing city without a franchise in any major U.S. professional sports league. In the absence of baseball or basketball, boxing ruled. Generally, Mexican boxers were looked down upon, but Casanova won over local fans who loved his style and aggression. Like many boys from the barrios who suddenly find themselves with money and fame, Rodolfo struggled to cope. He was regularly seen at local nightclubs, and rumors even swirled that he was hanging out with Mae West. When Casanova lost a world title fight to Sixto Escobar, it was reported that the young man had escaped from his hotel the night before and was found in the early morning drunkenly wandering the streets. His critics were vicious; the young man, it was said, had left his fighting skills along with his money in nightclubs.

A golden age cut short

Back home, the sport was helped by the opening of the Arena Nacional in 1930. This 30,000-capacity stadium was ideally suited for boxing, and a generation of fighters that included Kid Azteca, Baby Arizmendi and Juan Zurita produced magical nights there. Casanova was also back in the ring and forgiven. Like another flawed genius of a later generation and a different sport — Diego Maradona — his vulnerability seemed to identify him as a child of the barrios and made him even more popular. His three fights with Zurita during the mid-1930s were legendary for their passion and violence, while 30,000 fans packed into the city’s bullring to see him fight American Freddie Miller.

It was a golden age for the sport, with giant advertising posters around Mexico City previewing fights and promoting gyms. Boxing stories featured in comic books and magazines, and Olympic boxer Raúl Talán became a movie star thanks to the boxing movie “Todo un Hombre” (“A Real Man”). The general theme of the story, copied by nearly every other boxing movie, was that a poor boy makes good in the ring and wins a girl above his social class.

A blow to the sport

Boxing operated on many levels, and a man could gain prestige among his peers by fighting at a lower level. The taxi drivers’ society, for example, staged popular fight nights between its members. If it was tough at the top, it was harder still for the men who made their living further down the food chain fighting in grimy venues for pitiful rewards.

The sport then received two blows. On June 7, 1936, a promising 17-year-old, Paco Sotelo, was taken from the ring unconscious after a third-round knockdown against Jesus Najera. The crowd, believing the fight had been fixed, booed, but then came the news that Sotelo had died in the hospital. The following year, a fire ripped through the Arena Nacional, destroying the sport’s spiritual home in the city. By then, boxing was firmly established as part of Mexican culture, but a little of the magic had been lost.

Bob Pateman lived in Mexico for six years. He is a librarian and teacher with a Master’s Degree in History.

World.title: Alfonso Cuarón enters the gothic-horror realm of Dungeons & Dragons
World.content:
Alfonso Cuarón, the Mexico City-born director of “Y tu mamá también” and “Roma,” is heading back to Netflix — this time to executive produce a series set in the gothic-horror world of Dungeons & Dragons.

“Ravenloft” is a live-action series set in the Dungeons & Dragons universe that follows the transformation of Strahd von Zarovich into the evil Darklord, the vampire ruler of Barovia.

According to Deadline and other reports last week, Cuarón, 64, will executive produce through London-based Esperanto Filmoj, the company he co-founded in 2002. (Filmoj is an Esperanto word meaning “films.”)

The series marks Cuarón’s return to Netflix, which showcased his semi-biographical “Roma” in late 2018 following a short release in theaters — a flashpoint in the early debate over streaming films’ theatrical releases.

The black-and-white drama, set in Mexico City of the early 1970s, went on to earn Netflix its first Academy Award best-picture nomination, among 10 total nominations. It lost to “Green Book” for best picture, but did win Oscars for best director, best cinematography and best foreign language film, now called best international feature film.

“Ravenloft” is being written by John August, whose background in gothic fantasy is a good fit for the series’ horror and dark-romance premise. His co-writing credentials include five Tim Burton films, including “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory,” “Corpse Bride” and “Dark Shadows.”

What is Ravenloft?

Watch this video on YouTube

First introduced in 1983, Ravenloft became one of the tabletop game’s best-known settings. Its realm of Barovia is a mist-shrouded gothic-horror world ruled by Strahd, who is both its tyrant and its prisoner.

The project is separate from “The Forgotten Realms,” a previously announced Netflix Dungeons & Dragons series no longer in development.

For “Ravenloft,” Netflix has not announced a cast, director, production start date or release date. Late 2027 would be the earliest plausible release time, though 2028 is more realistic.

Cuarón won Oscars for directing and editing the 2013 space thriller “Gravity,” becoming the first Mexican-born winner of the Best Director award. He had already directed “Y tu mamá también” (2001), “Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban” (2004) and “Children of Men” (2006). He co-wrote “Y tu mamá” with his brother, Carlos.

More recently, he wrote, directed and executive produced the limited series “Disclaimer,” and he is also co-writing and executive-producing the forthcoming drama “Ascension,” both for Apple TV.

With reports from Excélsior, EFE and Deadline

World.title: 2 years into operations, Olmeca Refinery reports its best month yet
World.content:
The Olmeca Refinery in the Gulf coast state of Tabasco had its best-ever month for fuel production in July, according to data from the state oil company Pemex.

The refinery, built on the Tabasco coast during Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency, produced an average of 252,498 barrels of fuel per day in July.

That figure — which includes premium and regular gasoline as well as diesel, among other fuels — represented a 78.8% increase compared to June and an annual gain of 62.4%. Production of regular and premium gasoline rose even more sharply at the Olmeca Refinery in July, increasing 127.9% on a month-over-month basis and 89.5% annually to reach an average of 108,548 barrels per day (bpd).

The sharp increases in production in July came after refinery equipment was restored and upgraded between April and June. A number of fires have occurred at the US $21 billion facility, including in March, April and July of this year.

Output from the Olmeca Refinery in July exceeded 200,000 bpd across an entire month for just the third time. López Obrador inaugurated the refinery, located at the Dos Bocas port, in July 2022, even though it was unfinished and not refining crude at the time.

The facility is one of seven refineries operated by Pemex in Mexico. The Salina Cruz Refinery had the highest output in July, followed by Olmeca, which contributed 21.2% of Pemex’s total production of 1.19 million bpd of fuel in July.

Olmeca had its second-best month for crude processing in July

Pemex data also shows that the Olmeca Refinery processed an average of just under 229,000 barrels of heavy Maya crude per day in July. That figure represented a 62.2% month-over-month increase and a 53.9% year-over-year gain. The only month when the Olmeca Refinery processed a larger quantity of crude was last December. Before July, its processing volumes declined on a sequential basis during six consecutive months.

The Olmeca Refinery only refines heavy “Maya” crude, whereas other Pemex facilities also process light and super light crude. In July, it was Pemex’s second-largest refiner after the Salina Cruz Refinery, which processed an average of 246,838 barrels of crude per day. Pemex’s seven refineries in Mexico collectively processed an average of 1.22 million bpd of crude in July.

At full capacity, the Olmeca Refinery can process 340,000 bpd of crude. The processing volume it achieved in July represented 67.3% of that capacity.

With reports from La Jornada, Imagen Radio, El CEO and El Financiero

World.title: 16 presumed Los Ardillos cartel members arrested in Guerrero
World.content:
Guerrero state authorities took into custody 16 cartel members linked to the “Los Ardillos” crime gang as part of an operation deployed after the dismembered body of a vacationing National Guard member was identified along the Mexico City-Acapulco highway.

The Guerrero Attorney General’s Office (FGE) reported the arrest of the 16 people, the result of a coordinated response carried out on Sept. 5 along with the Army, the National Guard and state police.

On Sunday afternoon, the Defense Ministry (Defensa) confirmed the FGE report about the arrest of the alleged cartel members in the towns of Pablo Galeana, Río Verde and Xaltianguis, all within the municipality of Acapulco.

Among those apprehended was a person identified as Los Ardillos’ “financial operator.”

Among four mangled bodies discovered was that of National Guardsman Eduardo Bustos, who was off-duty. Prior to being murdered, Bustos was apparently forced to film a video in which he stated that state security agents — identifying two by name — receive payments of up to 600,000 pesos per month (US $35,500) from the “Los Tlacos” crime gang to harass their rivals in Guerrero, Los Ardillos.

Defensa issued a statement confirming the death of the guardsman, condemning the violence in Guerrero and “reaffirming its commitment to collaborate closely with civilian authorities in the investigations to clarify the facts, including the circumstances surrounding the statements” made by Bustos in the video.

Also in Guerrero, feds raid and dismantle 3 meth labs

Federal forces deployed in the state of Guerrero located and dismantled three clandestine laboratories used to produce methamphetamine, officials announced over the weekend.

In a statement on social media, federal Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the three drug labs were situated in remote areas in the mountainous state. He praised the Army for the successful operations in “inaccessible, high-risk places.”

Two of the labs were in Zirándaro de los Chávez and one in Coahuayutla de José María Izazaga. García Harfuch did not specify when the operations took place.

A trove of drug-producing chemicals and equipment was seized, including more than 260 200-liter drums, 11 500-liter containers, nine reactors, more than 60 gas tanks, 150 sacks of caustic soda, 663 kg of ammonium chloride, approximately 2,400 kg of chemical substances, reactors, condensers, distillers and approximately 1,000 kg of chemical precursors.

Besides ingredients and equipment used for drug production, the operation seized 12 firearms, more than 36,700 cartridges, 17 doses of methamphetamine, 10 slot machines, two motorcycles and a vehicle.

With reports from Milenio, El Financiero, Proceso and Infobae

World.title: After renaming the Gulf and a Great Lake, Trump proposes a ‘more prestigious and beautiful’ name for New Mexico
World.content:
The Gulf of America, Lake America and … New America?

U.S. President Donald Trump has already renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” for U.S. federal purposes. Similarly, Trump renamed Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, “Lake America.”

Now, he would apparently like to rename New Mexico “New America,” even though he has no legal authority to change the name of a U.S. state.

Trump shared a map of the U.S. border state to his Truth Social account on Sunday. On the map, the word “Mexico” in “New Mexico” is crossed out and below it appears “America.”

Trump subsequently shared an AI-generated video showing him putting an “America” sticker over “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” sign. Above the video, he wrote:

“Many people suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote-cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA. So much more prestigious and beautiful for the people of that potentially incredible State. Wow, I Love It!!! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

Trump kept up his social media campaign on Monday, posting another map with New Mexico labeled as “New America.”

On Sunday, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Gresham rejected the president’s suggestion that the state she governs could be renamed.

“New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families,” Lujan Grisham wrote on X.

“… While the White House wastes time coloring on maps, Nuevo México is busy doing the work,” she wrote.

New Mexico’s name isn’t up for debate — it’s been ours since before the United States existed. What is up for debate? Who’s showing up for working families. While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring. Americans are… pic.twitter.com/tnX1gPItDH — Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham (@GovMLG) September 6, 2026

The New York Times reported on Monday that “Mr. Trump has no legal authority to rename any state, which in New Mexico’s case is written into its Constitution.”

“Any proposed change would have to originate within the state, a prospect that New Mexico’s Democratic leaders rejected forcefully on Sunday,” the newspaper reported.

The Times also wrote that the origins of New Mexico’s name predate the founding of the United States.

“In the 16th century, Mexicans called the territory north and west of the Rio Grande ‘New Mexico,’ according to the Bureau of Indian Affairs,” the Times reported.

Most of the land that now makes up New Mexico, as well as all of California, Nevada and Utah and parts of several other modern-day U.S. states, was ceded to the United States by Mexico under the terms of the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican-American War of 1846–48. New Mexico’s southwestern corner was acquired by the U.S. later, in the 1853 Gadsden Purchase.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Fireworks blast in México state kills 10, injures dozens more
World.content:
At least 10 people were killed and 82 wounded after an unknown quantity of fireworks detonated during a celebration for a patron saint in the town of Santa María Canchesdá, in the municipality of Temascalcingo, México state.

Local authorities said the explosion occurred at around 9:30 p.m. on Saturday night in the vicinity of the Nuestra Señora de la Luz (Our Lady of Light) church. Temascalcingo, a municipality of 66,000 residents, is located around 160 kilometers northwest of Mexico City.

Videos shared online show festival attendees carrying a straw bull, with fireworks shooting from the effigy. Shortly after, additional fireworks being stored next to the church ignited, which caused a roof and a nearby wall to collapse, burying several people in the rubble.

“It is with profound sorrow that I received the news of what happened in Santa María Canchesdá, Temascalcingo,” México state native and president of the Senate, Higinio Martínez Miranda, announced on social media.

“I contacted the mayor to reiterate my full support and offer my assistance… My solidarity and most sincere condolences go out to the families who are facing the loss of their loved ones. To those who were injured, I wish a speedy recovery.” Governor Delfina Gómez also communicated her condolences.

Hundreds of people from over 40 nearby communities were preparing to watch the fireworks display as part of the annual religious festival when the explosion occurred.

Civil Protection authorities, firefighters, state police and paramedics were quickly mobilized and continued recovering bodies from the debris and working to remove the collapsed structures until the early hours of Sunday morning.

Two priests were injured but are expected to survive, according to the diocese of the nearby municipality of Atlacomulco. Of the 82 total people treated, 62 have already been discharged, eight remain hospitalized and 11 have been referred to other medical facilities.

The state Attorney General’s Office has initiated an investigation into the cause of the accident.

This is not the first time that the storage of fireworks has turned deadly in Mexico. In 2016, an explosion at a fireworks warehouse in Tultepec, México state, killed 42 people.

With reports from Al Jazeera, CNN, NMás, Sol de México and Quadratín México

World.title: Mexico’s foreign affairs head seeks common ground with China in Beijing
World.content:
Mexico’s Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Monday, marking Velasco’s first official trip to the Asian country and signaling hope for improved political and economic cooperation amid an ongoing trade dispute.

The visit to China takes place under the shadow of trade tensions stemming from the tariffs Mexico applied in January to imports from countries without a free trade agreement, including China.

The package modified duties for 1,463 tariff lines across 17 sectors — with rates of up to 50%. Beijing has questioned the decision, while Mexican authorities maintain that it is not directed at any particular country.

However, a statement issued by the Foreign Affairs Ministry (SRE) downplayed the trade topic, instead describing the meeting as an opportunity to discuss mechanisms for strengthening political, economic, cultural and academic exchanges between Mexico and China.

Velasco highlighted the Mexican government’s readiness to maintain a constructive relationship with China, based on mutual respect, equal sovereignty and non-interference.

The Mexican official proposed strengthening the political consultation mechanism between the two foreign ministries in order to maintain communication and make progress on concrete agreements.

The areas of cooperation highlighted by Mexico include health, education, scholarships, science, technological innovation, the environment, rural development, and cultural exchanges.

The SRE indicated that both parties examined options to expand ties in these areas and leverage existing opportunities for collaboration.

During the meeting, Velasco highlighted coordination between Mexico and China in multilateral forums, including the Group of 20 (G-20) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. He also acknowledged China’s role as host of the upcoming APEC leaders’ summit, scheduled for November in Shenzhen.

Regarding culture, Velasco noted that artistic exchanges offer valuable opportunities to deepen mutual understanding between the two peoples and highlighted the exhibition “On Top of the World Tree: Ancient Civilizations of the Americas” at the Shanghai Museum, which brings together nearly 3,000 archaeological and artistic pieces from Mexico.

Velasco’s trip to China includes the inauguration of the Mexican Consulate in Chongqing, one of the major cities in the western part of the country.

With reports from La Silla Rota

World.title: Trump says Mexico is only good for ‘tamales and tomatoes.’ Trade data says otherwise
World.content:
Listen to this article

U.S. President Donald Trump reasserted on Friday that Mexico has “nothing” the United States needs — apart from “hot tamales” and “tomatoes” — and therefore the U.S. could cease trading with its southern neighbor.

However, Trump said he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico — a country that sent more than US $60 billion worth of exports to the U.S. in July alone — “because we get along very well” with President Claudia Sheinbaum.

🇺🇸🇲🇽 Donald Trump aseguró que México no tiene “nada que ofrecer” a Estados Unidos más allá de “tamales y tomates”, al hablar sobre su política comercial desde el Despacho Oval. Pese a la declaración, el presidente estadounidense descartó por ahora interrumpir el comercio con… — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) September 4, 2026

His remarks from the Oval Office came just hours after he threatened in a social media post to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT,” among which is Mexico, if the U.S. Federal Reserve doesn’t lower its benchmark interest rate, which is currently set at 3.50%-3.75%.

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader [Kevin Warsh], must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!” Trump wrote on Truth Social ahead of the Fed’s next interest rate decision on Sept. 16.

Later on Friday, the U.S. president told reporters that “we could do tremendous good for ourselves by just not trading with countries.”

“We lose with the European Union $200 billion a year. If I didn’t trade with them, we’d lose nothing — just one swipe of the pen,” Trump said.

“We lose with Mexico $195 billion a year,” he said, referring to the United States’ trade deficit with its southern neighbor in 2025.

“… They have nothing that we have to have — I mean hot tamales, tomatoes, a couple of things,” Trump said.

“But basically they have nothing that we need. We have oil, we have everything,” he said, adding that he didn’t want to end trade with Mexico “because we get along very well with the president.”

“We like the president, [we] respect her a lot, but if we didn’t want to trade with Mexico, if we didn’t want to trade with Canada, we’d save from $60 billion to $90 billion a year, just by not trading with Canada,” Trump said.

The U.S. president has previously asserted that the United States doesn’t need anything from Mexico and Canada, its two largest trade partners.

“With Mexico and Canada we have trade deficits. We should have surpluses with them. We don’t need their cars, we don’t need their lumber, we don’t need their energy, we don’t need anything that they have,” Trump said on June 10, the same day that he declared that he wasn’t seeking to renew the USMCA free trade pact.

Three weeks later, the United States announced that it had declined to renew the trilateral agreement in its “current form,” a move that paved the way for annual reviews of the USMCA, which remains in force.

Trump’s assertion that Mexico has “nothing” that the United States needs collides with the reality that the U.S. and Mexican economies are highly integrated and that Mexico ships huge quantities of goods to its northern neighbor on a daily basis. Among Mexico’s exports to the U.S. are vehicles, auto parts, machinery, medical devices, AI servers, alcoholic beverages and fresh food, including tomatoes.

In July alone, Mexico exported goods worth $60.55 billion to the United States, according to the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. Mexico’s exports to the U.S. in the first seven months of 2026 were worth $358.7 billion, an increase of 16% compared to the same period of last year.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Guatemala Diesel Cap Proposed as Road Blockades Continue
World.content:
GUATEMALA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The proposal President Bernardo Arevalo announced a bill on 7 September 2026 to cap diesel at Q39 a gallon, about US$5.12.

— The current price Diesel is Q46.39 a gallon in the metropolitan region, roughly US$6.09, the highest in Guatemalan history.

— The catch It is a bill, not a decree. Congress has already declined to fast-track a related fuel tax measure.

— The protests Road blockades began on 31 August and peaked at 24 simultaneous points on 1 September.

— Who is protesting Transport associations, the 48 Cantones of Totonicapan, the Indigenous Municipality of Solola, market vendors and taxi drivers.

— The courts The Constitutional Court granted the chamber of commerce an amparo on 4 September ordering authorities to act on the blockades.

Guatemala diesel is at a record price and the roads keep closing. The president’s answer is a cap, and Congress has not passed it.

The Interamerican Highway at Barberena. Blockades on routes like this have run since 31 August. (Photo: “Carretera Interamericana, Barberena, Guatemala” by Christopher Aragón, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Guatemala’s president has proposed capping the price of diesel. The announcement came on Monday 7 September at the government’s weekly press conference.

The cap would be Q39 a gallon nationwide, about US$5.12. The reference rate that day was Q7.6222 to the dollar.

Diesel currently sells at Q46.39 a gallon in the metropolitan region, roughly US$6.09. That is the highest price in Guatemalan history.

The gap of about Q7.40 a gallon, near US$0.97, would be covered by the state. Bernardo Arevalo said the money would come from emergency funds identified by the finance ministry.

Why Guatemala Diesel and Not Petrol

Arevalo was asked why the measure targets diesel alone. He said diesel has three times the impact on the basic basket of goods.

The logic is freight. Trucks and buses run on diesel, so its price feeds into the cost of food and transport for everyone.

Superior petrol sells around Q43.09 and regular around Q41.09, roughly US$5.65 and US$5.39. Those affect car owners more directly than food prices.

The cap would be temporary, running to the end of 2026. A different mechanism is planned for next year.

The Roads Have Been Closing Since August

Blockades started on 31 August. They peaked the following day with 24 simultaneous closures, some cleared with tear gas.

By 7 September there were nine points. They included Rio Hondo and Santa Cruz in Zacapa, two in Coban and one in the capital’s historic centre.

Transport associations are the core, joined by the 48 Cantones of Totonicapan and the Indigenous Municipality of Solola. Market vendors, taxi and mototaxi drivers have also taken part.

Their demand goes further than a subsidy. Transport leaders want import duties, value added tax and the fuel distribution levy suspended instead.

Congress Is the Obstacle

The legislature has already balked once. Deputies declined to give national urgency status to an initiative suspending VAT and fuel taxes.

On 2 September the plenary closed its session without voting on a fuel exoneration. The blockades continued that day at eleven points.

Arevalo’s diesel bill now enters the same chamber. A cap financed by the treasury is a different proposition from a tax cut, but it still needs votes.

Business groups have pushed from the other side. The Constitutional Court granted the chamber of commerce an amparo on 4 September ordering authorities to act on the blockades.

The Budget in the Background

Guatemala submitted its 2027 budget on 2 September, the constitutional deadline. Article 171 requires it 120 days before the fiscal year begins.

The proposal totals Q192,045.1 million, around US$25.2 billion. That is 17.6 percent of projected GDP and 13.8 percent more than 2026.

More than 46 percent goes to social spending. Education takes Q27,898 million, near US$3.66 billion, and health Q18,615.5 million, about US$2.44 billion.

The projected deficit is 4.4 percent of GDP. A fuel subsidy financed from emergency funds sits awkwardly beside that figure.

What to Watch

The first marker is Congress. Without a vote, the cap is an announcement rather than a price.

The second is whether the blockades stop. Transport leaders have said they reject temporary subsidies, which is precisely what the bill offers.

The third is the international oil price. A cap financed by the treasury gets more expensive every time crude rises.

More: Guatemala news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Guatemala proposing on diesel?

A bill announced by President Bernardo Arevalo on 7 September 2026 would cap diesel at Q39 a gallon, about US$5.12, through the end of 2026. The state would cover the difference from emergency funds.

What is diesel costing now?

Around Q46.39 a gallon in the metropolitan region, roughly US$6.09 at the 7 September reference rate of Q7.6222 to the dollar. That is the highest recorded price in Guatemala.

Why are there road blockades?

Transport associations, indigenous authorities and market vendors have blockaded roads since 31 August over fuel prices and the cost of the basic basket. They want taxes and duties on fuel suspended rather than a temporary subsidy.

Sources: Prensa Libre, Infobae, La Hora, Emisoras Unidas, TN23, Banco de Guatemala, Ministerio de Energia y Minas, Rio Times.

World.title: Guyana Qatar Talks in Doha End With Nothing Signed
World.content:
GUYANA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Guyana’s President Irfaan Ali held official talks with Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani in Doha on 8 September 2026.

— The visit A state visit that began on 6 September.

— The catch No agreement, memorandum or investment figure was announced from the talks.

— Who else he met Qatar Investment Authority chief executive Mohammed Saif al-Sowaidi, Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al Kaabi and Finance Minister Ali bin Ahmed Al Kuwari.

— The existing link QatarEnergy holds 35 percent of Guyana’s offshore Block S4, signed in November 2025.

— On the table A hospitality and real estate project in Georgetown, unnamed and unpriced.

The Guyana Qatar talks spent Tuesday on money. No agreement was announced, and the existing energy tie-up already runs deep.

Doha at night. Guyana’s delegation spent three days there. (Photo: “Al Aaliya Street in Al Mirqab Doha” by Isabell Schulz @ Flickr.com, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.)

Guyana’s president spent Tuesday in Doha. Irfaan Ali held official talks with Qatar’s Amir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani.

The state visit began on 6 September. The talks covered bilateral relations, investment and regional issues.

Nothing was signed. No agreement, memorandum or investment figure came out of the meeting.

That is worth stating plainly. The Guyana Qatar relationship already has substance, and this visit did not add a document to it.

Who Was in the Room

Guyana’s delegation included Foreign Minister Hugh Todd. Presidential assistant George Andrew Hallaq and Director of Presidential Affairs Marcia Nadir-Sharma also travelled.

Ali met Qatari officials separately from the Amir. One was Mohammed Saif al-Sowaidi, chief executive of the Qatar Investment Authority.

He also met Energy Minister Saad Sherida Al Kaabi and Finance Minister Ali bin Ahmed Al Kuwari. That is the sovereign wealth, energy and treasury side of the Qatari state.

The composition of those meetings is the signal. It says what Guyana went to discuss.

What the Guyana Qatar Talks Covered

The Qatar Investment Authority is reported to be advancing a hospitality and real estate development in Georgetown. The project has not been named and no value has been given.

A possible collaboration between the Qatar Development Bank and the Guyana Development Bank was also raised. Again, no instrument has been signed.

Guyana’s economy has been transformed by offshore oil since 2019. Georgetown has a visible shortage of hotel rooms and commercial property.

That gap is what a Gulf sovereign fund would be looking at. It is also why the hospitality project is the item most likely to become real.

The Energy Relationship Already Exists

QatarEnergy is already a partner in Guyanese waters. It holds 35 percent of offshore Block S4.

TotalEnergies operates that block with 40 percent and PETRONAS holds 25. The production sharing agreement was signed on 11 November 2025.

Block S4 covers 1,788 square kilometres. It lies 50 to 100 kilometres offshore in water 30 to 100 metres deep.

The agreement carried a US$15 million signing bonus, paid into Guyana’s Natural Resource Fund. It was the first petroleum agreement under the country’s new fiscal regime.

Two Things Worth Not Confusing

Guyana and Qatar did sign agreements in 2023, when the Amir visited Georgetown. Those covered economic, commercial and technical cooperation and biodiversity.

Those documents are three years old. They are not outcomes of this week’s talks, and they circulate online in a way that makes the two easy to conflate.

There is also an air services agreement between the two countries. It dates from September 2019, and no Qatar Airways route to Guyana has been announced.

Ali was re-elected on 1 September 2025 and sworn in for a second term a week later. This visit falls almost exactly a year into that term.

What to Watch

The first marker is the Georgetown property project. A named developer and a value would turn it from a discussion into a deal.

The second is the development bank link. Bank-to-bank arrangements are usually signed rather than merely discussed.

The third is Block S4 itself. Exploration results there would matter more to both countries than any hotel.

What did Guyana and Qatar agree in Doha?

Nothing was announced as signed. President Irfaan Ali and Qatar’s Amir held official talks on 8 September 2026 covering bilateral relations, investment and regional issues, but no agreement, memorandum or investment figure was reported.

What is the existing Guyana Qatar energy link?

QatarEnergy holds 35 percent of offshore Block S4, alongside operator TotalEnergies with 40 percent and PETRONAS with 25 percent. The agreement was signed on 11 November 2025 with a US$15 million signing bonus.

Is Qatar investing in Georgetown?

The Qatar Investment Authority is reported to be advancing a hospitality and real estate development in Georgetown. The project has not been named and no value has been disclosed.

World.title: Jamaica Tourism Runs 17 Percent Below Last Year After Melissa
World.content:
JAMAICA · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The arrivals 2.34 million visitors through 31 August 2026.

— The earnings US$2.5 billion in tourism revenue over the same period.

— The gap Arrivals are 17 percent below the same months of 2025 and earnings 18 percent below.

— The catch About 30 percent of hotel room inventory is still offline, so the shortfall is partly a capacity limit.

— The cause Hurricane Melissa made landfall in Westmoreland on 28 October 2025 as a Category 5 storm.

— Who said it Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett, at a briefing in Kingston on 2 September 2026.

Jamaica tourism is recovering with three in ten hotel rooms still offline. The gap to last year is the measure of what Melissa cost.

Negril. Three large resorts there reopened on 25 August 2026. (Photo: “Jamaica – Negril – 017” by Oleg Yunakov, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Jamaica tourism has recovered a long way and is still well short of last year. The island received 2.34 million visitors through 31 August.

Earnings over the same period were US$2.5 billion. Tourism Minister Edmund Bartlett gave the figures in Kingston on 2 September.

Arrivals are 17 percent below the same months of 2025. Earnings are 18 percent below.

The reason is not demand. It is that the island cannot house everyone who wants to come.

Why Jamaica Tourism Is Capacity-Limited

Hurricane Melissa made landfall near New Hope in Westmoreland on 28 October 2025. It was a Category 5 storm with sustained winds of 185 miles per hour.

Somewhere between 40 and 50 percent of hotels were damaged. Ten months later, about 70 percent of room inventory is operational.

That leaves roughly three in ten rooms offline. A shortfall of that size caps arrivals regardless of interest.

Bartlett has also said airlines are not providing pre-Melissa levels of airlift. Flights, he said, are flying full.

What Has Reopened

Negril moved first. Royalton Negril, the Hideaway at Royalton Negril and Grand Lido Negril all reopened on 25 August 2026.

In Montego Bay, Half Moon is fully operational. Royalton Blue Waters and its Hideaway are due to reopen on 15 September.

Larger properties are further out. Three Sandals resorts are in a US$200 million refit due to finish in December 2026.

Seven Hyatt-affiliated properties around Rose Hall are scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. Those are the rooms that would close most of the gap.

Reading the Numbers Carefully

The 17 and 18 percent declines are official. The 2025 comparison figures behind them have not been published in the same release.

The nearest verified 2025 datum is from July of that year. Jamaica had 2.3 million arrivals and US$2.4 billion in earnings by 11 July 2025.

That is a shorter period, so it is not a like-for-like comparison. Anyone reconstructing the 2025 totals arithmetically is estimating.

Earnings falling slightly faster than arrivals is the more interesting detail. It suggests visitors are spending a little less per head, or staying in cheaper rooms.

What It Means for the Economy

Tourism is Jamaica’s largest foreign exchange earner. A fifth of it missing for a year is a macroeconomic event, not just an industry one.

Employment follows room capacity closely. Resorts that are closed for refit are not employing housekeeping, kitchen or grounds staff.

Against that, reconstruction spending is itself economic activity. The US$200 million Sandals refit is capital investment in the island.

The net position depends on how quickly rooms return. Every reopening date above is a step in that calculation.

What to Watch

The first marker is 15 September, when the Royalton properties in Montego Bay are due back. It is the next scheduled addition to capacity.

The second is the winter season. December to April is the peak, and it will be the first full high season since the storm.

The third is airlift. Airlines set schedules months ahead, so seat capacity for winter is already largely fixed.

More: Caribbean news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How is Jamaica tourism performing in 2026?

The island recorded 2.34 million visitors and US$2.5 billion in earnings through 31 August 2026. Arrivals are 17 percent below the same period of 2025 and earnings 18 percent below.

Why are the numbers down?

Hurricane Melissa struck on 28 October 2025 as a Category 5 storm, damaging 40 to 50 percent of hotels. About 30 percent of room inventory is still offline, which caps how many visitors the island can accommodate.

Which resorts have reopened?

Royalton Negril, the Hideaway at Royalton Negril and Grand Lido Negril reopened on 25 August 2026. Half Moon in Montego Bay is operational, and Royalton Blue Waters is due back on 15 September.

Sources: Jamaica Information Service, Jamaica Gleaner, Caribbean Journal, Jamaica Star, NOAA National Hurricane Center, Rio Times.

World.title: Uruguay AI Centre Opens in Montevideo on a US$10 Million Loan
World.content:
URUGUAY · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts — What opened Uruguay’s national artificial intelligence centre, branded Instituto Vidart, launched on Monday 7 September 2026.

— Where The Los Ombues building at the LATU innovation park in Montevideo.

— The money US$10 million from an Inter-American Development Bank loan, spread over four and a half years.

— The catch The research body still has to be formed. No headcount or annual budget has been published.

— Who runs it Diego Garagorry as executive director and Matias Di Martino as scientific director, both named in mid-July.

— First projects Early autism detection and satellite-image analysis to identify crop types.

Uruguay AI policy now has an institution behind it. The money is a loan, the staff are not hired yet, and the ambitions are specific.

Central Montevideo. The centre sits at the LATU innovation park on the city’s eastern side. (Photo: “Durazno y Wilson Ferreira Aldunate (ex Rio Branco)” by Estudiante1969, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Uruguay has opened a national artificial intelligence centre. It was launched in Montevideo on Monday 7 September.

The venue was the Los Ombues building at the LATU innovation park. The centre is branded Instituto Vidart.

The name honours Jorge Vidart, a Uruguayan computing pioneer. Uruguay AI policy has had strategy documents for years and now has an institution.

Funding is US$10 million from an Inter-American Development Bank loan. It is spread across four and a half years.

Who Runs the Uruguay AI Centre

Diego Garagorry is the executive director. Matias Di Martino is the scientific director, and both were designated in mid-July.

The centre sits under the Uruguay Innova programme. That places it with SENCI, the national science secretariat that reports to the presidency, and with AGESIC, the digital government agency.

It is incubated by ANII, the national research and innovation agency. LATU, Ceibal, the state telecoms operator Antel and universities are also involved.

No single ministry owns it. That is deliberate and is also the reason it took eighteen months to stand up.

What It Will Actually Do

Garagorry named two first projects at the launch. One is early detection of autism.

The other is analysis of satellite images to identify crop types. Both are narrow, measurable problems rather than general research.

Health, agriculture and education are the stated priority areas. Agriculture matters here because Uruguay’s exports are largely agricultural.

Garagorry said the research body still has to be formed. He described more than eighty meetings with around two hundred people to define the work.

Where Uruguay Stands on AI

AGESIC said in early September that Uruguay is among the region’s better performers on responsible AI governance. The reference is the 2026 Global Responsible AI Index.

The detail is worth having. Uruguay ranks 22nd globally with a score of 56.99, out of 135 countries and jurisdictions.

Within South and Central America that is third, behind Brazil on 63.3 and Chile on 61.9. The regional average is 38.85.

So Uruguay is well above the regional average and not the regional leader. AGESIC’s own headline said it leads the region, which overstates the index.

The Private Side

Uruguayan AI companies have been raising money independently of the state. Six of them raised more than US$26.3 million between August 2023 and August 2026.

One firm dominates that figure. Zapia has raised US$19.3 million across three rounds, including US$7 million in March 2026.

The rest are smaller. Horizon AI raised US$3.5 million in January, Roma AI US$1.2 million in August, Flipando AI US$1 million and Mozart US$600,000.

Microsoft also opened an AI for Good Lab at LATU, announced in March 2026 and described as the first in South America. No investment figure was disclosed.

What to Watch

The first marker is hiring. A centre with two directors and no announced staff is an intention rather than a capability.

The second is the loan structure. Multilateral loan funding sets a clock, and what happens after four and a half years is not defined.

The third is the first outputs. Autism screening and crop mapping are both testable, which makes this easier to judge than most technology announcements.

More: Uruguay news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Uruguay’s national AI centre?

The Centro Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial, branded Instituto Vidart, launched on 7 September 2026 at the LATU innovation park in Montevideo. It sits under the Uruguay Innova programme and is incubated by ANII.

How is it funded?

With US$10 million from an Inter-American Development Bank loan, spread over four and a half years. No annual budget or staff headcount has been published.

What will it work on first?

Early detection of autism and analysis of satellite images to identify crop types, according to executive director Diego Garagorry. Health, agriculture and education are the stated priority areas.

USA & Canada Intelligence Brief — Tuesday, September 8, 2026

Parliament Hill in Ottawa, seat of the government whose C$27.6 billion in counter-tariffs on American goods took effect at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, hours after President Trump threatened to ban Bombardier jet sales in the United States.
