World.title: Tico Time and Why Life in Costa Rica Doesn’t Always Run on Schedule
World.content:
I don’t want to hear about Tico Time. Where did that expression even originate? It has been around for at least the 35 years I have lived here. It was likely coined by some impatient gringo who first said it in a voice of irritation and disgust. Personally I’ve never had a problem with a casual approach to punctuality.

If I wanted to be controlled by the clock, I’d have never left my nine to five phone company job in Washington, DC. One of the many positives of life here is the laid back, pura vida outlook that says that being late for social gatherings and other appointments is not a crime. And the reality is that even if you leave with time to spare to make a meeting, there are obstacles awaiting you as soon as you step out the door. Take what happened to me last week.

I had a doctor’s appointment in town. I left early, to allow myself time to park in a public lot and walk to the medical building. I took my usual route, only to find that the one-lane bridge by the river was closed as rains had swollen the river, which then washed away much of the earthen structure supporting each side of the bridge.

I turned around, headed back up the hill, past my house and came to a crawl behind the municipal garbage truck. Something was happening at the barrio grade school and cars were parked along both sides of the narrow street. For the next few minutes, unable to pass, I breathed the pungent air and watched the workers fling leaking bags of garbage into the grinding maw of the truck. Finally, the truck made a turn and I was able to proceed.

At the intersection to the four lane highway, traffic crawled. There had been a small crash, a fender bender, and the drivers waited outside their cars for the guy from INS to show up and write up an accident report. Five minutes later, I was passing the barely damaged cars, already late for my appointment.

These are but minor inconvenience compared to the delays that mount when extreme nature decides to make its presence felt. Landslides close important highways for days at a time. Flooding chases people to higher ground. About ten years ago, I arrived in San Jose for an outgoing flight that was cancelled because Volcan Turrialba erupted.

The runways were covered in ash and visibility was limited. Juan Santamaria airport looked like a hostel for stranded vagabonds. Hundreds of passengers stuck waiting, lounging in chairs, hunkered down on the floor. I spent the night at a hotel Alajuela and was lucky to catch a flight out the next day.

There is a week every year– the final week of July leading to the Dia de la Virgin on the second of August. Depending on where you are in the country, you may be delayed by groups of true believers, walking toward Cartago. And there was a time in Costa Rica when it was common for protesting groups to block highways, sometimes for days, to get the attention of the government, but that practice was made illegal a few years back, so that is one less delay to encounter.

As for my doctor’s appointment– I arrived fifteen minutes late– and waited another 30 minutes until the doctor could see me. Pura Vida!

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Panama Canal May Restrict Ship Traffic as El Niño Worsens
World.content:
The Panama Canal has not ruled out further restrictions on ship traffic because of a drought worsened by the El Niño climate phenomenon, its new administrator, Ilya Espino de Marotta, said in an interview. The waterway, which connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and handles 5% of global maritime trade, has begun gradually reducing daily transits from 36 to 32 as of September 15.

The 80-kilometer (50-mile) Panama Canal operates primarily with rainwater stored in the artificial Gatun and Alhajuela lakes. Their levels have fallen because of a drought that is shaping up to be the most severe ever recorded. Between 2023 and 2024, restrictions caused by El Niño, whose effects are intensified by climate change, resulted in 2,700 fewer ship transits.

Espino de Marotta, a 64-year-old engineer and the first woman to run the canal, which the United States built in 1914, hopes to avoid measures that restrictive. But she stressed the need for a new reservoir to support operations at the canal, where she has worked for about four decades.

Q: What are the canal’s main challenges?

A: Climate change is one, and that is why the Rio Indio reservoir project is our No. 1 priority. We see what is happening in 2026 and would like to finish this project to ease the impact on customers. We want (…) to expand. We are going to build a gas pipeline and two ports.

Q: What is El Niño’s impact?

A: We have to reduce the permitted draft of ships, which means they must carry less cargo. In 2023–2024, we had to reduce the number of transits to avoid affecting the population’s water supply. Fewer transits mean less revenue.

Q: Could there be restrictions similar to those in 2023–2024?

A: We think not (…) but we cannot rule out having to reduce transits in February or March, probably not to 24 a day, but to 29 or something close to that. That could have an impact.

Q: Does this affect international trade?

A: Shipping can adapt by using vessels as large as our permitted draft allows. With fewer transits but more cargo, they achieve economies of scale, and we do not need to use more water.

Q: Analysts say the United States, the canal’s main user, could be affected.

A: If it lasts less than a year, there will be no significant consequences for the economy. If it lasted five or seven years, I would say yes (…) Limiting the number of ships for four or five months will not necessarily have a lasting impact.

Q: Is there a risk that shipping companies will leave?

A: We experienced that in 2024. Bulk carriers had practically disappeared, but they returned because the canal route offers major advantages (…). That is why the Rio Indio reservoir project is so crucial (…). We are going to store enough water to live with El Niño without affecting the number of transits or the population.

Q: But this new reservoir will not be ready before 2031?

A: I cannot shorten the construction period. We will probably include a clause in the tender stating that if the contractor delivers ahead of the contractual deadline, there will be an incentive. The tender is expected to be launched in 2027.

Q: How do you envision relations with the United States?

A: I hope we will have a cordial relationship, as we have for the past 25 years.

World.title: Costa Rica Vehicle Thefts Hit a Ten-Year High
World.content:
If you own a car here, it is more likely to be stolen now than at any point in the past ten years. Costa Rica recorded 5,146 vehicle thefts in 2025, according to open statistics from the Organismo de Investigación Judicial (OIJ). That is the highest annual figure of the decade, up from 4,289 in 2016 — a 20% increase.

What makes the number worth paying attention to is what happened around it. Over the same ten years, almost every other property crime went the other way. Muggings, larcenies, break-ins at homes and businesses, and thefts of items from inside parked cars all trended downward.

Vehicle theft did not follow and after bottoming out at 3,217 cases in 2020, it climbed every single year from 2021 through 2025. Part of that is simple arithmetic as there are far more cars to steal than there used to be. Costa Rica finished 2025 with 2,087,356 vehicles covered by mandatory SOA insurance, 9.1% more than the 1,913,266 registered a year earlier.

But more cars on the road does not really explain why this one category rose while everything else fell. Something changed about the crime itself and the answer, according to specialists whose analysis accompanied the OIJ data, is that stealing a car stopped being a job for one or two opportunists and became a supply chain.

Organized networks now handle it in stages — one person takes the vehicle, another strips it, and intermediaries move the parts to workshops, to businesses, or directly to buyers who want a cheap replacement bumper or gearbox. That matters in order to show you how you protect yourself.

A car is no longer stolen because someone wants to drive it. It is stolen because its parts are worth more disassembled than the whole vehicle is worth intact, and because those parts are easy to sell without anyone asking where they came from. Which means the thing that keeps your car safe is not just making it hard to break into. It is making it slow to move and slow to take apart.

A steering lock, a tracker, a car that gets parked somewhere visible rather than somewhere convenient — these work because they add minutes, and the whole model depends on the vehicle disappearing fast. The OIJ statistics do not show how many of the 5,146 thefts were committed by organized structures rather than by individuals acting alone, so treat that as a pattern the investigators describe rather than a number you can verify.

Where you live changes the picture considerably. Eight of the country’s cantons finished 2025 with fewer vehicle thefts than they recorded in 2016, bucking the national trend entirely. Santa Ana posted the largest drop in raw numbers, falling from 76 cases in 2016 to 31 in 2025 — 45 fewer thefts. It also slid from 14th place to 44th out of 84 cantons ranked from most to fewest.

That decline was not a straight line. Santa Ana dipped to 29 cases in 2021, then rose again to 44 in 2022, 45 in 2023 and 66 in 2024 before dropping sharply last year. Escazú, San Rafael, Heredia, Sarapiquí and Aserrí also closed below their 2016 figures, though their paths were similarly uneven and several saw rebounds in the intervening years.

Heredia is the useful cautionary case. It went from 207 thefts in 2016 to 178 in 2025, a 14% reduction — and still finished fifth in the country, having been fourth a decade earlier. Falling numbers do not automatically mean a low-risk canton. They can just mean a slightly less bad one.

One technical note on the rankings. In 2016 Costa Rica had 81 areas; it now has 84. Position changes between the two years reflect that shift as well as actual movement in theft numbers, so a area that dropped a few places has not necessarily improved.

If your vehicle is stolen, report it to the OIJ immediately rather than waiting to see if it turns up. The parts chain moves within hours, and a report filed the same day is the only realistic window in which a vehicle gets recovered whole. Have your plate number, chassis number (VIN) and your cédula or passport ready before you call, because you will be asked for all three.

World.title: Belize takes major step to protect Global Ocean Biodiversity
World.content:
Belize takes major step to protect Global Ocean Biodiversity

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Government of Belize, through the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation (MBEMC), officially launched the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Implementation Project marking a significant step toward translating Belize’s international ocean commitments into national action.

The BBNJ Agreement is an international treaty under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) aimed at conserving and sustainably using marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.

These waters account for approximately two-thirds of the world’s oceans and are considered critical to global efforts to protect marine ecosystems and achieve the international goal of conserving at least 30 percent of the ocean by 2030. Belize became the first Caribbean country to ratify the agreement in 2024, strengthening its position as a regional leader in ocean governance.

The 18-month project is funded by the Global Environment Facility (GEF), with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) serving as the implementing partner, and is scheduled to conclude in December 2027. The initiative will support Belize in strengthening its capacity for marine scientific research, accessing and benefiting from marine technology, building technical and institutional expertise, and participating in the governance of marine genetic resources.

Speaking at the launch, MBEMC Chief Executive Officer Beverly Wade emphasized the importance of connecting Belize’s international commitments with its national ocean priorities. “Internationally, BBNJ gives Belize an additional platform to protect the wider ocean systems upon which our prosperity and resilience depend, while opening pathways to knowledge, technology and partnerships that can strengthen our national agenda,” Wade said.

Ambassador Janine Coye-Felson also highlighted the need to turn Belize’s international leadership into tangible national benefits. She said the agreement must be translated “from international commitments into national laws, capable institutions, scientific expertise, and tangible opportunities for our people.”

The Ministry said it will work with national and international stakeholders throughout the project to strengthen Belize’s preparedness under the BBNJ Agreement and advance sustainable ocean management for present and future generations.

World.title: Belize @45: Magical History tour brings National history to San Ignacio
World.content:
Belize @45: Magical History tour brings National history to San Ignacio

By Zoila Palma: The Belize @45 Magical History Tour made its way to San Ignacio Town, Cayo District, bringing students, community leaders and residents together for discussions on Belize’s history, the struggle for independence and the country’s ongoing process of decolonization.

The tour is being led by the Institute for Social & Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) in partnership with historian Dr. Assad Shoman.

The initiative aims to encourage Belizeans, particularly young people, to critically examine the events, struggles and diverse perspectives that have shaped the nation’s journey to independence.

On September 3, Dr. Shoman met with students at Sacred Heart College, where he facilitated thought-provoking discussions on Belize’s history and encouraged students to examine the stories and experiences that have influenced the country’s development. Students and representatives from Eden SDA High School and St. Ignatius High School also participated in the discussions.

The engagement continued that evening at the San Ignacio & Santa Elena House of Culture, where community leaders and residents gathered for a public forum.

Participants engaged in discussions and shared perspectives on Belize’s historical journey, creating an opportunity for meaningful reflection beyond the classroom.

The Magical History Tour will be hosted in Belize City today as part of Belize’s 45th Independence celebrations.

World.title: International News: Powerful El Niño developing as Pacific ocean heats up
World.content:
International News: Powerful El Niño developing as Pacific ocean heats up

By Zoila Palma: Sea surface temperatures in the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the region at the heart of the El Niño climate pattern, are already significantly above average and continue to climb, according to information from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

The Niño 3.4 index, a key measure used to monitor El Niño conditions, recorded sea surface temperatures 1.5°C above average from May to July 2026, rising to 2.0°C above average in July. Weekly measurements from late July through mid-August showed even warmer conditions, ranging between 2.2°C and 2.6°C above average. Subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average in some areas during July and early August.

Forecasts indicate that El Niño conditions could strengthen considerably over the coming months, with multi-model projections suggesting Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomalies could reach approximately +3.6°C.

The event is currently expected to peak around November and December 2026, potentially producing significant impacts on weather and climate patterns in areas far beyond the Pacific.

The WMO also expects a positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole to develop, reaching an average value of about +0.9°C between September and November 2026, while the equatorial Atlantic is forecast to remain warmer than normal. The combination of these climate patterns could reinforce, weaken or alter the typical effects of El Niño in different parts of the world.

El Niño can influence weather patterns thousands of kilometres from the tropical Pacific, potentially affecting rainfall, temperatures and other climate conditions in different regions.

The WMO is urging everyone to rely on their National Meteorological and Hydrological Services for official warnings and region-specific climate information as conditions continue to develop.

World.title: International News: U.S. Secretary of State heads to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to strengthen ties
World.content:
International News: U.S. Secretary of State heads to Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to strengthen ties

By Zoila Palma: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit Colombia, Ecuador and Peru this week as Washington seeks to strengthen ties with newly elected leaders who have closely aligned themselves with President Donald Trump’s administration.

Rubio is scheduled to travel to Colombia today to meet newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella, before heading to Ecuador to meet President Daniel Noboa and Peru to meet President Keiko Fujimori.

The US State Department said Rubio’s agenda will include discussions on support for Colombia’s earthquake response, increased cooperation in the fight against narcoterrorism and opportunities to deepen commercial relations.

The trip comes amid a broader conservative shift across Latin America, with Trump-backed or closely aligned leaders also emerging in Honduras and Bolivia, while Washington maintains strong relationships with Argentina’s Javier Milei and El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele.

Security and the fight against drug trafficking are expected to feature prominently during Rubio’s meetings.

Colombia recently joined the US-led “Shield of the Americas,” whose members have pledged to use military force against cartels and terrorist networks. Ecuador has also expanded security cooperation with Washington under Noboa, including US military operations targeting suspected drug-trafficking groups, while Fujimori has pledged closer US ties and a tougher military response to criminal organizations in Peru.

Rubio’s tour comes as the Trump administration seeks to expand US influence across the Western Hemisphere and pursues what it has described as a more aggressive approach to combating drug trafficking.

World.title: NICH congratulates Benque House of Culture on 25 years
World.content:
NICH congratulates Benque House of Culture on 25 years

By Zoila Palma: The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) has congratulated the Benque House of Culture on reaching its 25th anniversary, recognizing the institution’s longstanding contribution to cultural and historical preservation in Benque Viejo del Carmen. The milestone was celebrated on September 7, 2026, with NICH President Albert Vaughan in attendance.

NICH also extended special recognition to the Community of Artists for Cultural & Historical Endeavours (CACHE), which was organized in January 1999 and served as the founding organization of the Benque House of Culture.

NICH said CACHE’s partnership has played an important role in nurturing and promoting the town’s vibrant cultural heritage.

As part of the Jubilee celebration and in keeping with this year’s theme, “Rooted in Culture,” 25 trees were planted to mark the 25 years of cultural and historical work. The initiative was carried out in collaboration with the Forestry Department’s Greening Belize Initiative, stakeholders and members of the local community.

NICH said the tree planting symbolizes Benque Viejo del Carmen’s deep cultural roots and the shared commitment to preserving and promoting Belizean culture and history for future generations.

World.title: Belmopan to host St. George’s Caye Day citizen ceremony and block party
World.content:
Belmopan to host St. George’s Caye Day citizen ceremony and block party

By Zoila Palma: The Belmopan City Council will host a St. George’s Caye Day Citizen Ceremony and Block Party on September 10, bringing residents together to celebrate Belizean heritage, culture and community.

The event will take place at Sir George Brown Park, beginning at 3:00 p.m., with residents of Belmopan and surrounding communities invited to attend and take part in the festivities.

The celebration will feature a citizen ceremony alongside music and entertainment, providing an opportunity for residents to come together and recognize Belize’s national heritage as the country continues its September celebrations.

The Belmopan City Council is inviting residents to come out and make the St. George’s Caye Day celebration a memorable community event.

World.title: Fisheries Department warns fishers to sell sea cucumbers only to licensed buyer
World.content:
Fisheries Department warns fishers to sell sea cucumbers only to licensed buyer

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Sea cucumber fishers are being advised to take note of new purchasing arrangements for the opening of the 2026 to 2027 fishing season.

The Belize Fisheries Department says MAD’s Seafood Export is presently the only business authorized to legally purchase and export sea cucumbers in Belize.

Purchasing will begin on September 9, with the company operating from Independence Village and authorized buyers stationed in Belize City.

The Department issued a clear warning that transactions involving unlicensed buyers remain illegal. Fishers should therefore ensure that their catch is sold only through authorized channels.

The announcement is particularly important as the season opens and commercial activity increases around the valuable marine product.

While MAD’s Seafood Export currently holds exclusive authorization, the Fisheries Department says other applications are being reviewed. Additional companies could therefore enter the market later in the season if their applications are approved.

Any new licences will be announced publicly by the Department.

Fishers seeking purchasing information can call 610 0664, while questions regarding licensing or regulations can be directed to the Belize Fisheries Department at 224 4552.

World.title: 18 year old detained after police find motorcycle insurance and licence expired
World.content:
18 year old detained after police find motorcycle insurance and licence expired

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An 18 year old Carmelita Village resident was escorted to the Trial Farm Police Station on Monday after police say he was found riding a motorcycle with expired insurance and an expired vehicle licence.

Police report that officers were on mobile patrol along Manatee Boulevard in Trial Farm Village when they observed a black Jiyo motorcycle travelling in the same direction.

The rider was stopped and asked to produce his driver’s licence, but police say he was unable to do so.

A subsequent check found that the motorcycle’s insurance had expired in July, while its licence had expired the month before.

The rider was identified as George Richard Orlando Lopez, a labourer of Carmelita Village.

Police say Lopez was cautioned and informed of his constitutional rights before being taken to the Trial Farm Police Station.

The motorcycle, bearing licence plate CZL M 0978, was also taken to the station and impounded.

World.title: Rough start
World.content:
Grade two students at Holland Primary School seated during their outdoor class under a bamboo structure on Monday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

THE education ministry on Monday reported a generally smooth reopening of schools across the island for the start of the 2026/27 academic year but principals, mostly in hurricane-ravaged western Jamaica, highlighted a raft of difficulties.

Among the complaints were incomplete repairs as well as classes held in heat-trapping tents that turn into sweltering ovens under the tropical sun.

“Based on preliminary data received from all seven educational regions covering approximately 1,000 schools, only three schools did not open today, meaning that approximately 99.7 per cent of the schools captured in the data were able to open on the first day of the new school year,” the ministry said in a news release.

While the ministry said late furniture delivery was among the most frequently reported challenges on Monday, Jamaica Observer journalists received first-hand reports of the rough start to the academic year in the sections of the island that suffered the brunt of Hurricane Melissa’s fury last October.

Stories on Pages 3 to 10.

World.title: Two traditions, one future
World.content:
Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon (centre), along with former Hydel High Principal Dr Walton Small (right), as well as teachers and students of the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School, release balloons in celebration of the official opening of the merged institution on the first day of the new academic year, Monday. (Photos: Garfield Robinson)

EDUCATION Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon officially unveiled the newly merged Hydel Cumberland High School Monday, declaring that the unification wasn’t about erasing either school’s identity, but rather combining the best of their traditions to create a single learning environment better equipped to serve students and make fuller use of existing resources.

“I love to see the new motto: ‘On the wings of excellence, endeavour to soar.’ And that’s a merger of the two mottos of the two schools. So even starting with the name, we merged the two schools. With the motto, we have merged the two schools and their ethos,” Morris Dixon said Monday while delivering greetings at the name unveiling ceremony at the school’s campus in Portmore, St Catherine.

As she helped to officiate both the historic first day of the school and the start of the 2026-2027 academic year, Morris Dixon explained that Cumberland High School had a capacity for 1,200 students but had only been operating with just over 300 students when she visited about a year ago. She added that the infrastructural challenges at Hydel High, coupled with Cumberland’s available space, made the merger a practical option.

“One of the things we had thought about was potentially moving the children in little groups to different schools, putting them all around St Catherine. But I think this is the best option. I think this was quite strategic in nature, and that’s how we’re going to continue to do this restructuring of education in Jamaica — be strategic — because now that we have one institution instead of two, it means we can direct more resources to one… that is our plan,” said Morris Dixon.

Already, significant investment is being made in the new school. The minister announced that $70 million is being spent to improve its electrical system while work is also being done on the home economics laboratory.

She added that the school’s parking lot will be expanded to accommodate the increased number of staff, while upgrades to the sporting facilities are also planned.

“So there’s a lot that will happen here, and Principal [Carlon Pitt] can ask for everything he wants. Principal, we’ve already granted your first wish, which was more students, but your success, the success of this merged institution, is really important to the Ministry of Education. We are very much committed to it. We’re committed to seeing the traditions work together and to achieve so much more,” she said.

Morris Dixon acknowledged, however, that bringing together two established school communities would not be without challenges but promised that her ministry would be strongly supporting the school’s leadership to smoothly navigate any trials that may arise.

“There are understandable emotions when schools merge. I know there is sadness from some who are, you know, leaving a space that they’re used to. There are those who are seeing all these new children come and these new teachers come. There are a lot of emotions involved in this, and so I want to acknowledge those emotions. Change is never easy; it’s always hard. And us adults, we sometimes have a harder time than the children with change,” she said.

“So teachers, I know this is an emotional period for you… I know that you’re great, I know you’re wonderful, I have no doubt that we have the best teachers in this world in Jamaica, so I know we can get through this. The ministry is here to support, in whatever way we can, to the students who may be coming to this new environment. You have a good principal, you have a good team here; you’re going to be okay,” Morris Dixon assured.

Principal Pitt told the Jamaica Observer that as the former head of Cumberland High he was highly receptive to the idea of a school merger.

Welcoming this new chapter in his career, Pitt emphasised that his vision focuses heavily on academics while prioritising students’ holistic development.

Highlighting Cumberland’s status as a leading Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institution in St Catherine, alongside Hydel’s strong culture of sports and academics, the principal noted that the merger offers the perfect opportunity to fulfill his goals.

“Whatever we do in school, it must result in student outcome, the students must be the biggest beneficiary of whatever we do. And so the primary focus is on adding value, value-added education, adding value to the students with respect to their starting point and where they exit. So far we have added more sciences to the curriculum. We have now the traditional sixth form… we have a sports programme to roll out that we are excited about, and so with all of these things it is about the holistic development of the child,” Pitt said.

World.title: Jahshii to embark on islandwide tour; aims to reconnect with his fans
World.content:
JAHSHII...the fanbase a grow and mi just waa continue grow with the fans.

IN a move to reconnect with his fan base, dancehall artiste Jahshii is set to embark on a multi-stop tour across the island in November.

The Born Fighter artiste says the tour will feature performances backed by Tower Band and he’s also bringing along some special guests at each stop.

“The fanbase a grow and mi just waa continue grow with the fans,” he told the Jamaica Observer recently.

“The islandwide tour will kick off in November, and you can expect high-energy performances, special guests at each stop. We’ll be going across the island, and it will be a live music experience like no other,” Jahshii assured.

He added, “We really want to get the fans dem closer, like in an up close and personal vibe, so we have been doing rehearsals while locking in the venues.”

Jahshii, who is best known for songs like Pieces featuring Masicka, Cream of the Crop and

Born Fighter, revealed that it wasn’t an easy journey to get to where he is today.

“Mi a come from nobody naw do nuttin fi mi; a fight wi fight to get up deh. But it is very satisfying to help other emerging talent and see how they develop and make it in the music,” he shared.

Father to a young son, Jahshii says fatherhood has changed his perspective on life.

“It has changed my outlook on life; family comes first and my priorities come first. That’s what we get from being a father,” he shared.

Jahshii’s latest single Auto Pilot, produced by Troublemekka, was released two months ago. He says new music is on the way.

“We definitely have some new music coming especially for the ladies, because we not leaving them out,” he said.

World.title: CPL Hall of Fame award named in honour of Sir Garfield Sobers
World.content:
Garfield Sobers

BRIDGETOWN, Barbados (CMC) — The Republic Bank Caribbean Premier League (CPL) has announced that the trophy presented to each year’s player inducted into its hall of fame will be officially named the Sir Garry Sobers Award, in tribute to the man universally recognised as the greatest all-rounder West Indies cricket has ever produced.

The naming follows the recent launch of the CPL Hall of Fame which will honour two inductees annually, one player and one off-field contributor.

Dwayne Bravo and Ian Bishop were confirmed as the inaugural class, and the CPL has now secured the Sobers family’s blessing to attach Sir Garry’s name to the award, marking one of the most significant moments in the league’s history.

As one of the finest cricketers the game has ever seen and a defining figure of West Indies cricket, Sir Garry’s name gives prestige to the Hall of Fame recognition.

The Sir Garry Sobers Award will be presented for the first time at the CPL Hall of Fame Gala Dinner on September 15, 2026 at the Hilton Barbados.

The evening is being held in support of the Sir Clive Lloyd Healthcare Foundation’s prostate cancer awareness, testing, and early detection work across the Caribbean.

With the trophy carrying Sir Garry’s name the gala brings together two of West Indies cricket’s most respected figures for a single showpiece night in support of the region.

Pete Russell, CEO of CPL, said “Sir Garry Sobers was, without question, the greatest all-rounder the game has ever seen, and having his name on this award means a great deal to everyone at CPL. We are enormously grateful to the Sobers family for trusting us with his name and his legacy. It gives this trophy, and this hall of fame, a weight our players will carry with real pride. To present it for the first time at a gala dinner in support of Sir Clive Lloyd’s Healthcare Foundation makes 15 September an even more prestigious night for West Indies cricket.”

World.title: ‘SPOILT KIDS’
World.content:
RICKETTS... FIFA has supported us and I’ll be very ungrateful not to show some regard, and show some respect, and say thanks to a man that has supported Caribbean football (Photo: Observer file)

JAMAICA Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts has come to the defence of FIFA President Gianni Infantino, saying he doesn’t deserve the treatment he’s receiving from stakeholders. Ricketts also labeled UEFA “spoilt kids” for its stance against the FIFA boss.

On Sunday, football’s world governing body confirmed that Infantino intends to stand again in next year’s elections for a fourth term, despite mounting criticism over recent months. Infantino proposed selling stakes in FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s World Cup, to private investors and offered FIFA’s 211 member associations US$40 million ($6.3 billion) each if they backed the plan.

However, the 56-year-old Swiss ultimately scrapped it following widespread opposition, including European football governing body, UEFA, who voted to boycott all World Cups if it went ahead. Concacaf, who governs North America and the Caribbean, also rejected the proposal.

Infantino, though, attempted to smooth things over with several Concacaf members after attending a Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Presidents’ Meeting and the CFU Under-14 series in the Dominican Republic last month, where Jamaica reached the final. Concacaf President and FIFA Vice-President Victor Montagliani had written to Infantino, asking him not to attend.

Reports from England stated many of the Concacaf members were “infuriated” by Infantino’s behaviour.

However, while not providing the details of the meeting, Ricketts told the Jamaica Observer that the FIFA boss was treated with the utmost respect.

“That’s how reporting and that’s how media is — some people try to sensationalise certain events to suit their own agenda — but that’s the farthest thing from the truth,” he said. “I think Infantino was warmly, warmly welcomed; he was embraced by almost every single CFU member.”

Ricketts, who has served as JFF boss for nearly a decade, admits that Infantino should have approached the proposal differently, although he had no issue with its premise.

“Infantino might have made a mistake, but the intentions were to help Caribbean countries or help smaller countries. Can you imagine Jamaica getting 40 million US dollars to invest in football? Can you imagine the difference that would make in four or five years?” said Ricketts.

“In my very first utterance, I did say that the gesture would suit me but we thought [there] was [a] lack of communication, lack of discussions, it seemed non-transparent. But I don’t think Infantino meant to hurt anybody or would have tried to make himself a beneficiary of the gesture.”

The fallout from the proposal continues Belgium Football Association, on Monday, the latest to oppose Infantino’s re-election. At least 11 other FIFA member associations have publicly withdrawn their support including major European football nations such as England, Germany, Norway and the Netherlands.

UEFA has led calls for Infantino to step down and is preparing legal action against him, accusing the FIFA president of “criminal mismanagement” over the proposal. FIFA, in return, has accused the Euopean governing body of a “smear campaign against it and its leadership”.

Ricketts believes UEFA are being unreasonable and has no intention of following its stance.

“People will have different views and different opinions for different reasons. But I am not supporting UEFA because I think that they always want to be in opposition and always want to oppose. It doesn’t matter who is president, they are going to have issues. It doesn’t matter how well the president does, they are going to have issues and I think that UEFA is behaving like a set of spoilt kids,” he said.

“From a commercial standpoint, they really don’t need FIFA. They probably have as much money as FIFA does so they can do and say anything. I can’t do that because I need support and FIFA has supported us and I’ll be very ungrateful not to show some regard and show some respect and say thanks to a man that has supported Caribbean football.”

More than 20 FIFA member associations, including 2026 World Cup finalists Argentina, World Cup co-host Mexico and African champions Morocco, have publicly expressed support for Infantino .

Ricketts praised Infantino’s performance but says the decision on Jamaica’s support for rests with the JFF board.

“This is something I probably don’t even have the right to speak on because it’s a decision that the board will have to make. But personally, I think Infantino has done a good job,” he said.

The nominations for FIFA presidential candidates must be submitted by November 18. Infantino is currently the only candidate, though Concacaf President Victor Montagliani is being touted as a potential challenger.

World.title: Wedding, Fashion & Interior Design
World.content:
Inspired by the beautifully curated spaces they encounter worldwide, couples are choosing venues like boutique hotels to evoke those same unforgettable feelings on their wedding day. -

New York Fashion Week is upon us, and it got me thinking about how much fashion and interior design influence the wedding industry. We often look at weddings as their own creative world, but they are actually incredibly responsive to what is happening around us. What we wear, how we decorate our homes, the restaurants and hotels we are drawn to, even the way luxury brands present themselves all eventually find their way into weddings.

And increasingly, I think the most interesting weddings are borrowing ideas rather than following wedding trends.

The Runway Has Always Found Its Way to the Aisle

Fashion is perhaps the most obvious influence. What happens on the runways of New York, Paris, Milan and London eventually changes what brides and grooms want to wear, but its influence goes much further than the dress.

The current fashion conversation is full of personality: sculptural silhouettes, interesting textures, dramatic draping, bows, metallics, sheer fabrics, unexpected colour and a renewed appreciation for beautiful tailoring. Those ideas translate remarkably well into weddings.

A beautifully draped fashion silhouette can inspire the treatment of a tent. A couture floral appliqué can become the starting point for an invitation, cake or tablescape. A runway colour combination can suddenly make traditional wedding palettes feel completely different.

Even bridal fashion itself has become less formulaic. Brides are changing looks throughout the celebration, experimenting with shorter dresses, statement accessories, dramatic veils and fashion-forward reception looks. Grooms, too, are embracing more colour, texture and individuality.

Weddings Are Beginning to Look More Like Beautiful Interiors

Interior design is having an even greater influence on weddings.

For years, wedding décor was largely about flowers, linens and centrepieces. Couples are paying attention to chairs, lamps, rugs, bars, shelving, interesting furniture, textured fabrics and architectural details. The lounge is no longer simply somewhere to put a sofa; it can feel like the living room of an incredibly stylish home. Bars are becoming statement pieces. Dinner spaces are layered with lighting and objects in much the same way an interior designer would style a room.

I particularly love the move towards residential-style lighting. Table lamps, shaded pendants and warm pools of light immediately change the feeling of a wedding. They make large spaces feel intimate and give outdoor celebrations a sense of permanence and warmth.

This is where I think the influence of boutique hotels, restaurants and private members’ clubs has become especially important. Couples travel. They dine out. They experience beautifully designed spaces around the world, and naturally they want their celebrations to evoke some of those same feelings.

They may not say, “I want an interior-designed wedding.” They say, “I want it to feel like this hotel in Paris,” or “I loved this restaurant in New York.” That distinction matters.

The New Luxury Is Atmosphere

I think we will continue to see couples becoming more confident about mixing influences — vintage furniture with contemporary florals, fashion-inspired fabrics with traditional tablescapes, chrome against soft linen, sculptural pieces beside organic greenery.

The objective isn’t necessarily for everything to “match.” It is for everything to belong to the same story.

Fashion Is Also Teaching Weddings to Be More Personal

Perhaps my favourite influence from fashion is individuality. For a long time, weddings came with an unwritten formula of what was considered “bridal”. White, blush, certain flowers, certain chairs, certain stationery, certain photographs. That vocabulary has expanded enormously.

Today’s couple can create a wedding that is minimalist, maximalist, tropical, editorial, romantic, architectural, vintage, fashion-forward or wonderfully difficult to categorise.

Looking Beyond the Wedding Industry

As New York Fashion Week begins, I’ll certainly be watching the clothes, but I’ll also be looking at the sets, colour combinations, fabrics, styling and tiny details that make a collection memorable.

Because inspiration doesn’t always arrive labelled “wedding.”

Sometimes it is a handbag. A hotel lobby. A fashion show. A restaurant in another country. A fabric you can’t stop touching. A beautifully designed room. A colour combination you would never have thought to put together.

The best wedding professionals know how to notice those things, reinterpret them and make them relevant to the couple, the location and the celebration. For me, that is where wedding design becomes most exciting.

The future of weddings isn’t simply about following the next wedding trend. It is about looking at the wider world of design, fashion, travel and culture — and asking: how can we turn that inspiration into something that feels entirely our own?

Shikima Hinds

Managing Director
