World.title: Has Karol Nawrocki’s first year as Poland’s president been a success?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Poland’s right-wing president has been largely successful at transforming his office into an assertive centre of resistance to the liberal centrist-led government, frustrating its agenda through extensive use of constitutional powers. He has emerged as the leading unifying figure on the fragmented Polish right but faces new challenges moving towards the next election. Scuppering the government’s reform agenda Last month, Polish President Karol Nawrocki marked the first anniversary of his inauguration following a surprise victory in the May-June 2025 presidential election over Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, the candidate of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Poland’s main governing party since autumn 2023, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. A relatively unknown conservative historian and head of the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), a state historical research institute, Nawrocki ran formally as an independent but was backed by the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping. The election result represented a significant upset, ushering in a period of tense “cohabitation” between the Tusk government and a hostile president. The Polish presidency is not a day-to-day governing role, and in many respects largely ceremonial, but retains important constitutional powers. Karol Nawrocki has now issued more vetoes than any other president in Polish history Three vetoes on Thursday took his total to 37 in just ten months since taking office, surpassing the 35 issued by Aleksander Kwaśniewski during his ten years as president https://t.co/xf27K8Fyn6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 These include a legislative veto, which the government lacks the required three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, and the ability to suspend a piece of legislation coming into law by referring it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Given that a majority of tribunal members were appointed under previous PiS-dominated parliaments, this also functioned as a de facto veto. As a result, Nawrocki was able to severely complicate the Tusk government’s plans to push through its legislative and elite replacement programme, notably efforts to roll back PiS’s judicial reforms. This, combined with the political authority that stemmed from Nawrocki’s strong electoral mandate, meant that the government faced continued resistance for the remainder of its term of office until the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027. An assertive presidency From the outset, Nawrocki has been a much more assertive president than his predecessor Andrzej Duda, leveraging his mandate to carve out a role as an active centre of resistance to the government. Although both presidents were PiS-aligned, during cohabitation with the Tusk administration, Duda used his powers more selectively and occasionally sought common ground. Nawrocki, by contrast, interpreted his strong electoral mandate as authorising a more confrontational approach. He has surrounded himself with a strong political support base who have helped him to develop and carry forward a blaze of independent initiatives in both the domestic and foreign policy spheres. As well proposing a series of his own draft laws, Nawrocki has used the legislative veto far more frequently than Duda (who issued only 19 across two full five-year terms) or any previous post-1989 president in a comparable period. By mid-2026, he had already surpassed previous records, blocking over 40 government-sponsored laws on issues such as judicial reform, socioeconomic policy and defence financing. In foreign policy, where the president’s formal competencies are more limited, Nawrocki pursued independent initiatives that often diverged from, or complicated, the government’s line. He has, for example, prioritised close personal and strategic ties with the USA, positioning Washington as Warsaw’s primary security guarantor. He cultivated a high-profile relationship with the Trump administration that yielded commitments to ongoing US troop deployments in Poland, sometimes bypassing or challenging the Tusk government. On Ukraine, while supporting continued military and diplomatic aid, Nawrocki has adopted a more transactional and assertive approach, opposing rapid Ukrainian EU and NATO accession until bilateral issues are addressed, and taking symbolic steps such as removing a Polish state honour from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over unresolved historical grievances. Polish President Nawrocki has announced that he will strip @ZelenskyyUa of Poland’s highest honour in response to him naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles during WWII Ukraine's foreign minister condemned Nawrocki's "reckless" decision https://t.co/CEqj4aaHYg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 These have drawn criticisms that he is playing into Russian hands by weakening regional unity, but were clearly in line with changing Polish public attitudes towards its eastern neighbour. Uniting the fragmented right? Nawrocki has also emerged as the most important unifying figure on the increasingly fragmented Polish right. PiS, long the hegemonic force on the conservative side, has seen radical-right challengers, the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), gaining ground. In July, PiS also suffered its biggest ever internal split, with a significant group of parliamentarians aligned with former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki breaking away. All of this weakened PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński’s once unquestioned authority as the central broker on the Polish right; he is now one leader among several. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 Alone among leading right-wing politicians, Nawrocki possesses genuine crossover appeal across the fractured conservative landscape. His 2025 presidential victory showed that he could consolidate a broad right-wing coalition and attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists, capturing the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. Although he was the PiS candidate, Nawrocki operates as an independent authority outside of direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative independent figure, which gives him greater moral and symbolic stature than any partisan leader. Nawrocki’s assertive use of his constitutional powers has further reinforced his position as a natural focal point around which the broader right can unite. Many conservatives now look to him as a potential patron or broker ahead of the 2027 election. Nawrocki can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. However, he has no unifying mandate and his ability to bring together the right depends ultimately on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally non-partisan and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, Nawrocki lacks the party organisational levers needed to enforce messy backroom deals. Focus of government attacks The Tusk government knows that Nawrocki’s is now the most potent counterweight to its authority and potential unifier of the fragmented right, which is precisely why he has become the main focus of its attacks on the opposition. An essential element of this has been trying to portray Nawrocki’s more active presidency as destructive and undermining the unity of the Polish state. This forms a principal component of its broader “security” narrative, a calculated strategy to reframe political debate around the ongoing Russian threat. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk with hybrid threats against Poland, the government has portrayed presidential obstruction as undermining the country’s military readiness and ability to co-ordinate with its allies. Karol Nawrocki has sought to redefine Poland's presidency and become the figurehead of the right-wing opposition. So far, it is working, but questions remain over what his end goal is and whether these tactics will get him there, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/TNDRGGv2QT — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 22, 2025 The Tusk administration cites Nawrocki’s veto of legislation enabling Poland to access its €43.7 billion allocation from the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defence procurement initiative as an apparently perfect example of this, although the president argues that the loans saddle future generations with a huge, long-term debt and undermine Polish sovereignty. In fact, Nawrocki is fairly relaxed about the government’s attempts to portray his more active presidency as obstructive. Rather, he feels he needs to be assertive because that is precisely what those who voted for him expect: action and change, not passivity or compromise. Nawrocki’s 2025 presidential victory was based on a sharp critique of the Tusk administration and framed, and widely interpreted, as a vote of no confidence in the government’s performance. The president believes that this gives him a strong mandate to confront the ruling coalition across a wide range of issues and that the greater political risk lies in undermining the political momentum that his win created and appearing weak or inactive, rather than in the government’s counternarrative that he is a “blocking” president. A clash between the right-wing president and more liberal government over Poland's receipt of EU defence loans has sharpened polarisation and turbocharged the ruling coalition’s “Polexit” and security narratives, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/Iu7rcJfj5e — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 2, 2026 More broadly, Nawrocki is not too concerned about what the Warsaw opinion-forming elites say about him. His approach stands in stark contrast to earlier presidents, even right-wing ones such as Duda, who, conservative critics argue, paid excessive attention to elite and liberal media criticism and received no meaningful political reward or pay-off for doing so. Instead of seeking to present himself as a “president of all Poles” in the traditional, consensus-seeking sense, Nawrocki has deliberately prioritised appealing directly to his core electoral base: Polish voters living beyond the large urban agglomerations in smaller towns, rural areas, and the provinces. By maintaining an assertive, unapologetic style that resonates with this electorate’s sense of cultural and political marginalisation, Nawrocki has sought to consolidate that support rather than diluting it in pursuit of metropolitan elite approval. Poland’s most popular politician There have obviously been plenty of missteps along the way. One clear risk has been the sheer volume and sometimes seemingly indiscriminate nature of the legislative vetoes. While this has successfully blocked key elements of the government’s agenda and reinforced Nawrocki’s image as an assertive counterweight, it has also handed the Tusk administration a ready-made narrative that the president is simply an obstructive “veto machine”. A number of Nawrocki’s more high-profile vetoes, such as the cryptocurrency regulation law, have proved highly contentious. PM @donaldtusk called a classified meeting of parliament in a bid to persuade opposition MPs to overturn the president's veto of crypto-asset regulation, which Tusk said threatens national security. However, in a subsequent vote, the veto was upheld https://t.co/Vj0Zh9wxpH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 5, 2025 Moreover, some of the other constitutional instruments that he has sought to utilise have not been particularly successful or even proved counterproductive. These include attempts to introduce his own legislation or referendum initiatives that have been stymied in parliament, as well as his original idea of holding the government to account via the so-called “Cabinet Council”, a formal meeting of the Council of Ministers chaired by the president. Nonetheless, in general, Nawrocki’s strategy appears to have delivered political dividends for him. He can, for example, point to a number of foreign policy successes, particularly in cultivating close personal and strategic ties with the USA under the Trump administration and positioning himself as a significant actor on security issues. President @NawrockiKn has recorded the highest ever level of trust (54.8%, up 8.4pp since May) of any politician in the history of regular polling by @IBRiS_PL for @onetpl Foreign minister @sikorskiradek (42.6%) was second and PM @donaldtusk (38.1%) third https://t.co/POuUFR3Khk — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 26, 2026 At the same time, Nawrocki has asserted a greater degree of independence from PiS than Duda was ever able to achieve. This has been helped by the simple fact that PiS is now in opposition rather than in government, which reduces the formal and informal constraints that tied his predecessor more closely to the party. As a result, Nawrocki has emerged as Poland’s most popular politician, with consistently high approval ratings that set him apart from both the government and right-wing opposition party leaders. Challenges ahead There are clear challenges ahead for Nawrocki in the run-up to next year’s election and beyond. The first is how to respond to the argument that electing a right-wing government would concentrate excessive power in one side of the political spectrum. This is an awkward point for Nawrocki because he himself used a version of this argument during the 2025 presidential campaign, presenting his candidacy as a necessary check on the Tusk government. Opponents of the right will inevitably turn this logic against the broader conservative camp in the run-up to the 2027 election, claiming that the combination of a sympathetic president and a right-wing parliamentary majority risks the very imbalance Nawrocki once warned against. A second, related strategic challenge arises if a right-wing government does take office, and Nawrocki finds himself cohabiting with an ideologically and programmatically aligned administration rather than a hostile one. In that situation, he would still need to carve out a distinct and independent role for himself. The risk is falling into the trap that afflicted Duda during the years of PiS government: being widely perceived as little more than the government’s “notary” or a passive rubber stamp for its agenda. Maintaining personal authority, visibility, and a sense of autonomy, while avoiding conflict with an ideologically allied government, would demand a different style of presidency from the approach that has defined his first year. The very assertiveness and independence that have served him well in cohabitation with the Tusk government will prove harder to sustain if the political balance shifts after 2027. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” those among the right-wing opposition who have celebrated Sunday’s state election victory by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted. The rise of the AfD has been watched with concern by many in Poland due to the party’s attempts to downplay the significance of Germany’s Nazi history and its sympathy towards Russia. W Polsce tylko idioci albo zdrajcy mogą się cieszyć z tryumfu AfD w Niemczech. Trochę się ich nazbierało w Konfederacjach i PiS. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) September 6, 2026 The AfD came first by a large margin in Sunday’s election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, with preliminary results giving it around 44% of the vote. The centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz is trailing in second on around 17%. The victory continues a recent rise for the AfD, which also came first in the Thuringian state election in 2024, with 33% of the vote, and second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition party. The AfD’s latest result was welcomed by some figures from Poland’s right-wing and far-right opposition. “Germany is waking up,” tweeted Jacek Wilk, a former member of Poland’s parliament who is part of the radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party. Wg tej prognozy AfD brakuje już tylko 3 miejsc do samodzielnej większości Landtagu Saksonii-Anhalt. Niemcy się budzą. https://t.co/oHUIkYV1aQ — Jacek Wilk (@JacekWilkPL) September 6, 2026 Zdzisław Krasnodębski, a former deputy president of the European Parliament for the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s main opposition party, described the Saxony-Anhalt elections as “a great celebration of democracy”, pointing to the almost 80% turnout. Krasnodębski called on the minister-president of the German state, Sven Schulze of the CDU, to “end the anti-democratic ‘firewall’ [Brandmauer]” policy under which mainstream German parties refuse to form administrations with the AfD. However, other PiS figures expressed concern over the AfD’s victory, including former education minister and current MEP Anna Zalewska, who said that “the AfD is a powerful threat to European values and Polish-German cooperation”. Sven Schulze ist ein besonnener, konservativer Politiker (den ich persönlich aus dem Europäischen Parlament kenne). Er sollte einer Koalition mit der angeblich demokratischen, postkommunistischen „Linken“ nicht zustimmen. Er sollte vielmehr mit Merz’ Politik der… https://t.co/10rtEnO4yN — ZdzisławKrasnodębski (@ZdzKrasnodebski) September 6, 2026 On Sunday evening, Tusk also commented on social media. “In Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany. Quite a few of them have gathered in Confederation and PiS,” he wrote. Confederation is another far-right opposition group. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, who is from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, called those celebrating the AfD’s victory in Poland “a modern-day Targowica” – referring to a group of 18th-century Polish nobles who allied with Russia against the Polish national cause and are a symbol of treachery. Another government minister, Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, leader of KO’s coalition partner Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), pointed to the fact that one of the two parties that make up Confederation is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. “Neo-fascists aligned with Russia won the elections in Saxony [sic],” she wrote, misnaming the German state. “For Polish patriots, it was a defeat for the values ​​of our world. For Mentzen and half of Confederation, it was a victory for an ally.” Sławomir Mentzel is the leader of the New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja) party that makes up one of the two main factions in Confederation and which sits in the Europe of Sovereign Nations group alongside the AfD. Mentzen has, at the time of writing, not commented on the election result in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD’s growth has been watched with concern by many in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation in World War Two. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. Last year, Tusk also criticised remarks by billionaire Elon Musk at an AfD election rally, in which he urged Germans to “move beyond” their guilt over Nazi crimes. The Polish prime minister called them “ominous”, especially as they were delivered hours before the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further concern in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. On Sunday evening, responding to Tusk’s latest social media post, AfD MEP Tomasz Froelich, who holds both German and Polish citizenship, wrote: “Herr Tusk, eat a Snickers!” – a reference to an advertising campaign for the chocolate bar suggesting that people should eat one when they need to calm down. Late on Monday morning, a senior aide to right-wing Polish President Karol Nawrocki – who is aligned with the opposition and an opponent of Tusk’s government – told broadcaster Kanał Zero that “the AfD is pursuing a programme that is contrary to Poland’s interests”. “The AfD’s pro-Russian agenda, such as the proposal to lift sanctions against Russia, is dangerous and unacceptable from Poland’s perspective,” said Paweł Szeferneker, who is head of the president’s cabinet. However, he also argued that the AfD’s rise has been the result of a backlash against policies previously implemented by former German Chancellor Angela Merkel as well as by Tusk himself when he served as president of the European Council. 🗣️ @jprusinowski: "AfD i lokalne wybory w Saksonii – 45% prawie. World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague Castle to Celebrate Václav Havel With Four-Month Festival
World.content:
Prague Castle will host a four-month festival celebrating the legacy of Václav Havel, with theatre, film, music, design and public debates taking place from October through January.

The Havel ALIVE festival will mark what would have been Havel’s 90th birthday and explore the continued relevance of his ideas. Most events will be free.

One of the main highlights will be the Czech premiere of The Warning, an unfinished Havel play that remained hidden for almost 40 years. The manuscript was discovered by David Dušek among the papers of writer Zdeněk Urbánek.



The production has been prepared by Jiří Havelka, artistic director of Dejvické Theatre, and will feature actors Martin Myšička and Ivan Trojan. The theatre will also present We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here at Prague Castle’s Riding Hall.

The festival will also focus on Havel’s influence on Czech design. In cooperation with Designblok, Prague Castle will present Design for Václav Havel, featuring objects connected with his presidency, including Bořek Šípek’s Olga chair, original glass pieces and Castle Guard uniforms designed by Theodor Pištěk.

For the first time, the exhibition will also show the entire presidential office, including Havel’s library. It will open during Designblok on October 7 and remain at the Riding Hall from October 21 to January 17.

Music and dance will feature prominently as well. On November 18, students and teachers from the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague will present a gala evening directed by Magdalena Švecová. Other performances will draw on Havel’s writings, his Anticodes poetry collection, his relationship with the underground music scene and the events of November 1989.

The programme will also include screenings of Citizen Havel and Leaving, a musical evening led by Pavel Klusák, and discussions about art, architecture, freedom and democracy.

Selected festival events

October 4 — Guided tours of Lány Chateau and Prague Castle focused on Havel’s presidency. Free.

October 7 — Opening of Design for Václav Havel at the Prague Castle Riding Hall.

October 8 — Pavel Klusák’s All the President’s Rockers: Václav Havel & Music. Free.

October 14 — Citizen Havel screening followed by a discussion. Free.

October 22 — Thinking Havel Live: Democracy and the Future of Europe. Free.

November 4 — Dejvické Theatre presents We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 5–6 — Czech premieres of Havel’s The Warning. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 12 — Thinking Havel: Between the Individual and the System. Free.

November 18 — Havel: Inspiration for a New Generation, a gala evening at the Prague Castle Riding Hall from 7 p.m. Tickets CZK 250.

November 26 — Lecture on Havel’s designer and architect Bořek Šípek at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 3 — Thinking Havel: Politics and Spiritual Values, a debate with Alice Koubová, Milena Bartlová and Petr Kratochvíl at the Riding Hall from 6 p.m. Free.

December 8 — Literature at the Castle: Writing Havel, a lecture at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 15 — Screening of Leaving, followed by a discussion with Dagmar Havlová and other guests at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 6 p.m. Free.

January 14 — Ceremonial presentation of the Jindřich Chalupecký Award 2027 at Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Airport to Expand Border Control at Terminal 1
World.content:
Prague Airport is expanding and modernising the border control area for arriving passengers at Terminal 1 to increase capacity and reduce waiting times.

The project will add five new passport control desks and four EasyGoGate (EGG) self-service gates for eligible European passport holders.

The work is scheduled to begin in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by the end of April 2027.



The expansion comes as Prague Airport faces increased pressure at border control, particularly during peak hours. The introduction of the European Entry/Exit System (EES) in October 2025 has added to the workload at the airport.

The project will also enlarge the waiting area before passport control and upgrade the ventilation system throughout the border control area.

The total investment is estimated at CZK 290 million, including construction, design and engineering work, technical supervision and safety coordination. The new passport control equipment will be supplied and installed by the Police of the Czech Republic.

Police representatives said the changes are also intended to strengthen security at the Schengen Area’s external border while ensuring the new facilities meet current security and legal requirements.

Some queues and restrictions are expected

The renovation will take place in stages to limit disruption to airport operations. However, passengers may encounter temporary restrictions at passport control and longer queues during some phases of the work.

At one stage, three passport control desks will be temporarily closed. This phase will be scheduled during a period of lower passenger traffic.

EU citizens will continue to be able to use the passport control desks and EGG self-service gates designated for European passport holders. They are not required to register through the EES.

During the other stages of construction, restrictions will mainly affect the area immediately before passport control. Passenger routes will be adjusted around the construction zones, while the overall flow through border control will remain unchanged.

World.title: Prague Bids to Host 2029 European Figure Skating Championships
World.content:
Prague is preparing a bid to host the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships, with the O2 Arena expected to serve as the main venue if the Czech capital wins the right to stage the competition.

Prague City Council approved the candidacy on Monday following an approach from the Czech Figure Skating Union.

The proposal comes several months after Prague hosted the 2026 World Figure Skating Championships in March.



City councilor for education and sports Antonín Klecanda (STAN) said the success of that event helped encourage the city to pursue another major international competition.

“The response was very positive, and other countries asked whether another event of this kind could be held in Prague,” Klecanda said on Monday. “We reached an agreement, and today we approved our candidacy to host the European Figure Skating Championship in 2029.”

The 2026 World Championships attracted a record number of spectators for a figure skating world championship, according to Klecanda. He also said international visitors had responded positively to Prague’s role as host city.

The city has not yet determined when the 2029 championship would take place. The date will be discussed at a later stage, while Prague currently expects the competitions to be staged at the O2 Arena.

The financial impact of hosting the championships has not yet been calculated. The city would have to cover not only the direct costs of organizing the competition but also additional expenses linked to public services, including increased public transport capacity, emergency services and police deployment.

Klecanda said these costs could reach tens of millions of Czech crowns. He argued, however, that part of the expenditure could be offset by additional tax revenue generated by the event, while the championship would also strengthen Prague’s international profile.

The final decision on the host city for the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships has yet to be made.

World.title: Pickles Prague Festival: A Celebration of Pickled and Fermented Vegetables
World.content:
The Pickles Prague Festival will take place on September 19-20 at the Prague Exhibition Grounds, bringing together producers, food enthusiasts and visitors interested in pickled and fermented vegetables.

The festival will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and will focus on the wide variety of vegetables preserved through pickling and fermentation.

More info here.

Visitors can expect everything from traditional pickled cucumbers, peppers and beets to less familiar varieties from the Czech Republic and abroad.

Alongside tastings and opportunities to buy pickled products, the programme will include workshops and educational talks covering pickling techniques, fermentation, the nutritional aspects of fermented vegetables and the role of preserved foods in different culinary traditions.



The event will also feature live music throughout the day, while a dedicated children’s area will offer activities for younger visitors, making the festival suitable for families as well.

Admission to the Pickles Prague Festival is free.

World.title: Czech Politicians Divided Over AfD Victory in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has secured a major victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, prompting different reactions from Czech politicians.

While some have congratulated the party and called for dialogue with its leaders, others have warned that the result reflects the growing strength of political extremism.

The result has also renewed debate in the Czech Republic over migration, security and how mainstream parties should respond to the AfD.



Martin Kupka, chairman of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS), described the result as a warning for Europe. He said democratic parties could not counter extremist movements simply by labeling them or ignoring issues that concern voters.

“Democratic parties must offer clear solutions: a tough migration policy, security, less regulation and no populist waste of public money,” Kupka said.

He added that the Czech Republic should avoid following the same political path.

Vít Rakušan, leader of the Mayors and Independents (STAN), similarly said the election should serve as a lesson for Czech politicians.

According to Rakušan, mainstream democratic parties risk losing voters when they leave issues such as migration and social problems to populist movements.

Rather than focusing solely on the AfD’s success, he said, democratic parties should develop practical and sustainable responses to issues that voters consider important.

Former Prime Minister Petr Fiala offered one of the strongest warnings. In a post on social media, the ODS politician called the result a “political earthquake” and said the AfD’s success could not be explained solely by the failure of mainstream democratic parties to address voters’ concerns.

Fiala argued that the reasons were more complex than economic dissatisfaction alone. “The causes are deeper and far from just economic,” he wrote.

The response from the Czech government’s current Foreign Minister Petr Macinka was more cautious. Macinka said the next steps by the AfD and Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) would be particularly significant.

He said it would be important to see how the winning party uses its strong mandate and how the CDU responds to the result.

Tomio Okamura, chairman of the Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party and speaker of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, took a more positive view of the AfD’s performance.

He congratulated the party and said the election showed that voters were dissatisfied with the policies of Germany’s established parties, particularly the CDU.

“The people of the former East Germany have made it clear that they no longer want this policy to continue,” Okamura said in an interview with Czech Television.

Okamura also rejected criticism based on the AfD’s classification as a far-right party. He questioned the credibility of reports concerning extremism and pointed to similar accusations involving his own SPD.

Radek Vondráček of the ANO movement also called for a different approach to the AfD. Speaking to Czech Television, the chairman of the Chamber of Deputies’ foreign affairs committee said the election had given the party a clear mandate and expressed hope that it would be able to form a stable government.

“I hope that the time for dialogue is coming, when citizens will receive some appropriate result for what they have chosen,” Vondráček said.

World.title: Boris Brejcha Brings his High-Tech Minimal Show to Prague in October
World.content:
One of the world’s most sought-after producers and the king of the high-tech minimal genre, German DJ Boris Brejcha, is returning to the Czech Republic.

As part of his Reflections world tour, he will perform at Prague’s O2 Arena on Friday, October 2, 2026. For electronic music fans, one of the highlights of the season.

Boris Brejcha, whose identity is inextricably linked to a mysterious Venetian mask, promises a show full of spectacular lighting and a breathtaking visual spectacle.

He is recognized worldwide as a creator and pioneer of the “high-tech minimal” genre. The concert will be the artist’s only performance in the Czech Republic.

Official ticket sales have already begun. Tickets are available exclusively through the official Ticketmaster and Ticketportal sales networks.

Where did the iconic mask come from?

At the age of six, Brejcha suffered serious injuries in a plane crash. He sustained severe burns to his face and body. Music became his escape, and he began producing it on his own at the age of twelve.

He launched his official career in 2006. He made his debut at the Universo Paralello festival in Brazil, where he was inspired by the local carnival and chose his iconic Joker mask, which has become an integral part of his image.

Brejcha is best known as a creator and pioneer of high-tech minimal—a musical genre that combines electronic music with elements of techno, house, and trance, featuring distinctive melodies. He plays exclusively his own original music.

“Hello, Prague! Returning to your beautiful city is always a special experience for me. This time, I’m bringing the ‘Reflections’ show to the O2 Arena, which will feature a unique visual stage and my exclusive extended set. I’m already looking forward to the amazing atmosphere we’ll create together in the arena. It’ll be a night we’ll never forget. See you there,” says Boris Brejcha.

The unique atmosphere will be further enhanced by artistic support from Brejcha’s own label, FCKNG SERIOUS.

World.title: Langdon Appears in Prague! Netflix Presents New Series Based on Dan Brown
World.content:
Netflix has begun filming its new series based on Dan Brown’s The Secret of Secrets, bringing Harvard symbologist Robert Langdon back to Prague.

The production officially started in the Czech capital this week, with Netflix releasing a first look at Morgan Spector as Langdon and Rebecca Hall as scientist Katherine Solomon. The series is currently untitled and does not yet have a release date.



Netflix has now added five more actors to the production. Mamoudou Athie will appear as Michael Harris, Ben Levi Ross as Alex Conan, Anamaria Marinca as Dr. Gessner, Richard Sammel as Karl Muller and Elena Saurel as Susan Housemore.

The series is being developed by Carlton Cuse, who co-created Lost and later worked on Jack Ryan, Locke & Key, Bates Motel and Five Days at Memorial. Cuse serves as co-creator, showrunner, writer and executive producer. Emma Forman is also an executive producer for Genre Arts, alongside Cuse and Brown.

Brown is involved in the project as a co-writer and executive producer.

The novel takes Langdon through several recognizable parts of Prague, including Charles Bridge and the Klementinum, as he searches for answers following Solomon’s disappearance. Netflix says the television adaptation will combine scientific ideas, historical mysteries and mystical elements.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dan Brown (@authordanbrown)

The Secret of Secrets was published in September 2025 and became the latest installment in Brown’s Robert Langdon series. The book was released simultaneously in multiple countries, including the Czech Republic, and Prague is closely tied to its plot.

The Czech Republic is expected to play a significant role in the new television production. Prague has previously served as a filming location for a wide range of international productions, making the city a familiar setting for foreign film and television crews.

The arrival of the Netflix series could also have an impact beyond the production industry. Czech travel companies and Argo, the publisher of Brown’s books in Czech, have previously pointed to the potential for two waves of tourism connected with the project: first from readers discovering the novel and later from viewers of the television adaptation.

World.title: Prague Planetarium to Become a Concert Venue Under the Stars
World.content:
The Prague Planetarium in Stromovka will host a new series of chamber concerts combining live music with projections of the universe from September 2026.

Called Niche Nites, the series will feature 10 concerts between September 2026 and June 2027. Each performance will be accompanied by visuals projected across the planetarium’s 22-metre-wide dome, with the imagery responding to the music in real time.



The programme will take place on the final weekend of each month. Rather than staging repeated performances, each musician or group will appear at the planetarium only once, giving every concert its own programme and visual design.

The series will open on September 25 with cellist Terezie Kovalová, whose work combines classical music with pop, alternative and electronic influences.

Other performers confirmed for the programme include guitarist and composer Michal Pavlíček, who will appear with singer Bára Basiková, pianist and composer Beata Hlavenková, and singer-songwriter Lenka Dusilová. Further names will be announced by the organisers in the coming months.

Producer and dramaturg Michala Komrsková said the project is intended to present established Czech musicians in a more intimate setting than the large concert halls where they usually perform.

The planetarium’s technology will play a central role. Its dome is fitted with an LED system containing millions of diodes, allowing large-scale visual sequences to accompany the performances. The imagery will be prepared specifically for each concert rather than using a single projection throughout the series.

More recently, the planetarium was used during this year’s Spectaculare festival, which combined music by composer Rafael Anton Irisarri with visual work by Czech artists Dalibor Cée and Alex J. Jindrák.

World.title: Danube falls to historic low water levels in Budapest: just 1 centimetre
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water-level gauges showing just 1 centimetre on Tuesday, according to Időkép.

The Danube’s water level is at its lowest ever in Budapest

The reading is significantly lower than the levels recorded during the severe drought conditions earlier in the summer. In July, the Danube had already broken the previous negative record set in 2018, when the water authority measured a level of 27 centimetres at the end of the month, reports Időkép.

The river continued to recede throughout August, falling by almost another 20 centimetres. By Tuesday, the water level had dropped to just 1 centimetre. The exceptionally low level is creating serious difficulties for river navigation and can also pose a direct safety risk to vessels, as obstacles normally hidden beneath the surface become exposed or much easier to encounter.

Some of the consequences of the unusually low water level have already become visible elsewhere along the Danube. Near Baja, a shipwreck emerged from the riverbed to such an extent that it could reportedly be walked around. In Budapest, the remains of the former Ferenc József Bridge, which sank near what is now the Liberty Bridge, also became clearly visible.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

There might be light at the end of the tunnel

Water management experts attribute the extreme conditions to prolonged rainfall shortages and exceptionally dry conditions across the Danube’s catchment area. There could, however, be some relief in sight. A weather front is expected to bring rain to the Danube basin on Wednesday and reach Hungary by the evening. The rainfall could lead to a rise in the river’s water level.

The record low water levels show how Hungary, and all of Europe has become the victim of the all-summer-long dry conditions, with consequences extending beyond the river itself to navigation and water safety.

World.title: Remarkable: Remains of Ice Age animal found in Hungary’s River Tisza
World.content:
An extraordinary prehistoric discovery has been made in River Tisza, in Hungary, where water management workers found what is believed to be the skull of a cave bear that lived during the Ice Age.

Workers first thought they found an old anchor

Staff from the Middle Tisza District Water Directorate (Kötivizig) spotted the object while kayaking between Szolnok and Kisköre. Initially, they thought the object protruding from the riverbed might be an old anchor.

A closer inspection, however, revealed the remains of a large animal. Around three-quarters of the find was buried in the gravel bed, from which the workers were able to recover it thanks to the Tisza’s low water level.

The remains were taken to the Damjanich János Museum in Szolnok, where experts conducted an initial examination. Their preliminary assessment is that the find is probably the skull of an Ice Age cave bear.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What to know about cave bears?

Cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) lived across much of Europe during the Pleistocene and became extinct thousands of years ago. Their remains are often associated with caves, where the animals sought shelter and hibernated.

The exact age of the newly discovered skull has yet to be established. Museum specialists will carry out further examinations to determine when the animal lived. The discovery demonstrates how falling water levels can expose objects and remains that have been hidden beneath river sediments for centuries or even millennia.

This is how cave bears used to looked like. Illustration. Photo: Sergiodlarosa/Wikimedia Commons

World.title: Russian senator claims Hungary was forced to “prove its loyalty” to Brussels
World.content:
Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats accused of carrying out activities incompatible with diplomatic status, in a move that could mark a significant change in Budapest’s approach to Russian intelligence operations. Moscow has already warned of a “tough and painful” response. The deputy speaker of Russia’s upper house of parliament said that the decision was an unfriendly and confrontational act.

Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomatic personnel to leave the country after authorities determined that they had engaged in activities deemed unacceptable under the Vienna Convention.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the decision on Tuesday, saying the Foreign Ministry had informed Russia’s ambassador in Budapest that Hungarian authorities had identified activities by 10 members of the Russian diplomatic mission that were incompatible with their diplomatic status.

“The decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” Orbán said, while stressing that the move does not amount to a severing of diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary, she added, intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with Moscow based on mutual respect and compliance with international rules.

Expert: The diplomats were Russian intelligence officers

According to Russia expert András Rácz, the wording used by the Hungarian government strongly indicates that the 10 individuals were actually Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover. Rácz, deputy director-general responsible for research and academic affairs at the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, told MTI that the phrase “activities incompatible with diplomatic status” traditionally refers to espionage.

In practical terms, he said, Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats who were allegedly working as intelligence officers under diplomatic cover in Budapest.

The scale of the move is particularly significant. According to Rácz, more than 600 Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover have been expelled from EU member states since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Until now, Hungary had been the only EU member state not to carry out such a large-scale expulsion. Rácz therefore described the decision as Hungary effectively joining its EU and NATO allies in efforts to reduce Russia’s intelligence capabilities across the bloc.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Why has Hungary acted now?

The timing of the expulsions is particularly noteworthy given Hungary’s historically close relationship with Moscow under the previous Orbán government.

Rácz said he could not determine precisely why Budapest had chosen this particular moment to act. However, he argued that the decision represents a significant shift in Hungary’s position towards Russian intelligence activities. He also pointed out that, according to official Foreign Ministry figures, 47 Russian diplomats are currently accredited in Hungary, accompanied by 41 spouses.

It is not publicly known how many of the remaining diplomats are connected to Russian intelligence services. However, Rácz noted that a Russian investigative outlet recently identified 15 of the 47 Russian diplomats in Budapest as having links to various Russian intelligence agencies based on publicly available information.

He added that while there had been some “quiet expulsions” of Russian intelligence personnel during the previous Hungarian government, there had never before been a publicly announced expulsion on this scale.

Budapest sends a message to its Western allies

The decision could have implications beyond Hungary’s bilateral relationship with Russia. Rácz argued that Russian intelligence officers based in Hungary can potentially operate elsewhere in the Schengen Area, making their presence a security concern for Hungary’s allies as well. He pointed to Prague as a previous example of how Russian diplomats could use one European capital as a base for intelligence operations in neighbouring countries.

According to the expert, Russian intelligence personnel operating from Budapest have similarly been able to conduct operations elsewhere in the Schengen Area and in Balkan countries outside the zone.

For this reason, Rácz described Hungary’s decision as a long-overdue step towards its EU and NATO partners. He argued that Hungary’s failure to expel such personnel over the previous four and a half years had potentially harmed the security interests of its allies.

Moscow threatens retaliation

Russia has responded angrily to the expulsions. Konstantin Kosachev, deputy speaker of Russia’s upper house of parliament, told the RIA Novosti news agency that the decision was an unfriendly and confrontational act. He argued that the simultaneous expulsion of 10 diplomats was “many times more unfriendly” and amounted to an open challenge to Moscow. Russia, he said, would respond accordingly.

Kosachev also claimed that the decision had been driven by Brussels, arguing that the “post-Orbán” Hungary had been pressured to demonstrate its loyalty to what he described as the anti-Russian policies of the EU and NATO.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova likewise warned that Moscow would deliver a “tough and painful response”, referring to what she called the “Russophobic lobby” in Budapest. A reciprocal move is therefore widely expected, with Rácz saying Russia is almost certain to respond proportionally by expelling Hungarian diplomats.

World.title: Hungary waves goodbye to historical county titles, and reintroduces modern forms
World.content:
Hungary’s Parliament has voted to restore the terms “county” and “government commissioner”, reversing the controversial renaming of counties and government commissioners introduced by Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz government in 2022.

Historical titles are gone

The Tisza-majority Parliament approved the legislation on Tuesday with 134 votes in favour and 52 against. Fidesz, the Christian Democrats (KDNP) and Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) voted against the proposal. Under the changes, Hungary’s vármegyék (literally translated to castle counties) will once again officially be known as megyék, while főispáns (lord lieutenants) will again be referred to as government commissioners.

The 2022 terminology was introduced as part of the 11th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law. The Fidesz government argued at the time that restoring the historical term vármegye would preserve the constitutional traditions of Hungary’s thousand-year statehood, strengthen national unity and reinforce the national character of Hungarian democracy.

Government cites clarity and practicality

The newly adopted legislation takes a different approach, stressing practical and legal considerations. According to the proposal, abandoning the terms vármegye and főispán will make the administrative system more transparent and easier to understand, while promoting consistent application of the law.

The changes are primarily terminological and technical. They do not alter the powers or responsibilities of the affected authorities, nor do they change the substance of administrative, regulatory or local-government relationships. The law will enter into force on the day after its promulgation, while amendments changing the terminology in other legislation will take effect on 1 October.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

From historic tradition to a controversial revival

The term vármegye has deep roots in Hungarian history. It was used for a fundamental administrative unit from the foundation of the Hungarian state until 1949, although the county system developed gradually over several centuries. The system underwent major reforms in the late 19th century, including a significant administrative restructuring between 1876 and 1881.

County boundaries changed repeatedly, including before the Treaty of Trianon. The historical name survived these changes and remained in use after Trianon and during the years following the Second World War. It was officially replaced by megye in 1949, when Hungary adopted a new constitution modelled on the Soviet system.

Stay up-do-date: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat

Lázár once opposed the name change

Interestingly, János Lázár, who was a senior minister in Orbán’s fifth government, voted in favour of the 2022 renaming despite having previously criticised the idea. When the change was considered during the drafting of the Fundamental Law in 2011, Lázár argued that the historical term carried negative associations for many Hungarians, particularly those whose families had worked as servants or labourers.

He eventually supported the 2022 change, saying he did so because it formed part of the constitutional amendment before Parliament. The latest vote now reverses that decision, bringing Hungary’s official administrative terminology back to the terms used between 1949 and 2022.

World.title: New documents reveal why Orbán minister Lázár kept his Switzerland trip a secret for 13 years
World.content:
After more than 13 years, new documents have shed light on one of the longest-running mysteries surrounding Hungarian politician János Lázár: what he was doing in Zurich on 22 and 23 March 2013. The details were revealed by investigative outlet Direkt36, which obtained an internal government document from the Tisza government, which took office this spring.

Newly revealed documents show what János Lázár was doing in 2013

According to the document, Lázár, who was then heading the Prime Minister’s Office as a state secretary, met a person identified as “Prof. Mangold” in Zurich to discuss potential cooperation between the Hungarian government and Western European companies.

Direkt36 says the name almost certainly refers to Klaus Mangold, a prominent German businessman with extensive contacts in European and Russian business circles. Mangold established links with the Hungarian government in the early 2010s and later worked as an adviser to Viktor Orbán’s governments. The newly released report was prepared by his consultancy, Mangold Consulting GmbH.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Rothschild, SAP and government communications

The report says Lázár and Mangold discussed three main areas. The first was whether Rothschild could act as an “independent adviser” to the Hungarian government, including assessing the country’s financial risks and advising on the banking sector. A meeting involving then Economy Minister Mihály Varga and newly appointed central bank governor György Matolcsy was reportedly planned, with Orbán himself potentially attending part of the meeting.

The pair also discussed cooperation with business software giant SAP, particularly in financial administration and healthcare. The third topic was the Hungarian government’s marketing strategy. The report mentions German consultancy firms Schuppner and CNC, which Mangold was said to know well and which could advise on responding to critical media. A joint brainstorming session was reportedly proposed.

Rothschild later did work for the Orbán government, including producing a report during the European Union’s investigation into the Paks II nuclear project. The report concluded that the investment could be economically viable under market conditions. Rothschild also later participated in the creation of the partly state-owned MBH Bank.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat

A mystery that began with expensive hotel bills

The Zurich trip had attracted attention because of its unusually high costs. Lázár and his companion spent HUF 189,000 on one night’s accommodation in Zurich. Two other trips also raised questions: HUF 596,000 for one night in Milan and HUF 920,000 for two nights in England.

At the time, Lázár’s office refused to reveal the purpose of the trips, citing national security concerns. Lázár was also responsible for Hungary’s foreign intelligence service. Journalist András Pethő, then working for Origo, sued for access to the information. The case became politically explosive and contributed to pressure on Origo’s editorial team. Editor-in-chief Gergő Sáling was later dismissed, prompting many journalists, including Pethő, to leave the outlet.

Lázár eventually repaid the travel expenses, but the purpose of the Zurich meeting remained secret for years. The former minister declined to comment to Direkt36. Mangold’s consultancy also refused media questions, while SAP said it was unaware of any cooperation linked to the meeting. Rothschild and CNC did not respond.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat
World.content:
Hungary has ordered 10 employees of the Russian Embassy in Budapest to leave the country, saying their activities were incompatible with the conduct expected of diplomats under the Vienna Convention. A spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry said Budapest should expect a “harsh and painful response”.

FM Orbán announces letting go of 10 embassy employees

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the decision, describing it as unprecedented in scale. She said the relevant official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had informed Russia’s ambassador to Budapest of the decision on her instructions. According to Orbán, the Hungarian authorities assessed that the 10 representatives had engaged in activities that were not acceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention.

“The decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” the minister said. She stressed, however, that the move does not mean a break in diplomatic relations with the Kremlin. Hungary intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with Moscow, provided that both sides respect one another and comply with international rules.

UPDATE: Russia’s threat

Russia will respond to Hungary’s expulsion of ten Russian diplomats, according to the Russian state news agency TASS, citing a statement from the Russian Foreign Ministry. Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry, promised a “harsh and painful response.”

“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” she told TASS.

A tougher approach towards Moscow

The expulsions mark a notably tougher public response towards Russian diplomatic activity than previous measures taken by Hungary. Péter Magyar also raised the announcement in Parliament, reading out Orbán’s statement and saying that a Tisza government would protect Hungary’s sovereignty, reports Telex.

Anita Orbán has adopted a more distant diplomatic approach towards Russia than her predecessor, Péter Szijjártó, according to the supplied sources. On 13 May, shortly after taking office, she summoned Russia’s ambassador following a Russian drone attack against Transcarpathia. Szijjártó had last summoned a Russian diplomat in February 2022. The latest move also follows reports of a quieter expulsion of a Russian intelligence officer earlier this year.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Kremlin intelligence officer reportedly expelled in May

VSquare reported in May that Artur Sushkov, allegedly a Russian intelligence officer operating under diplomatic cover at the Embassy in Budapest, left Hungary on 4 May. According to the report, Hungary’s Constitutional Protection Office had established that Sushkov had spent years collecting information on institutions close to the Hungarian government. VSquare’s government sources claimed that Hungarian intelligence had recommended his expulsion as early as February, but that the previous Orbán government had blocked the proposal.

Stay up-to-date: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine

2018 Skripal case provides a different precedent

Hungary also expelled a Russian diplomat in 2018 following the poisoning of former Kremlin intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Britain. However, a subsequent Direkt36 investigation suggested that Budapest deliberately handled the expulsion in a way that would minimise damage to its close relationship with Moscow.

Diplomatic sources reportedly said the expelled Russian was a GRU military intelligence officer whose posting was due to end within months. The latest decision is considerably larger in scale, as the 10 embassy employees have now been ordered to leave Hungary. Despite this, Budapest insists that diplomatic relations with Moscow will continue, with the government presenting the expulsions as a measure to protect Hungary’s security and sovereignty rather than a move towards severing ties with Russia.
