World.title: Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?
World.content:
The panel discussion starting at 12:30 pm on September 10 brings together stakeholders to identify safety gaps and develop community-led solutions to protect children

MANILA, Philippines – Concerned about your child’s safety and how you can ensure a more secure environment for them?

Watch the live panel discussion as Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH launches “Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?” This will be streamed on Rappler’s YouTube channel live from the Rappler Civic Hub in Pasig City on Thursday, September 10.

Organized in partnership with CyberGuardiansPH and Mental Health Youth Hub, this pilot initiative tackles rising school violence and digital risks by turning community discussions into concrete, multisectoral solutions.

Rappler head of community Pia Ranada moderates the conversation with key decision-makers and child protection advocates:

Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte shares local government strategies on community governance, child protection policies, and campus safety.

Police Capt. Wallen Arancillo, spokesperson for the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group, addresses online grooming, cyberbullying, and digital protection in off-campus hotspots.

Dr. Princess Gairanod, child protection specialist from the Philippine Pediatric Society, discusses student mental health, psychosocial care, and health safeguarding protocols.

After the panel discussion and Q and A, participants joining on-site can take part in a hands-on workshop to collectively develop concrete and actionable responses to threats facing children and schools across four Civic Circles:

Campus security and physical safety

Psychosocial care and mental health

Policy, governance, and accountability

Digital safety and off-campus hotspots

The solutions generated during the session may be featured on Rappler to encourage a broader discussion and possible adaptation by local governments, schools, families, and communities.

Bookmark this page to watch Rappler’s live broadcast.

To join the conversation, download the Rappler App on iOS or Android, tap the Chat tab, and enter the Education chat room while watching the stream. – Rappler.com

World.title: IN CHARTS: Literacy of Filipino students in Grades 1 to 3
World.content:
FIRST DAY. Students of Navarro Elementary School in General Trias City, Cavite, attend the first day of classes on June 8, 2026.

Around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still did not have proficient reading skills by the end of SY 2025-2026, the Department of Education's assessment shows

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines faces a daunting challenge to fix the decades-long learning crisis in the country, starting with literacy in children’s early years of schooling.

Rappler checked the Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment (CRLA) results from the Department of Education (DepEd) for school year (SY) 2025-2026 to better understand the reading profiles of Key Stage 1 learners, or students in Grades 1 to 3. The data sets were accessed in early June.

Reflected in the data were literacy rates for mother tongue in Grade 1, Filipino in Grade 2, and English in Grade 3. Under the enhanced K to 10 curriculum, the DepEd offers English and Filipino starting Grade 2.

The DepEd’s curriculum standards also suggest that by the end of Grade 3, students are “becoming literate and increasingly fluent” in the use of English, while using their mother tongue to understand and express “familiar and developmentally appropriate texts” or discuss content in various learning areas.

Here are some data visualizations of the literacy of Grades 1 to 3 pupils in the Philippines:

How many struggling readers are there?

Struggling readers are students assessed to be in low reading profiles. In terms of CRLA results, these are pupils in Grades 1 to 3 who were classified as emerging, broken down into lower or higher emergent.

By the end of SY 2025-2026, there were around 519,000 students from Grades 1 to 3 who struggled with reading. That’s 10% of all assessed students in Key Stage 1.

But the CRLA results also revealed that around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still cannot read “at grade level” or at the standard expected for their current grade.

By 2028, the Philippines is targeting 75% of Key Stage 1 learners to be reading at grade level, according to the National Education Plan 2026-2035, which was introduced by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) in January. (READ: [ANALYSIS] What does ‘at least nearly proficient’ mean in Philippine education?)

Where are the struggling readers?

Among the regions, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has the highest percentage of struggling readers.

Focusing at the end of Key Stage 1, over 22% of Grade 3 pupils in BARMM remain at low proficiency in literacy.

In its January report, EDCOM 2 stressed that children should be literate by the end of Grade 3 so they do not fall behind in later stages of schooling.

Senior technical officials of BARMM and various national government agencies are already preparing for the first meeting of the newly formed Bangsamoro Education Coordination Forum (BECF).

The BECF, a coordinating mechanism between the national and Bangsamoro governments, will attempt to address issues in early childhood care and development, curriculum and learning, learner support, governance and finance, teacher education, and higher and technical-vocational education in the autonomous region.

You can also check the percentage of struggling Grade 3 readers per schools division office in the table below.

Did Key Stage 1 learners show improvement in reading?

There are improvements seen in the reading profiles of Grades 1 to 3 pupils, as data showed decreases in the share of struggling readers by the end of SY 2025-2026.

Still, half of the students remain below the proficient level.

That trend is seen throughout the Philippine basic education system.

In its analysis, EDCOM 2 found that while the results show “consistent improvement” within SY 2025-2026, around 18% or 3 million out of 16.5 million students remain in non-proficient reading levels. (READ: Most Grade 11 students struggle with reading. What now?)

The assessment was done after the first full year of implementation of the DepEd’s Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program.

The DepEd was given P8.9 billion for the initiative in 2026. However, for next year, the Department of Budget and Management did not include an allocation for the ARAL Program in the proposed budget.

The ball is with Congress as Education Secretary Sonny Angara appealed for an additional budget to fund the ARAL Program, as well as beef up various aspects of the sector.

Funding for basic education reached P1 trillion in 2026. Will the government push to at least keep the education budget at this level to address the country’s learning crisis? – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines’ reading, math, science scores improve in 2025 PISA
World.content:
BACK TO SCHOOL. Students of Carmona National High School in Carmona City, Cavite, attend the opening of academic year 2024-2025 on July 29, 2024.

The Department of Education says the Philippines’ ‘strongest PISA performance’ to date ‘should be seen as a starting point,’ with much more to be done

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ performance in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) improved in 2025, with the country climbing out of the bottom 10 in the subjects covered.

The Philippines ranked 72nd out of 90 countries in reading, 74th out of 90 countries in mathematics, and 77th out of 91 countries in science, according to the 2025 PISA results released on Tuesday, September 8.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which conducts the test, found that Filipino students had average scores of 373 in science (up by 17 points from the previous PISA edition), 371 in mathematics (up by 16 points), and 367 in reading (up by 20 points).

The Department of Education (DepEd) noted that this is the Philippines’ “strongest PISA performance” to date since the country first joined the global assessment in 2018 and again in 2022, where it saw dismal results both times.

Although an improvement, it “should be seen as a starting point” and “highlights the work that remains,” added the DepEd.

“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system. But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a press release.

“We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”

The Second Congressional Commission on Education said the task now is to sustain the momentum, stressing that education reforms require “consistency of purpose, continuity in implementation, and the commitment of the entire country.”

In 2018, the Philippines was ranked lowest in reading, and second to the last in science and mathematics. Four years after that, the Philippines was still among the bottom 10.

Play Video

The average scores among OECD countries for 2025 were 482 in science, 463 in mathematics, and 461 in reading.

“PISA 2025 recorded the lowest OECD-average performance observed so far in science, reading, and mathematics,” the international group said. “Reading has declined after peaking around 2012, while science has declined more gradually over the past decade, and mathematics has fallen especially sharply after 2018.”

Globally, the Chinese jurisdictions of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, along with Singapore, were the highest performers across science, mathematics, and reading in 2025.

Also among the top 10 performing education systems in all three subjects were Estonia, Japan, Korea, Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, and the United Kingdom.

According to the DepEd, around 8,000 15-year-old students from 208 schools in the Philippines took part in PISA 2025 through a computer-based assessment. Most of the participating schools were regular public schools, but there were also public science-oriented schools and private schools. – Rappler.com

World.title: As peso lingers at record-low P62, what does it mean for Filipinos?
World.content:
The Philippine peso has never been this weak. Here's how that could affect everything from fuel prices to remittances.

The Philippine peso has pushed deeper into territory it had never entered before.

For the first time in history, the currency sank past P62 to the US dollar on August 28, closing at a then-record low of P62.265. The peso then touched an unprecedented P62.775 intraday on Monday, September 7, before closing slightly stronger at P62.586.

On Tuesday, September 8, it weakened again to a fresh record-low closing rate of P62.625 to $1.

The peso’s slide began in March 2026, when it sank to an all-time low of P60 to the dollar. A month later, it sank to an all-time low again, breaking past P61. Now, it has sunk to an all-time low yet again, this time beyond P62.

So what does a peso sinking deeper into record-low territory actually mean for the economy?

A weaker peso can make its way to fuel pump prices and grocery checkouts, raise costs for businesses, complicate the central bank’s fight against inflation, and weigh on the Philippines’ economic growth.

For OFW families, a weaker peso might provide some relief since they get more pesos for every dollar sent home. But that gain is partly eroded if the same currency weakness pushes up the cost of fuel, food, transport, and other everyday expenses anyway.

Currency depreciation hits the Philippines particularly hard because it is a country of imports – bringing in large amounts of fuel, food, machinery, raw materials, and other goods all priced and paid for in dollars.

As the peso weakens, Philippine importers have to spend more pesos to pay for exactly the same dollar-priced shipment. Companies can absorb some of that increase through lower profit margins, but they’re more likely to pass the cost on to consumers.

More expensive fuel

Fuel is one of the clearest examples of how quickly the exchange rate can ripple through the economy.

At the Department of Energy’s September 7 briefing, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the peso’s depreciation was adding pressure to domestic pump prices because petroleum products are bought in dollars.

DOE officials said the peso weakened by around 68 centavos during the latest pricing period, compounding an increase of roughly $9 to $10 per barrel in petroleum import costs caused by renewed Middle East tensions.

In other words, Filipinos are being hit twice because global oil prices are rising at the same time as the peso is falling. The fuel itself becomes more expensive in dollars, while each dollar needed to buy it also costs more pesos.

The impact goes beyond just motorists having to pay more for their trips. Diesel powers trucks moving food and merchandise around the country too, while businesses depend on imported machinery, fertilizers, ingredients, and other inputs. As those costs rise, companies may eventually pass on at least some of them through higher prices.

Inflation, and the BSP’s reserves

BPI lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. warned that the recent peso depreciation could fuel further inflation through higher import costs, with headline inflation in August already at a worrying 6.1%. That’s why peso weakness is also becoming a headache for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) as it tries to bring inflation back within its 2% to 4% target range.

The BSP will not, however, defend the currency at a particular level. At an August 27 Senate budget hearing, BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank can smooth out sharp movements in, but trying to fix the peso at a particular rate would burn through the country’s dollar reserves.

Nevertheless, BSP data show that ammunition remains substantial.

Photo from the BSP.

The country’s gross international reserves rose to $104.8 billion at end-August, from $103.3 billion in July, largely because higher gold prices boosted the value of the BSP’s holdings and because of income from its overseas investments. The increase was partly offset by government withdrawals of foreign currency to service external debt.

Still, the buffer has thinned from $110.8 billion at the end of 2025. At its August level, reserves could cover about 6.8 months of imports and around 3.7 times the country’s short-term external debt.

“These provide sufficient foreign currency to meet the country’s import needs, service its external debt obligations, and serve as a buffer against external economic shocks,” the BSP said in a statement on Monday.

If depreciation keeps inflation elevated, the BSP may instead have to keep interest rates high for longer or tighten further. Higher borrowing costs can then weigh on household spending, business expansion, housing, and investment, creating another drag on an economy already struggling with slower growth. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

World.title: Prevent outside influence in Bangsamoro polls, groups urge Marcos
World.content:
SPEECH. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address at the House of Representatives on July 27, 2026.

Civil society also urges the Moro Islamic Liberation Front 'not to fan the flames of division'

MANILA, Philippines – Civil society groups urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday, September 8, to prevent external actors from attempting to influence the outcome of the Bangsamoro parliamentary polls and undermine the autonomy the region fought hard for.

Duyog Bangsamoro, a coalition comprised of regional and national civic organizations, urged the national government to continue supporting the peace process “regardless of which parties win the elections.”

“They have to make sure that this election turns out to be peaceful and credible,” Josua Mata, secretary general of labor group Sentro ng mga Nagkakaisa at Progresibong Manggagawa, said in a press briefing Tuesday.

Duyog Bangsamoro said there is a “persistent perception” in the region that Malacañang has been meddling with the affairs of the regional government.

This started when Malacañang made “irregular appointments” to the transition government, the group said, which deepened cracks within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).

“We call on the AFP and PNP personnel assigned to the region to observe the highest level of professionalism and reject influence from any actor that would deprive the Bangsamoro people of a genuine exercise of their autonomy,” their statement read.

The historic election is a milestone in the peace process between the Philippine government and the MILF.

But other things have yet to be done, such as decommissioning former combatants and the implementation of transitional justice. (READ: Transitional justice for Bangsamoro should be a ‘national project,’ say peace advocates)

MILF’s prerogative

The call for peaceful and credible elections followed MILF’s recent move to dismiss a number of its commanders and strip Abdulraof Macacua of his position as the organization’s military chief.

Macacua is the Bangsamoro interim chief minister, running in the 3rd parliamentary district of Maguindanao del Norte. Macacua has refused to run under the banner of United Bangsamoro Justice Party, the MILF’s official regional parliamentary political party.

This move manifested a long-running conflict inside the MILF. However this affects the election outcome, Amina Rasul, president of the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy, said that MILF’s decision is their prerogative.

“It’s within their right,” Rasul said on Tuesday. “In truth, we don’t know the rationale for that. We have to accept the decision and just make sure that everything is going to proceed as peacefully as possible.”

To the MILF, the coalition said: Don’t fan the flames of division, continue to engage in debates, and instruct the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces to “stand down.”

Over 2.3 million voters are expected to participate in the September 14 parliamentary elections. The Bangsamoro region is electing political party and district representatives. The elected parliament will eventually choose one member to become the chief minister. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – The intense rivalry between these parties can be both good and bad for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

With 13 regional parliament political parties and a total of nearly 700 candidates seeking just 80 seats, political participation in the region could broaden and offer BARMM voters a wider range of choices, according to the Asian Network for Free Elections (ANFREL).

World.title: NLEx completes dredging of Tulaoc River section
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines — Dredging of the NLEx section of the Tulaoc River is complete, and as of Sept. 8, NLEx Corp. reports there is no more pooling of rainwater on the expressway shoulder.

The company added that the work is continuing upstream from the Manila Bay outfall toward Tulaoc and the expressway, carried out with government and private sector partners. Deployment upstream was not possible during the flooding itself, when standing water blocked truck access.

Sheet piles installed along the alignment to keep water out of the NLEx system are being monitored through the rainfall now forecast.

Article continues after this 

Dredging is one part of the flood mitigation measures on the corridor. A mobile pumping unit is deployed at the kilometer 56 marker, with L-type flood barriers and modular mesh-and-liner units along the alignment and crews pre-positioned at Meycauayan, Paso de Blas, San Fernando and Balintawak.

Toll relief for journeys the expressway did not deliver—P113 for Class 1, P281 for Class 2 and P338 for Class 3—was credited to motorists’ RFID accounts the following day, with no claim form required.

“Our section of the river is dredged, and there is no water on the shoulder,” NLEx Corp. said. “The work is moving upstream from the bay, and we are watching the sheet piles perform through the next rainfall.” /cb

World.title: Aquaculture players seek say in Pangasinan projects amid flooding
World.content:
Vendors and market-goers endure rising floodwaters at Malimgas Market Phase II in Dagupan City, Pangasinan, where flooding worsens during high tide as seen in this photo taken on Aug. 31, 2026. — Photo by Willie Lomibao

CALASIAO, Pangasinan — Aquaculture industry players in Pangasinan are urging authorities to include them in consultations for development projects, saying they are often left to bear the consequences of decisions in which they have little or no say.

“We are a big part of the country’s food security, but we are often overlooked by the government when projects, such as solar farms in the mountains, are being planned and implemented,” said Christopher Sibayan, president of the Samahan ng Magbabangus sa Pangasinan (SAMAPA) in a recent interview.

Sibayan said massive flooding this year inundated fishponds for weeks, causing them to overflow and allowing fish stocks to escape into rivers and other waterways.

Article continues after this 

READ: Massive fish kill hits Pangasinan town

Binmaley, Labrador, Lingayen and Bugallon, major aquaculture areas, were severely affected by nearly monthlong flooding brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, and tropical cyclones Luis, Maymay and Neneng.

Industry players believe developments in upland areas, including solar farms in Bugallon and Labrador, may have worsened the flooding.

William Go, a SAMAPA coordinator, said some solar farm projects involved cutting trees that could have helped lessen the impact of heavy rains.

Sibayan said solar companies should have installed water-impounding facilities so rainwater collected by solar panels would not rapidly flow downhill into rivers and fishponds.

Article continues after this 

“Without the panels, rainwater could flow more slowly. But the water is collected by the panels and ran rapidly flow downstream all at once,” Go said.

READ: Erratic weather harmful to Pangasinan ‘bangus’

Article continues after this 

Vita Mamaril, a fisheries industry leader in Bugallon, said the flooding this year was unusually severe.

“Bugallon has always experienced flooding, but it was only this year that the flooding became so massive and took weeks to subside,” she said.

She also disputed claims that all mountains where solar farms were established had already been denuded.

“It is not true that all the mountains were denuded. Cayanga was still forested before a solar farm was put up there,” she said.

Sibayan said the flooding showed how developments upstream could affect the fisheries sector downstream.

“What is happening in the mountains directly or indirectly affects us in the lowlands, including those of us in the fisheries sector,” he said.

Fishpond operators also lost millions of pesos in fish stocks and inputs after floodwaters overtopped pond embankments.

One Binmaley operator, who requested anonymity, estimated his losses at about P5 million in fingerlings and feeds. The fish weighed about 200 grams each when they escaped.

“That does not even include the income we would have earned if the stocks had grown to harvestable size and were sold after another two to three months,” he said.

Another bangus producer in Labrador said he lost about 500,000 fingerlings being raised in a nine-hectare fishpond.

Manuel Estrada of Labrador said high-value fish, including malaga, lapu-lapu and talakitok, were also affected after the salinity of river water dropped to zero because of the flooding.

Workers also lost their livelihood.

Melchor Valdez, a fishpond “harvester” in Bugallon, said many ponds now had few or no fish stocks left to harvest.

“Bugallon fishponds have no stocks to harvest, so I have no work,” Valdez said.

He said flooded palay farms were also leaving agricultural workers without income.

World.title: 76 nabbed in Ilocos anti-illegal gambling drive
World.content:
Arrested individuals are presented following a series of anti-illegal gambling operations conducted by the Police Regional Office 1 across the Ilocos Region from Sept. 1 to 6, 2026. Police arrested 76 people and seized P33,457 in alleged bet money. — Photo courtesy of Police Regional Office 1

SAN ILDEFONSO, Ilocos Sur — Police arrested 76 people in 20 operations against illegal gambling across the Ilocos Region from Sept. 1 to 6, the Police Regional Office 1 (PRO 1) said.

The operations resulted in the confiscation of P33,457 in alleged bet money, according to PRO 1.

Police said the operations targeted various forms of illegal gambling, including illegal number games, jueteng, dice games, coin games and sports betting.

Article continues after this 

READ: Ilocos Sur cops nab 10 in illegal gambling raid

Brig. Gen. Crisaleo Tolentino, PRO 1 regional director, said the campaign against illegal gambling would remain intensified, urging police personnel and the public to remain vigilant against such activities.

“Our fight against illegal gambling does not end with these arrests. We will sustain our operations and strengthen our presence in communities to prevent these unlawful activities from spreading,” Tolentino said.

He also called on communities to cooperate with the police to keep their neighborhoods safe, peaceful and orderly. —Kenneth P. Tabin/Contributor /das

World.title: San Roque Dam stops spillway discharge in Pangasinan
World.content:
The spillway gates of the San Roque Multipurpose Dam in San Manuel, Pangasinan, as seen in this photo taken on Sept. 8. (Photo courtesy of Tommy Valdez/San Roque Power Corp.)

CALASIAO, Pangasinan — The two spillway gates of the San Roque Multipurpose Dam in San Manuel, Pangasinan, were closed at 7:30 p.m. on Tuesday (Sept. 8), ending the dam’s discharge, according to the National Power Corp. (Napocor).

The gates, 2A and 2B, were closed at one meter and 1.5 meters, respectively. The dam’s water elevation was 277.14 meters above sea level (masl) at the time.

READ: San Roque Dam to discharge water, ease reservoir pressure

Article continues after this 

The San Roque Power Corp. (SRPC), which operates the dam, initially opened the two spillway gates by one meter each on Sept. 2, when the water level was 283.68 masl.

Continued rain and inflow from the Binga Dam pushed the water level to 285.13 masl on Sept. 5. The SRPC opened an additional 0.5 meter on Sept. 6 and increased the total gate opening to three meters at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, an hour before the gates were closed.

The dam’s mandatory spilling level is 280 masl. /mcm

World.title: Highlights: Day 23 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 8, 2026
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Day 23 of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday centered on two major procedural developments: a looming decision on the voting threshold needed for conviction, and the formal pivot to Article II, the unexplained-wealth charge.

Presiding officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero announced that amici curiae (friends of the court) will be heard on September 16, with oral arguments of the parties scheduled for September 23, when the Senate is expected to vote on whether to retain the 24-member voting base for the trial.

READ: Highlights: Day 22 of Sarra Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 7, 2026

Article continues after this 

Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo had raised the issue, citing concerns about senators who may be unable to physically participate in the final conviction or acquittal vote, given that Sens. Loren Legarda is on sick leave, Ronald dela Rosa is in hiding, and Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada are detained in connection with plunder cases.

On the evidentiary front, the prosecution told the court it would skip the remaining 15 of 27 witnesses for Article I and instead reserved the right to call Duterte herself to the witness stand to address all articles of impeachment.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan announced the move, saying the prosecution had already presented 10 witnesses and stipulated two others, making the remaining Article I witnesses unnecessary.

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison immediately objected, invoking the Constitutional prohibition against compelling an accused to testify against herself, calling the prosecution’s possible move an attempt at impermissible testimonial compulsion.

With Article I witnesses concluded, the court set September 14 as the start date for Article II proceedings on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

Article continues after this 

Rep. Chel Diokno, lead prosecutor for Article II, told the court on Tuesday that more than 1,800 documents, including bank and insurance records produced under court-issued subpoenas, are set for marking on September 9 and 10, with trial proceedings suspended on those days so both sides can participate.

The Senate impeachment court separately gave Duterte’s lawyers 15 days to respond to the prosecution’s Request for Admission covering 104 items related to Article II, including bank records the prosecution seeks to confirm belong to the vice president.

Article continues after this 

Escudero also announced the broader trial schedule running through November, with whole-day trial sessions scheduled for October 1, 2 and October 5 to 15, and a break from October 16 to November 8 to make way for 2027 national budget hearings and plenary debates. The revised calendar was approved in an all-senators caucus, according to Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri. /dp

World.title: Police: No incident at 2 Quezon City schools amid alleged threat
World.content:
Quezon City Police District logo. — File photo by Grig C. Montegrande/INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — The Quezon City Police District (QCPD) on Tuesday said no violent incident had been reported at the Batasan Hills National High School and E-Claro Academy amid an alleged threat.

In a statement, the QCPD said the Batasan Police Station had coordinated with the respective schools’ managements and conducted a verification of the purported security concern.

“As of Sept. 8, 2026, no violent incident related to the alleged threat has been reported or recorded at either school,” the police noted.

Article continues after this 

READ: Quick reaction teams eyed to handle school emergencies

It explained that the threat stemmed from a social media post, but it did not expound on the nature of the security concern.

“The QCPD likewise coordinated with the Quezon City District Anti-Cybercrime Team to verify the authenticity and determine the source of the alleged Facebook Messenger threat, as well as to identify the individual who may be responsible for the post,” it added.

In response, the city police district detailed that it had heightened police visibility and intensified security measures in coordination with the schools’ stakeholders.

The police also urged the public to remain calm, refrain from sharing unverified information and report suspicious activity.

“The QCPD assures the public that all reported threats are taken seriously and are subject to immediate verification and appropriate police action,” it stressed. /das

World.title: Remulla: Negotiations underway with Bato dela Rosa’s ‘protectors’
World.content:
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla and Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa (INQUIRER FILES)

MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said negotiations were underway with purported protectors of Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

“We know where he is, but there are negotiations now with his protectors and I think we’ll get to him soon,” Remulla said in an interview on One News’ Storycon program on Tuesday.

“I cannot really talk at length about it, but he’s being protected by very powerful people.”

Article continues after this 

READ: NBI receives ‘many leads’ on Dela Rosa’s whereabouts

The Philippine National Police (PNP) and the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) have been searching for dela Rosa since last May to serve an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant for his arrest over his alleged involvement in former President Rodrigo Duterte’s bloody drug war.

Dela Rosa was last seen leaving the Senate premises and supposedly getting off in Makati City in the early hours of May 14, shortly after a shooting incident in the chamber.

Remulla justified the supposed negotiations, saying, “We don’t want casualties involved. That’s number one. They have to surrender peacefully.”

“And we will use all the levers of the government to get him out of his hiding, using all the economic and military levers that we have in order to force him out,” he stressed.

Article continues after this 

The DILG chief further noted that the PNP was working to take custody of a total of 117 firearms registered to dela Rosa.

At least 26 firearms had been surrendered by the senator’s camp since last June.

Article continues after this 

This came after the PNP Firearms and Explosives Office revoked dela Rosa’s firearms license and gun registrations as part of the government’s bid to locate him.

In a statement on Tuesday night, dela Rosa’s legal counsel, Israelito Torreon, said he had no personal knowledge of the “protectors” Remulla alleged.

“What we do know is that Senator dela Rosa is a deeply prayerful man who places his faith in Almighty God, his one and only Protector,” Torreon said.

He also said that Remulla’s concern of casualties was “unfortunate.”

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Air Links to Southeast Asia with New Singapore Route
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is continuing to broaden its aviation network across Asia, with SCAT Airlines set to launch flights from Shymkent to Singapore via China’s Sanya on Oct. 20. The new service comes amid a wider expansion of routes by Kazakh carriers to China and other Asian destinations.

Via Sanya

The Shymkent-Sanya flight will take around 6.5 hours, followed by an approximately two-hour transit in Sanya. Passengers will remain in the airport’s sterile transit zone and continue their journey without passing through Chinese passport control.

The Sanya-Singapore segment will take nearly three hours, the airline reported on Sept. 7.

The new route comes as Kazakhstan’s airlines continue to expand connectivity with China and other Asian destinations.

Growing Asian Connectivity

The Air Astana Group reported an 81% increase in capacity to China during the 2026 summer season, reaching 49 flights per week across seven destinations.

The group launched new services from Almaty to Shanghai and Xi’an, from Astana to Guangzhou and from Aktau to Urumqi. FlyArystan is also scheduled to launch twice-weekly flights between Almaty and Chongqing on Sept. 23.

Across the wider network, the group increased services to Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe, Türkiye and Asia during the summer season.

Passenger Advisory

FlyArystan has advised passengers traveling to or from China to arrive at the airport at least three hours before departure following updated entry and exit procedures that will take effect on Sept. 15.

The airline said immigration checks may take longer and advised passengers to check passport validity and current entry requirements in advance.

The visa-free regime between Kazakhstan and China remains in effect, allowing Kazakh citizens to stay in China for up to 30 calendar days per trip.

World.title: Expert: Kazakhstan Residents See Infrastructure Gains, Demand Further Development
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan residents are largely positive about improvements in their towns and villages, but their expectations are shifting toward further development of everyday infrastructure and services, according to a nationwide survey presented on Sept. 7.

National Analytical Center expert Roza Tleukhan said the findings show that people continue to expect the development course to move forward.

“The survey clearly shows that people retain a strong demand for further development – they notice the changes, value them and expect this course to continue,” Tleukhan said.

Conducted in July-August among 1,000 adult residents through telephone interviews, the survey found that 68% believe conditions in their settlements have improved over the past three years. 82% are satisfied with their current living conditions, while 68% expect further improvement over the next three years.

Visible improvements shape expectations

Residents most often notice improvements in areas they encounter in daily life. Roads were identified by 32% of respondents, followed by landscaping and public amenities (29%), parks and greenery (22%), schools and kindergartens (18%), and new housing (15%).

The results show that public perceptions of infrastructure development are shaped not only by the scale of investment, but also by how visible and usable its results are. The survey reflects residents’ perceptions rather than the actual volume of completed work.

A clear urban-rural distinction also emerged. City residents were more likely to notice improvements in parks, greenery, new housing and public transport, while rural residents more often pointed to roads and utilities.

The next demand is broader

Future priorities indicate where expectations remain high. Roads and landscaping ranked joint first at 26% each, followed by hospitals and clinics (21%), internet and mobile connectivity (20%), schools and kindergartens (19%), utilities (17%), and parks and greenery (16%).

Roads and landscaping rank highly both among recent improvements and future priorities, suggesting that progress has not reduced demand for continued investment.

Meanwhile, healthcare, connectivity and utilities feature more prominently among future priorities than among areas where residents have noticed major improvements. This indicates that public expectations are increasingly focused on service quality and accessibility.

Expectations will test implementation

Confidence in further progress remains relatively strong, with 70% of urban residents and 63% of rural residents expecting conditions to improve over the next three years. Among respondents aged 18-35, the share rises to 76%.

The findings suggest that infrastructure policy will increasingly be judged not only by new construction, but by whether projects improve access to healthcare, connectivity, utilities and other essential services.

For policymakers, the key measure will be whether visible infrastructure gains translate into improvements in the areas where demand remains highest.

The survey therefore points to a positive public assessment while setting a higher benchmark for the next three years: development is expected to remain continuous, visible and relevant to everyday life.

World.title: EDB: Kazakhstan Maintains Growth, Strengthens Position Amid Tighter Global Financing Conditions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s resilient economic growth, moderate public debt and strong external buffers are strengthening its ability to access global capital markets despite tighter borrowing conditions worldwide, according to the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) September Macroeconomic Outlook.

The EDB experts said the economy continued to expand this year, with GDP growing 4.1% year-on-year in January-July, while the non-oil sector increased by 5.4%. Construction rose 15.3%, manufacturing 9%, transport and warehousing 7.4%, and trade 5.9%.

“The key factor behind economic growth was the increase in output in the non-resource sector by 5.4% year-on-year,” the report said.

Investment activity also remained strong. Fixed capital investment increased 7.7% year-on-year to 11.5 trillion tenge (US$25.3 billion), supported by state-backed manufacturing projects and growing investment in electricity, information and communications.

At the same time, oil production fell 8.9% to 53.2 million tons in January-July, underscoring the need for continued economic diversification.

Annual inflation slowed to 9.8% in August from a peak of 12.9% in September 2025. The EDB expects inflation to moderate to 9.7% by the end of 2026, while the National Bank’s base rate stood at 16.25% in September.

“The strengthening of the tenge against the dollar by 8.5% since the beginning of the year reduces imported price pressure, while tight monetary conditions limit domestic demand,” the report said.

The report noted that Kazakhstan’s fiscal deficit widened to 1.7% of GDP in January-July, reflecting higher government spending and continued fiscal support for economic activity.

Kazakhstan’s external position remains a key strength. Gross international reserves stood at $63.3 billion as of Aug. 1, while National Fund foreign assets reached $66 billion.

The EDB also highlighted Kazakhstan’s improved sovereign credit standing. On Aug. 21, S&P Global Ratings upgraded Kazakhstan’s sovereign rating from BBB- to BBB with a stable outlook, citing the country’s economic resilience, substantial foreign exchange reserves and expectations of a declining non-oil deficit.

According to the EDB, Kazakhstan’s average public debt stood at 24% of GDP in 2023-2025, significantly below the average for selected A-rated economies. The bank projects the country’s gross public debt to rise moderately to 32% of GDP by 2031.

“Maintaining sustainable economic growth in a complex and rapidly changing external economic environment is another pillar of Kazakhstan’s investment attractiveness,” the report said.

According to the EDB experts, Kazakhstan retains the possibility of regularly accessing global capital markets “in the medium term on comfortable terms.” It added that the transition to the “A” category will depend on “the success of ongoing institutional reforms and the pace of economic diversification.”

The EDB’s regional outlook showed that the economies in its region of operations grew 1.5% year-on-year in the first half of this year, while Central Asian economies expanded by 6%. Domestic demand, investment activity and infrastructure projects remain key drivers of growth.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes Lead as Central Asia Expands Space Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a Central Asian space hub as the nation expands its satellite and spacecraft capabilities and deepens regional cooperation, including discussions on a proposed Central Asia Space Agency.

The ambitions were highlighted at Space Days Kazakhstan 2026, an international forum taking place in Astana on Sept. 7–9. The event brings together government representatives, space agencies, international organizations, scientists, technology companies and investors to discuss satellite communications, Earth observation, artificial intelligence and new space technologies.

Speaking at the opening, Deputy Prime Minister – Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s priority is to strengthen its space industry while making greater use of the country’s space infrastructure.

“Our task is to use the unique legacy of Baikonur to develop a modern and competitive space industry,” Madiyev said.

Kazakhstan is currently modernizing its satellite infrastructure and expanding its capabilities in Earth observation and spacecraft manufacturing.

By 2030, the nation plans to create an international Earth remote sensing satellite constellation comprising nine spacecraft. It will include six satellites from Kazakhstan, as well as spacecraft from Mongolia, the Republic of the Congo and Nigeria. Madiyev said Kazakhstan is open to cooperation with new partners and sees potential to expand the constellation to 14 satellites.

The country is also working to replace KazSat-3 with a new KazSat-3R spacecraft to maintain the stability of Kazakhstan’s national satellite communications system and meet modern technological requirements.

In July, the government allocated 10.4 billion tenge ($22.8 million) from its reserve fund for the creation of KazSat-3R. The new spacecraft is intended to enter service as KazSat-3’s expected service life ends in 2029.

At the same time, Kazakhstan is expanding its domestic space capabilities. A spacecraft assembly and testing center in Astana allows the country to build and test satellites, train engineers and participate in international space projects.

Kairzhan Kozhayev, chairman of Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary, Kazakhstan’s national operator for Earth remote sensing and high-precision satellite navigation systems, said the country is building the capabilities needed to strengthen its role in the regional space industry.

“We are gradually positioning ourselves as a kind of Central Asian space hub,” Kozhayev told The Astana Times.

Kozhayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s spacecraft assembly, integration and testing center in Astana and the growing pool of young engineers as important advantages for the country’s space industry. The Astana Times visited the facility in December 2025 to see how Kazakhstan’s spacecraft are assembled and tested.

“We have a lot of brave, smart and unique minds, new generations of engineers growing up so fast,” he said, emphasizing the importance of involving younger specialists in major space projects.

Regional cooperation gains momentum

The forum also highlighted efforts to build an integrated Central Asian and Turkic space ecosystem.

Uzbekistan is exploring closer cooperation with Kazakhstan in Earth observation and space-based monitoring, particularly for water management, agriculture, land use and environmental protection.

Shukhrat Kadirov, director of the Space Research and Technology Agency under Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, said the two countries were also discussing an initiative to establish a Central Asia Space Agency.

“I believe Central Asia has significant potential to become an active regional hub for the space industry, connecting East and West, and creating new opportunities for innovation, business, international cooperation, and investment,” Kadirov said.

He noted that common regional challenges, including water scarcity, climate change, land degradation and desertification, require solutions that extend beyond national borders.

Deputy Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States Merey Mukazhan said space cooperation was becoming an important part of the organization’s broader technological agenda.

The OTS has held five meetings of the heads of space agencies, alongside technical consultations and working groups. One of the most concrete outcomes is the joint OTS-SAT satellite project, which will support Earth observation, technology demonstrations in orbit and the development of joint space capabilities.

Mukazhan said the project shows how regional countries can combine expertise and resources to develop capabilities that would be difficult to build independently.

“We are determined to ensure that the Turkic world is not merely a consumer of new technologies but an active contributor to their development,” he said.

From satellites to practical applications

For Kazakhstan, the development of the space sector is increasingly tied to practical applications on Earth.

Madiyev stressed that satellites and launches should not be viewed as an end in themselves. Satellite data are used in Kazakhstan for emergency response and monitoring climate and environmental changes.

The next step, he said, is to move from individual satellite images toward integrated data analysis and practical digital services.

“Artificial intelligence allows us to process space data faster, detect changes earlier, and improve the accuracy of forecasting,” Madiyev said.

This approach is particularly relevant to water management, agriculture and environmental monitoring, areas where Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries face common challenges.

The European Union is also supporting the development of satellite ground infrastructure and digital connectivity in Central Asia. Ambassador of the European Union to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić highlighted the EU’s cooperation with Kazakhstan in satellite infrastructure and Earth observation.

She noted that satellite data can increasingly support farmers and improve water management across the region.

“This is space technology working best for farmers, for water management, and for us,” Simkić said.

Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s space strategy would continue to combine infrastructure development with international partnerships. Baikonur Cosmodrome, a major space launch facility in southern Kazakhstan, is expected to remain an active launch site while also developing as an international center for space technology, science, education and tourism.

He identified three priorities for the development of Kazakhstan’s space industry: data, technology and people.

These include improving analytical products based on satellite data, expanding the use of AI, integrating space data into government and sectoral digital platforms, attracting investment and commercializing technologies, as well as strengthening education and international training programmes.

For Kazakhstan, Space Days Kazakhstan is intended to become part of that longer-term effort.

“This forum is only the beginning of this journey,” Madiyev said, adding that Kazakhstan expects concrete agreements and joint projects to emerge from the event and plans to make Space Days Kazakhstan a regular international forum.

World.title: Caspian Sea’s Decline Raises Water Security Concerns As Kazakhstan Strengthens Management
World.content:
ALMATY – The rapid decline of the Caspian Sea is emerging as one of Kazakhstan’s most complex water and environmental challenges, with falling water levels threatening ecosystems, fisheries, coastal infrastructure and communities. As the country strengthens its broader water management system, the changing Caspian is adding urgency to efforts to improve how Kazakhstan monitors and uses its water resources.

The scale of the challenge is becoming visible along Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast. A newly emerged island, already referred to locally as Rybachy, has become a visible sign of the sea’s retreat, while scientists have warned of potentially significant ecological consequences.

Experts have compared some aspects of the current situation with the deterioration of the Aral Sea, although the two water bodies have very different causes and dynamics.

Vadim Ni, founder of the Save the Caspian Sea movement and director of the Social and Environmental Fund, said the consequences are already being felt in several sectors, including shipping, cargo transportation, fisheries, tourism and drinking water supplies in Aktau.

At the same time, speaking with the Inbusiness agency, he noted that the full economic cost of the Caspian’s decline has yet to be systematically assessed.

A changing sea creates economic risks

The Caspian is particularly important for Kazakhstan because its economic role extends far beyond the coastline. The sea supports fisheries, ports and tourism, while Kazakhstan’s ports form part of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, linking China and Europe.

A continued decline in water levels could therefore create additional costs for maritime transportation and port infrastructure. Shallowing waters can restrict access for larger vessels and require adjustments to navigation channels and coastal facilities.

Economist and financial adviser Arman Baiganov said declining water levels could disrupt port infrastructure because deep-draft vessels may no longer be able to access and dock at some facilities. However, the exact economic impact remains difficult to calculate because it will depend on the speed and extent of the decline, as well as the measures taken to adapt infrastructure.

The same uncertainty applies to tourism. Kazakhstan has invested heavily in developing Aktau and other Caspian destinations, but a retreating shoreline could eventually change the location and viability of existing recreation facilities.

“If the water significantly retreats from the shore, tourist bases and recreation areas located today along the coast may have to be relocated or rebuilt closer to the sea,” Baiganov said.

Fisheries face a double pressure

The reduction of shallow-water areas in the northern Caspian affects habitats that are important for fish feeding and reproduction. This is particularly significant for sturgeon species, historically associated with the Caspian ecosystem.

Ni noted that declining water levels are already making fishing more difficult in parts of northeastern Kazakhstan, including the Atyrau region. The geography of the industry has also changed. In 2006, Atyrau accounted for around 13,650 tonnes, or nearly 40%, of total fish catches, according to Ni. By 2024, its share had fallen to just over 20%, with catches of about 9,480 tonnes.

At the same time, Mangystau’s catch increased substantially, from 315 tonnes in 2006 to almost 5,000 tonnes in 2025. But the sea’s decline is only one factor affecting fisheries. Overfishing and poaching also place pressure on fish populations, making it difficult to attribute changes in catches to water levels alone. This mix of environmental and human pressures means adapting to the changing Caspian will require more than infrastructure measures.

Scientists warned about climate change

According to a forecast cited by Ni from researchers at universities in Bremen, Giessen and Utrecht, under a lower-emissions climate scenario the Caspian’s surface area could decline by 23% and its level fall by about nine meters by the end of the century. Under a more severe warming scenario, the area could decline by 34%, with a similar fall in water level.

These projections are long-term scenarios rather than forecasts of what will necessarily occur, but they illustrate the scale of potential change facing the region. Against this backdrop, Kazakhstan is simultaneously overhauling its wider water governance framework.

A new Water Code that entered into force last year introduced new principles for protecting and using water resources, including stronger requirements to protect small rivers and lakes and provisions for establishing water protection zones.

The legislation also provides for a General Plan and basin-level plans to protect and use water resources. Their recommendations are intended to be incorporated into state planning.

These measures do not directly solve the Caspian problem, but they form part of a broader strategy to make Kazakhstan’s water management more efficient at a time when the country faces increasing uncertainty over water availability.

The North Aral Sea experience demonstrates the potential impact of coordinated water management. Through agreed reservoir operating regimes on the Syr Darya, Kazakhstan has maintained stable inflows into the North Aral Sea, increasing its volume from 18.4 cubic kilometers at the beginning of 2023 to 23.5 cubic kilometers currently.

The Caspian presents a much more complicated challenge, but the principle is similar: reliable data, coordinated management and long-term planning become increasingly important as environmental conditions change.

As Water Resources and Irrigation Minister Nurzhan Nurzhigitov said, the next stage is to move from strategic and regulatory measures toward the timely completion of specific projects and tangible improvements in water security.

World.title: Experts Say Kazakhstan’s Youth Advantage Won’t Last Without Action
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has one of the relatively young population structures globally, with people under 18 accounting for 34.2% of the population in 2025 and placing the country 80th among 163 countries and territories. Experts say the large share of children gives Kazakhstan a potential demographic dividend, but realizing that opportunity will depend on education, healthcare, employment and long-term planning.

According to data from the UN Population Division Data Portal, Kazakhstan ranks between countries with substantially older population structures and the world’s youngest societies. The Central African Republic has the highest share of people under 18 at 56.2%, followed by Niger at 53.3%, Somalia at 53.0%, Mali at 52.9% and Chad at 52.7%.

At the other end of the ranking, children account for just 12.9% of South Korea’s population, while Japan, Taiwan and Singapore also have shares below 15%.

The contrast highlights two very different demographic challenges. Countries with large youth populations need to create enough schools, healthcare services and eventually jobs for growing generations. Countries with very small younger generations face a shrinking future workforce and increasing pressure from population aging.

For Kazakhstan, experts say the current age structure creates a window of opportunity, but one that is time-limited.

A young population is a potential dividend, not a guarantee

Independent financial analyst Andrei Chebotaryov said Kazakhstan’s relatively young population should be viewed as an economic opportunity rather than an automatic source of prosperity.

“A large number of children is by no means automatically wealth. It is a potential demographic dividend,” he wrote on his Telegram channel.

According to Chebotaryov, that dividend materializes only if a country provides younger generations with quality education, healthcare, skills and opportunities to find employment. If those conditions are met, a large youth cohort can eventually become a substantial workforce, a larger group of taxpayers and consumers, and a source of entrepreneurship and domestic demand.

“Kazakhstan is in an interesting position. Our population is noticeably younger. This means that Kazakhstan currently has a very valuable window of opportunity: the young generation is already here. Now the main thing is to use it correctly,” Chebotaryov wrote.

The demographic gap of the 1990s is still being felt

Kazakhstan’s current age structure, however, is also shaped by demographic disruptions that followed the collapse of the Soviet Union. Demography researcher and PaperLab Making New Experts graduate Darina Dauletbek, speaking on the Zhiza podcast on YouTube, said the country’s demographic situation cannot be understood without considering the sharp decline in births during the 1990s.

She described this as a demographic “pit” – a significant drop in the number of births that later moves through the population structure in waves. In the late 1980s, around 400,000 children were born in Kazakhstan, according to figures Dauletbek discussed. By 1999, the number had fallen to just over 200,000.

The decline coincided with the economic crisis following the collapse of the Soviet Union, as well as significant migration out of Kazakhstan. The effects are now visible in the size of the generation reaching adulthood.

People born in the late 1990s and early 2000s are now roughly in their late 20s and 30s — the age when many people marry, have children, and establish careers and businesses. Because relatively few people were born during that period, fewer people are reaching these life stages.

“This demographic pit creates the noise we are seeing today: falling birth rates and a decline in the number of marriages,” Dauletbek said in an interview with the Zhiza podcast.

Fertility matters, but so does the size of each generation

Dauletbek also highlighted the importance of the total fertility rate: the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her reproductive years. In Kazakhstan, the total fertility rate fell to about 1.8 in 1999, compared with approximately 3.5 during the Soviet period, according to figures cited in the interview.

A fertility rate of around 2.1 is generally associated with replacement-level fertility under stable mortality and migration assumptions. When fertility remains below that level over a prolonged period, population growth becomes increasingly difficult to maintain without other demographic factors.

Kazakhstan subsequently experienced a recovery in fertility, but the demographic effects of the 1990s did not disappear. They moved through the age structure and are now affecting the number of potential parents. This illustrates why demographic trends are difficult to reverse quickly. A smaller generation today means fewer potential parents tomorrow, regardless of whether those people individually want larger families.

Kazakhstan has a window, but it will not last indefinitely

The global comparison makes Kazakhstan’s position particularly notable. Africa dominates the countries with the largest shares of children: 28 of the top 30 countries in the ranking are African, with Afghanistan and Yemen the only exceptions. Higher fertility rates have contributed to these youthful population structures.

But a young population becomes an economic advantage only when institutions and infrastructure can absorb the coming generations. East Asian economies illustrate the opposite challenge. South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Singapore all have child shares below 15%, meaning substantially smaller generations are entering the future workforce.

Kazakhstan sits between these two demographic models. Its 34.2% share of people under 18 gives it a relatively young population and a potentially favorable labor-force trajectory, while the demographic consequences of the 1990s and the prospect of population aging create longer-term constraints.

As Chebotaryov put it, the demographic bonus cannot simply be postponed. The children who represent potential future workers, entrepreneurs and taxpayers will eventually become those people, and the policies adopted today will influence how large an economic dividend Kazakhstan ultimately receives.

World.title: Joint Statement by Ministers of Foreign Affairs of States Parties on Occasion of 20th Anniversary of Signing of CANWFZ Treaty
World.content:
We, the Foreign Ministers of the States Parties to the Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia (hereinafter referred to as the “CANWFZ Treaty”), on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of the signing of the CANWFZ Treaty in Semipalatinsk

reaffirming our commitment to humanity’s common goal of achieving a world free of nuclear weapons, and recognizing the catastrophic humanitarian consequences of any use or testing of nuclear weapons,

emphasizing that the establishment of nuclear-weapon-free zones is one of the most powerful universal tools for preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons and strengthening the global disarmament process,

noting the importance of the Treaty between the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Republic of Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and the Republic of Uzbekistan on Friendship, Good-Neighborliness, and Cooperation for Development of Central Asia in the 21st Century in strengthening peace and security in the region,

recalling that the idea of establishing a nuclear-weapon-free zone in Central Asia was first proposed by the Republic of Uzbekistan in September 1993 at the 48th session of the UN General Assembly,

convinced that the establishment of a nuclear-weapon-free zone in Central Asia represents a successful example of the consolidation of efforts by the countries of the region, and emphasizing that this was an important step toward strengthening the nuclear nonproliferation regime and the process of nuclear disarmament, regional and international peace and security, as well as the development of cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy and the environmental rehabilitation of areas affected by radioactive contamination,

welcoming the thirty-fifth anniversary of the closure of the Semipalatinsk Nuclear Test Site and the thirtieth anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, and paying tribute to the memory of the numerous victims of nuclear explosions and their consequences in all regions of the world,

we hereby declare the following:

1. We reaffirm our commitment to the historically significant CANWFZ Treaty, signed by the Republic of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, the Republic of Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and the Republic of Uzbekistan on 8 September 2006, in Semipalatinsk. As the result of collective efforts of all five Central Asian states in their aspiration to ensure security, stability and peace in the region, and as it remains the first and only such zone located entirely in the Northern Hemisphere and directly bordering two nuclear-weapon States, the Semipalatinsk Treaty continues to play an important role in strengthening the global disarmament and non-proliferation regime and serves as a symbolic example of Central Asia’s transformation from a region where nuclear weapons were once actively tested and deployed into one of the leaders of global efforts toward nuclear disarmament.

2. We reaffirm the key role of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) as the cornerstone of international efforts to prevent the proliferation of nuclear weapons and, ultimately, to achieve their complete elimination. In this regard, we regret that the Eleventh Review Conference of the States Parties to the NPT concluded without adopting substantive outcomes, reflecting continuing differences and a lack of trust in the field of nuclear disarmament and nonproliferation. We call on all NPT parties to continue negotiations in good faith on the effective implementation of obligations under all three interrelated and mutually reinforcing pillars – nuclear disarmament, nonproliferation, and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.

3. In light of the urgent and unprecedented challenges threatening global security and stability, we express serious concern over the lack of substantial progress in the field of nuclear disarmament in accordance with Article 6 of the NPT, as well as the cessation of key arms control agreements, coupled with an alarming trend toward the modernization of nuclear arsenals. At the same time, we note the special responsibility of nuclear-weapon States to engage in negotiations on nuclear disarmament and call for the urgent development of new, verifiable arms control mechanisms to prevent a nuclear arms race.

4. We affirm our unwavering support for the activities of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in implementing the provisions of the NPT, promoting cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and applying safeguards and monitoring of nuclear programs in the Agency’s member states.

5. We firmly advocate for the necessity of the earliest entry-into-force of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) which will mark exactly thirty years since its opening for signature on 24 September 2026. In this regard, we emphasize the need to preserve and further strengthen the international norm against nuclear testing and call for refraining from any actions that could undermine this norm.

We emphasize the important role of raising awareness on disarmament and non-proliferation in fostering a culture of peace, trust and responsibility, and note the particular importance of involving the youth in discussions on disarmament and international security. We support the continued promotion of the International Day for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Awareness, initiated by the Kyrgyz Republic and symbolically observed annually on 5 March – the date the NPT entered into force – as well as related regional educational initiatives.

In this regard, we note the relevance of the recommendations contained in the UN Study on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Education, as well as the UN Secretary-General’s Agenda for Disarmament, “Securing Our Common Future: An Agenda for Disarmament.”

6. We welcome the signing on 6 May 2014 by the nuclear-weapon States of the Protocol on Negative Security Assurances to the Treaty on the Central Asian Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone and its ratification by four nuclear-weapon states, and we express our hope for the earliest completion of the ratification process for the Protocol by the United States of America.

7. We express our interest in the institutional development of the CANWFZ Treaty and in expanding further partnerships with existing nuclear-weapon-free zones with the aim of strengthening the global nuclear non-proliferation regime and uniting international efforts to ensure peace and security. In this context, we welcome the signing of Memoranda of Understanding with the African Commission on Atomic Energy (AFCONE) and the Organization for the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons in Latin America and the Caribbean (OPANAL), as well as the holding in Astana on August 28–29, 2024, under Kazakhstan’s chairmanship, of the second meeting of representatives of all existing nuclear-weapon-free zones.

8. We note the great importance of strengthening regional security as a key factor for sustainable development and stability in Central Asia, and we reaffirm our intention to continue to cooperate closely in addressing common challenges and threats.

9. We support efforts to establish new nuclear-weapon-free zones in regions where they do not currently exist, including in the Middle East.

10. We welcome the adoption of the resolution “Treaty on a Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone in Central Asia” at the 79th session of the UN General Assembly as well as the holding, of an anniversary meeting of the Treaty’s participating States in Ashgabat on 5 December 2024, under Turkmenistan’s chairmanship, with the participation of representatives of other existing nuclear-weapon-free zones and international organizations.

World.title: US Lawmaker Urges End to Cold War-Era Trade Restrictions on Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — The United States should establish permanent normal trade relations with Kazakhstan and offer greater economic opportunities rather than pressure the country to choose between Washington, Moscow and Beijing, Congressman Jimmy Panetta said during a Hudson Institute discussion on Sept. 2, as Washington weighs how to deepen its economic and strategic engagement with Central Asia.

Panetta, a California Democrat and a member of the House Ways and Means Committee, said repealing the Jackson-Vanik amendment would send an important signal of Washington’s commitment as it seeks new critical-mineral suppliers and greater influence in Central Asia.

He noted that closer engagement would serve U.S. interests at a time when securing diversified critical-mineral supply chains has become a growing priority in Washington. His remarks followed a House Ways and Means Committee hearing in which lawmakers considered legislation granting Kazakhstan permanent normal trade relations.

Jackson-Vanik is holding back U.S.-Kazakhstan ties

At the center of that conversation was the decades-old Jackson-Vanik amendment, which Panetta described bluntly as a “Cold War relic.” The Jackson-Vanik amendment, adopted in 1974 to pressure the Soviet Union over restrictions on emigration, links normal U.S. trade relations to freedom of movement. Kazakhstan has met its requirements for decades but remains formally covered by the law.

Panetta framed the continued application of Jackson-Vanik as a contradiction in U.S. policy: Washington is seeking closer economic ties with Kazakhstan while retaining a trade mechanism created during the Cold War.

Panetta called the repeal a “huge step to take to demonstrate symbolically our commitment at a very low cost to the future of not just Kazakh-U.S. relations,” while also noting that it would benefit the U.S. by helping diversify supplies of rare-earth and other critical minerals.

Kazakhstan’s reforms

Yet the significance of Jackson-Vanik in this debate goes beyond economics, because the case being made in Washington is also about how the U.S. assesses Kazakhstan politically and whether it recognizes the context in which the country is pursuing domestic change. Panetta pointed specifically to reforms under President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. He cited Kazakhstan’s single seven-year presidential term as evidence of political reform, while acknowledging that “more can be done.”

“These are big steps that President Tokayev is taking in the face of a very tough history of this country in order to show that it is willing to make the types of changes that are needed to enhance its democracy and uphold its democratic values. I think it is a major reform not just for Kazakhstan, but for the region, because I guarantee you, Kazakhstan’s biggest neighbors, China and Russia, didn’t like to hear that,” Panetta said.

Panetta described Kazakhstan as a country with exceptionally deep ties to both Russia and China and said that expecting Astana to sever those relationships would be strategically unrealistic.

During the discussion, the possibility was also raised that Kazakhstan’s participation in both U.S.-backed Pax Silica and a Chinese AI initiative could create pressure for Astana to choose one technological ecosystem over the other. Panetta rejected that approach.

“I do not think that is the right strategy to have, and we have to continue to give them the options to choose America,” he said.

The U.S. should compete, not pressure

American engagement should be strong enough that countries choose the U.S. because doing so serves their interests, rather than because Washington has successfully compelled them to choose, he added.

For Kazakhstan, the argument is particularly relevant because the discussion does not present its balanced foreign policy as an obstacle to closer U.S. engagement, but rather as a reality Washington needs to understand and, potentially, use to its advantage.

As Ken Moriyasu, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, noted, Kazakhstan’s multi-vector approach may actually benefit the U.S., because Kazakhstan’s geography and economic position make close ties with China and Russia unavoidable, while its relationship with Washington provides another channel for influence. Panetta agreed, emphasizing that Kazakhstan’s position makes such a strategy understandable and that the U.S. should seek to become part of that balancing act rather than demand it abandon it.

This approach also rests on a practical calculation. The discussion repeatedly returned to Kazakhstan’s potential importance for U.S. critical-mineral supply chains, and therefore to the broader question of whether Washington is prepared to translate its renewed strategic interest in Central Asia into the kind of sustained economic engagement that could compete with the relationships China and Russia have already built.

Panetta noted that Washington is only beginning to move in that direction, pointing to the bipartisan support for Jackson-Vanik repeal and the lengthy effort required to bring the issue before the Ways and Means Committee.

“Passing legislation in Congress, one, it is a marathon. Two, it takes a lot of luck. Three, it takes a lot of timing,” he said, adding that the process is beginning to move in the right direction.

Trump visit could send a strong signal

When asked about a possible visit by President Donald Trump, Panetta declined to say whether one was likely but said a presidential trip would signal that Washington intended to remain engaged in a region where China and Russia maintain a strong diplomatic presence.

As leaders gathered in Bishkek recently for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit, including Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin, Narendra Modi, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistan’s leadership, Panetta pointed to the gathering as evidence of how quickly geopolitical space can be occupied when Washington is absent.

Panetta’s argument was that Washington does not need Kazakhstan to abandon its relationships with Moscow and Beijing; it needs to ensure that the U.S. is sufficiently useful, credible and economically attractive to become another indispensable partner.

World.title: Council of Europe rights commissioner intervenes in Georgia FARA case
World.content:
Council of Europe on FARA

According to the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O’Flaherty has intervened as a third party in a case before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) concerning Georgia‘s Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA).

The commissioner submitted written observations to the court which, according to GYLA, go beyond an assessment of the law itself and also address legislative changes adopted in Georgia over the past two years.

O’Flaherty called on the ruling Georgian Dream party to ensure a free and safe working environment for the country’s civil society sector in line with its international obligations.

The FARA law adopted by Georgian Dream came into force on 31 May 2025. The authorities say it was modelled on the equivalent US law. However, Georgia’s version of FARA targets civil society organisations and media outlets and restricts their activities, including their ability to work with foreign foundations and organisations.

According to GYLA, Michael O’Flaherty considers the adoption of the law to be part of a broader set of restrictions targeting civil society, which are having a negative impact on media outlets and non-governmental organisations working on human rights, democracy and the rule of law.

In his assessment, the law’s provisions do not meet the requirements of legality, legitimacy, necessity and proportionality established by the European Convention on Human Rights in relation to freedom of expression and freedom of association. The commissioner also pointed to the principle of non-discrimination.

The commissioner said the law contains vague wording and defines the concept of “political activity” too broadly. He argued that this makes it difficult to distinguish between legitimate international cooperation and foreign interference, while leaving it unclear who exactly is subject to the law’s requirements.

The commissioner also noted that the law establishes a strict system of administrative oversight which, in his assessment, approaches the severity of Russia’s “foreign agent” legislation. Deliberate violations of the law can result in criminal liability, including imprisonment for up to five years.

He also argued that the term “agent” carries negative connotations in public perception, meaning that the law’s entry into force contributes to the stigmatisation of civil society. The commissioner also pointed to what he described as a campaign by the authorities to portray non-governmental organisations and human rights defenders as “enemies of the state”.

The commissioner said the law targets specific individuals and legal entities on the basis of their foreign funding, resulting in unequal treatment.
