World.title: Azerbaijan and U.S. discuss peace process and TRIPP project (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. On September 8, Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov met with David Allen, the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Armenia, who is visiting Azerbaijan, and Amy Carlos, the U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Azerbaijan, to discuss the peace process and the implementation of the TRIPP initiative.

This was announced in a statement by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan.

According to the Ministry, during the meeting, the parties discussed ongoing efforts to normalize relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia, advance the peace process, ensure long-term and sustainable peace, and strengthen stability and security in the region.

The sides also exchanged views on the outcomes of Elnur Mammadov’s visit to the United States on the occasion of the anniversary of the Washington Peace Summit and the signing of the trilateral statement. Discussions also covered ongoing efforts to implement the “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP), as well as the establishment of the TRIPP Development Company, which will oversee the construction of the route’s infrastructure.

In addition, the parties reviewed the bilateral agenda between Azerbaijan and the United States and prospects for further cooperation in the areas outlined in the Charter on Strategic Partnership.

World.title: Azerbaijan, China deepen dialogue on strategic ties (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. On September 8, a meeting was held at the Central Office of the “New Azerbaijan” Party (NAP) between NAP Deputy Chairman and Head of the Central Office Tahir Budagov and a delegation led by Minister Liu Haixing, a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and head of the International Relations Department.

This was announced in a statement published by the “New Azerbaijan” Party (NAP).

The meeting highlighted that, as a result of the targeted policies of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Chairman of the New Azerbaijan Party, Ilham Aliyev, and the President of the People’s Republic of China and General Secretary of the Communist Party of China, Xi Jinping, relations between the two countries are successfully developing in the spirit of friendship and a comprehensive strategic partnership.

In addition, it was noted that, against the backdrop of constructive political dialogue, relations have further developed in the economic and trade, transportation and logistics, educational, tourism, cultural, and humanitarian spheres, as well as in the fields of digital technologies, “green energy,” and other areas.

In addition, it was noted that both countries have launched important initiatives on a global scale, and the geostrategic importance and prospects of the “Belt and Road” initiative and the Zangezur Corridor were emphasized.

China's support for the development of Azerbaijan’s relations with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization was cited as an example of sincere friendship and partnership.

The sides emphasized that the comprehensive strategic partnership between Azerbaijan and China is of great importance not only for the development of relations between the two countries but also for promoting cooperation among countries of the Global South.

The importance of resolutely supporting the independence, territorial integrity, and sovereignty of both countries, which pursue independent policies based on the norms of international law and condemn all forms and manifestations of separatism, was underscored.

The development of relations between the NAP and the CPC, as an important component of interstate relations, was highlighted as a priority. The importance of mutual visits and the exchange of views and experiences in assessing the current state of relations between the parties and determining future areas of cooperation was noted.

In addition, it was stated that the successful implementation of the tasks arising from the Memorandum of Cooperation, signed during the NAP delegation’s visit to China in November 2024, has made a significant contribution to further strengthening the comprehensive strategic partnership between the two countries.

The parties noted with satisfaction the meetings held between them during the NAP delegation’s visit to the friendly country on May 11–15, 2026, and expressed confidence that mutual visits aimed at deepening cooperation would become a regular feature and that joint efforts would lead to further, sustained success.

The importance of young people’s active participation in public and political life, as well as in government administration and party activities, was discussed, and the importance of cooperation between specialized educational institutions in this area was noted.

During the meeting, the parties exchanged views on future directions for inter-party cooperation and other issues of mutual interest.

World.title: Religious leaders visit historic mosques in Azerbaijan's Shusha (PHOTO)
World.content:
SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 8. A delegation of religious leaders from Türkiye, Georgia, and Iraq visited the Yukhari Govhar Agha and Ashagi Govhar Agha mosques as part of their visit to the city of Shusha, Trend's Karabakh bureau reports.

The guests were provided with detailed information about the history and activities of both mosques. The delegation was shown photographs depicting the mosques’ former condition, as well as the destruction they suffered during the occupation.

During the visit, it was noted that a total of 21 mosques had been in operation in the city of Shusha. During the occupation, most of the mosques were destroyed, and some places of worship were used for other purposes.

Furthermore, it was noted that during the occupation of Azerbaijani lands, the destruction not only of people but also of Azerbaijan’s national, spiritual, and religious values was an integral part of Armenia’s policy of vandalism.

XXX

SHUSHA, Azerbaijan, September 8. A delegation of Azerbaijani religious leaders operating in Türkiye, Georgia, and Iraq has begun a visit to the city of Shusha, Trend's Karabakh bureau reports.

The visit is part of the “Path of Victory: In the Footsteps of Victory” project, organized by the Moral Values Promotion Fund, which operates under the State Committee for Work with Religious Organizations.

The purpose of the visit is to protect national and spiritual values, strengthen the attachment of our compatriots living abroad to their historical homeland, and convey the realities of Azerbaijan to the international community.

As part of the visit’s program, the delegation will visit the “Bullet-riddled statues,” the Yukhari Govhar Agha, Ashagi Govhar Agha, Saatli, and Mamayi mosques in Shusha, the Jidir Duzu plain, the Vagif Museum and Mausoleum Complex, and other historical and cultural landmarks.

World.title: Kazakhstan, WCO discuss customs digitalization, transit development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 8. Kazakhstan and the World Customs Organization (WCO) discussed cooperation in customs administration, digitalization, and the development of transport and logistics links in Central Asia.

This was announced by the press service of the Kazakh President, following the meeting between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and World Customs Organization (WCO) Secretary General Ian Saunders in Astana.

According to the information, in the course of the meeting, Tokayev noted the important role of cooperation with the World Customs Organization in improving legislation and enhancing the efficiency of customs administration in Kazakhstan.

The president emphasized that Kazakhstan is making significant efforts to strengthen transport connectivity in Eurasia and create favorable conditions for cargo transit. He also noted that the country is consistently developing a “smart border” model by applying digital solutions to optimize customs procedures.

In turn, Ian Saunders highly praised the steady development of contacts between the World Customs Organization and Kazakhstan, noting significant progress in improving customs administration, introducing modern digital solutions and strengthening the institutional capacity of relevant authorities.

The interlocutors confirmed their commitment to further strengthening mutually beneficial cooperation, which has been successfully developing for more than 30 years. The sides also exchanged views on new challenges and trends in global trade.

Particular attention was paid to prospects for expanding trade and economic ties and strengthening the transport and logistics potential of Central Asia.

World.title: Five killed as Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv after pause for US envoys' visit
World.content:
Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks on the Ukrainian capital after a brief halt for the visit of US peace negotiators, and killing five people.

Russia's main targets in its attacks on Monday night and Tuesday morning were Kyiv and the Odesa region of southern Ukraine.

The overnight attack caused fires in several districts across the Ukrainian capital, damaging at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.

Two people were killed in a strike on a warehouse, bringing the total death toll in the city to five, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Close to 30 people have been injured, authorities said. Officials from Russia reported three people killed and 13 wounded in areas it controls.

Explosions reverberated across the city as Russia kept menacing it with jet-powered drones into Tuesday afternoon.

"Kyiv was exploding and burning," Katarina Mathernova, the EU ambassador to Ukraine, said in a social media post.

Explosions were heard in Kyiv for nearly five hours, according to Ukraine's Minister of Internal Affairs of Ukraine Ivan Vyhivskyi.

More than 50 sites were damaged during the overnight attack, including residential buildings, dormitories, schools, shops, gas stations and a flour production plant, he said.

In a separate strike, a Russian drone partially destroyed a Ukrainian TV channel building in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called it "a horrific attack" and accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of undermining US peace efforts.

"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Mr Sybiha said on X, referring to Mr Putin.

" Strike after strike on residential buildings brings him no closer to winning this war — it is nothing but senseless terror. "

Kyiv has been battered in recent months by near-nightly drone and missile attacks. (Reuters: Yan Dobronosov)

The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces overnight launched a massive strike on Ukrainian military industry facilities.

It provided a detailed list of its targets, including places storing Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles, as well as transport, logistics and distribution centres for military cargo in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, the ministry said.

Trump and Putin hold call

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff visited Moscow and Kyiv for separate talks with Mr Putin and Mr Zelenskyy over the weekend.

It signalled the Trump administration's renewed push to end Russia's four-and-a-half year war in Ukraine.

The meetings appeared to produce no substantial breakthrough but the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of three-way negotiations also including the United States.

Both Moscow and Kyiv halted strikes on their capitals for three days to ensure the security of the US peace negotiators after which both then resumed their deadly air war.

In a call held between the two leaders on Tuesday, Mr Putin assured US President Donald Trump Russia did not harbour aggressive intentions towards Europe, after Germany accused Russia of orchestrating sabotage attacks on its soil.

Yuri Ushakov, Mr Putin's foreign affairs adviser, said the hour-long conversation between Mr Putin and Mr Trump was "constructive and quite frank".

Vladimir Putin shows no signs of backing down from his demands for concessions from Ukraine. (Reuters: Anastasia Barashkova)

There was no immediate White House comment on the call.

Mr Ushakov told reporters that "in view of the speculation about Russia's alleged hostile intentions toward European countries, it was underlined that we don't have any aggressive plans regarding Europe."

Mr Ushakov also said Mr Putin told Mr Trump about the combat situation in Ukraine and Russia's plans to make battlefield gains and achieve its military goals.

He said that Moscow has a positive view of the results of the weekend visit to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner.

"An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation's goals and tasks was given," Mr Ushakov said.

Zelenskyy-Trump meeting flagged

Meanwhile, Mr Zelenskyy said he is counting on meeting with Mr Trump around September 20, about the same time that the UN General Assembly is being held in New York.

He indicated he will press Mr Trump to provide more Patriot air defence systems that Kyiv needs to counter Russia's ballistic missiles.

Ukraine needs 300 Patriot missiles from its partners' stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors and $US2 billion ($2.7 billion) for more drones, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told the meeting of countries providing help.

Also on Tuesday, the European Commission approved a loan of 3.2 billion euros ($5.1 billion) for Kyiv to purchase components for Patriot air defence systems, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on its Telegram channel.

Mr Zelenskyy thanked US officials for their efforts to unblock negotiations with Russia, which have been stuck since early this year with little progress.

"As for the peace package that Kushner spoke about and the new ideas, I'll tell you frankly, there were indeed a couple of very good, worthwhile ideas," Mr Zelenskyy said in audio messages answering reporters' questions.

Wires

World.title: New documents reveal what NYC knew about air toxicity after 9/11
World.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has released more than 170,000 pages of documents showing that the city did not disclose all it knew about air toxicity after the September 11, 2001 attacks.

The release comes ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that killed 2,977 people, in the United States, mostly from the collapse of the Twin Towers in New York.

More than 9,400 have died from illnesses linked to their exposure to the area in the years since, according to a federal medical monitoring program.

"These are documents that show what the city knew about the toxic air around Ground Zero, when they knew it, and how they acted to limit liability," the mayor told a news conference.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani held a large event with advocates and politicians to announce the release. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

Mr Mamdani said the thousands of documents contain information on health concerns, air quality and the city's response to the attacks.

The release is part of an agreement with 9/11 Health Watch, a victims' advocacy group that had taken legal action to compel the city to make the documents public.

"For 25 years, four different Mayoral administrations kept from the public, the US Congress, and the City Council documents showing what the City actually knew about the danger of the toxic chemicals in Lower Manhattan and Western Brooklyn after the World Trade Center collapse, even as City officials continued messaging to the public that the air was 'safe and acceptable'," the group's director Benjamin Chevat said in a statement.

When asked about the names of officials who had withheld information from the public, Mr Mamdani said, "this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted."

Rudy Guliani was mayor of New York City at the time of the attacks.

In recent days, politicians including Mr Guliani and some relatives of September 11 victims have called for Mr Mamdani, NYC's first Muslim mayor, to skip this year's memorial. Other families have defended the mayor who says he will attend despite the criticism.

AFP

World.title: Dozens injured as Yemen's Houthis launch strikes on Saudi oil facilities
World.content:
Yemen's Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, setting fire to oil facilities and injuring more than 70 people.

The Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of Yemen's populated areas including the capital Sanaa, said they have launched an operation deep into Saudi territory, deploying drones and missiles to strike a Saudi air-base in the southern city of Khamis Mushait.

They also claim to have targeted spots belonging to Saudi Arabia's state oil company in nearby Abha, Najran on the Yemeni border and Jazan, a major Red Sea port city that houses a large refinery and power plant.

The move appears to be a major expansion of the war in the Midlde East which is now in its sixth month.

What the Houthis' Saudia Arabia blockade means The Houthi rebels, described as one of Iran's "merchants of chaos", have threatened to widen the conflict in the Middle East by declaring a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia. Here's what could happen next.

The reports of such large numbers of injured people suggested the attacks were among the biggest carried out against Saudi Arabia since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

Saudi authorities said women and children were among the 73 people hurt in the attacks.

NASA satellite images showed a thick cloud of black smoke over the Jazan refinery and a column of white smoke rising from an oil distribution centre in Abha.

A satellite image shows smoke rising from the Saudi Aramco distribution centre. (NASA Worldview via Reuters)

Confirmed images of the aftermath of the attacks in Saudi cities were not immediately available, and witnesses could not be reached in a country where media is tightly controlled.

The Houthis released pictures showing thick smoke and explosions of what they said were trucks from Saudi Arabia that they had hit in separate strikes at the border on Monday.

Houthi-controlled media reported later on Tuesday that Saudi war-planes had carried out four air-strikes in Yemen's Jubah district east of Sanaa.

Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree accused Riyadh of having escalated the war by launching air strikes on Yemen, and said the Houthis would respond.

But Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said they "will take all necessary operational measures to deter this terrorist militia and resolutely confronts its hostile approach".

Saudi military spokesman Colonel Turki al-Malki says Saudi Arabia "will take all necessary operational measures to deter" the Houthis. (AP: Amr Nabil)

Tuesday's attacks hit Saudi oil facilities connected to an alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb, a strategic waterway off the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

The International Organization for Migration said more than 18,500 people had fled their homes because of fighting along Yemen's west coast over the past three days.

Global oil prices rise as fighting renews

Houthi attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia have the potential to worsen the war's global economic impact by disrupting Middle East energy supplies beyond the blockaded Strait of Hormuz.

These latest attacks, along with Iran and the US exchanging fire over the weekend, has sent global oil prices surging back towards the prices seen at the peak of the war.

Trump looks for exit in protracted war The Iran war is showing signs it could drag on into next year as Iran seemingly looks to prolong Donald Trump's political pain for as long as possible.

Brent crude oil reached $US99.46 ($138) on Tuesday, the highest since mid-July, although the price eased a bit later in the day.

Washington is trying to increase the flow of oil to world markets by guiding ships through the Strait of Hormuz, while cutting off Iran's exports with a blockade.

Tehran has announced new measures to seal off the strait, saying it will soon unveil details of a "maritime exclusion zone" that will extend from the perimeter of the US blockade, through the strait and into the Gulf itself.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Israel closes UK consulate in East Jerusalem as three G7 countries ban settlement imports
World.content:
Britain, France and Canada will ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, in a move that prompted a swift retaliation and could spark a broader geo-political storm.

While several smaller nations have already adopted similar policies, Tuesday's announcement from the three G7 powers is much more significant.

The United Kingdom's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband revealed the plan in a speech in parliament on Tuesday, and two hours later, his Israeli counterpart Gideon Sa'ar announced that in response, his country would close the British consulate in East Jerusalem, among several other measures.

That facility had served as Britain's representative office for occupied Palestine. The UK's embassy in Tel Aviv remains unaffected.

An estimated 700,000 Israelis live in settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which are considered illegal under international law, although Israel disputes this.

Ma'ale Adumim, near Jerusalem, is among the most established Israeli settlements in the West Bank. (ABC News: Tim Swanston)

The announcement was widely telegraphed and drew condemnation from right-wing politicians in Israel, the country's president Isaac Herzog and US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee even before it was made official.

Israeli's Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the British ambassador to be expelled.

Meanwhile, Mr Sa'ar said on top of closing the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, the country's representatives would be removed from a support centre in Gaza and a training program in the West Bank. He also said 12 UK politicians who were "antisemitic" would be denied entry to Israel.

Israel's government and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have been criticised by much of the international community for accelerating the construction of settlements in the West Bank and not doing enough to stop violent attacks by Israelis on Palestinians there, while multiple wars have raged in the Middle East over the past three years.

Miliband says 'settler terrorists' carrying out 'ethnic cleansing'

The announcement by France, Britain and Canada on Tuesday also included commitments from nine other European nations that they intended to introduce or support similar bans in the future.

In his speech, Mr Miliband said "settler terrorists" were carrying out "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in the West Bank, and accused Israel's government of turning a "blind eye" to this.

Israel's government and PM have previously condemned settler violence, although some ministers have also openly campaigned for it.

France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot announced his country's ban on imports from Israeli settlements in a post on social media.

"Why are we doing this? Because the West Bank is close to exploding — there is frenzied expansion of the settlements, a flare up of violence against Palestinians by extremist settlers, and acts of terror which have been attacked by Israeli authorities themselves," he wrote on X.

The import restrictions are not expected to have a significant impact on the economies of France, Britain, Canada or Israel, and experts have warned it will be difficult to enforce.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar did not take long to announce retaliatory measures on the UK. (Reuters: Agustin Marcarian )

Dr Julie Norman, an associate fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Program at London-based think tank Chatham House, said the announcement was still significant.

"I think this is really important for middle powers to think about, that maybe directly their own ban or prohibition may not have a huge financial weight, but collectively with others, it will," she said.

Dr Norman said the ban could be extended in the future to include, specifically, IT companies, which would could hurt Israel's economy more.

Australia was not part of Tuesday's announcement, and in parliament earlier in the day, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the government was "not at this time pursuing a blanket-style import ban" on goods from Israeli settlements.

However, she said Australia would look at "targeted measures" to "deter illegal settlements and settler violence".

Several countries, including the UK and Australia have in the past 12 months announced they would or have recognised a Palestinian state.

Israel's decision to press ahead with plans to build a settlement on a particularly controversial parcel of land near Jerusalem, called E1, has been denounced as a diplomatic red line by several Western governments, and was referenced specifically by the nations introducing bans as one of the reasons behind their decisions.

World.title: Legendary horseman Paddy Payne Sr dies aged 90
World.content:
Legendary horseman and patriarch of the famous Australian racing family, Paddy Payne Sr, has died aged 90.

He was father of Michelle Payne, the first woman to win the Melbourne Cup, and husband to late Mary Payne, whom he had 10 children with.

Daughter Michelle took to social media to pay a tribute to her father, saying "RIP Dad. You finally get to go and see Mum again".

Paddy Payne (left) with daughter Michelle (centre) and son Stevie (right). (ABC Ballarat: Dominic Cansdale)

Racing Victoria issued a statement acknowledging the passing of the "legendary Ballarat horseman".

"Paddy was the patriarch of the Payne family as they established themselves as one of the most famous surnames in Australian racing," the statement continued.

Racing Victoria Chief Executive Aaron Morrison said "Paddy was the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing and provided us with so many great memories".

" Whilst Paddy has passed, his contribution to the sport will not be forgotten and his legacy will live on. "

Eight of Payne's 10 children became professional jockeys.

Daughter Michelle enjoyed multiple Group One triumphs, including her trailblazing 2015 Melbourne Cup win.

Michelle Payne's father never doubted her Paddy Payne said unlike many punters he thought Prince Of Penzance had a good chance of winning Australian racing's biggest prize.

Son Patrick also achieved great success in Group One racing, both as a jockey and a trainer.

Paddy Payne was immortalised in a film about Michelle's Melbourne Cup victory titled Ride Like a Girl, where he was played by the late Sam Neill.

Payne's wife Mary died in a car accident in 1986, leaving him to raise their children when Michelle was just six months old.

Later in life, two of his daughters died — Brigid in 2007 and Bernadette in 2025 — both were jockeys.

In an interview with the ABC in 2015, Payne said: "We've had some good success and some bad luck as well."

World.title: Three attacks in Tehran could 'amount to war crimes', report finds
World.content:
Amnesty International is demanding formal investigations into three American and Israeli attacks on densely packed suburbs in Tehran that killed at least 41 civilians, arguing the devastating impact and choice of weapons may amount to war crimes.

The advocacy group examined the March incidents, analysing photos and videos of the attacks available on social media as well as eyewitness accounts and official reports in Iranian state media to question the legitimacy of the strikes.

It found that the targets of the strikes, namely police stations and paramilitary compounds, may have been justified under international law.

But Amnesty said the damage to the surrounding areas, specifically civilian apartment blocks and businesses in congested neighbourhoods, should have been cause to rethink the attacks because of "entirely predictable consequences for civilians".

"Military combatants have to take feasible precautions to avoid civilian casualties," Andrew Witheford, a spokesperson for Amnesty International Australia, told the ABC.

"If it's possible, they need to give warning, and the strike itself and the action taken need to be proportionate to the military objectives that are being sought.

" Our analysis of these three attacks indicate that this bar wasn't cleared. "

Amnesty, which describes the US and Israel's war with Iran as unlawful, said the two countries must allow independent investigations of their conduct relating to the three attacks, as well as the widely criticised strike on the Minab school on the very first day of the war which killed 150 people, including 120 children.

When asked whether those countries would launch independent investigations, Mr Witheford said: "It saddens me to say that it's not looking good so far."

Loading...

'Horrific' scenes after early air strikes

One of the attacks investigated by Amnesty was on Niloufar Square in central Tehran on the evening of March 1, the second day of the war.

A police station appeared to be the target, but significant damage was reported to nearby apartment buildings and shops in the area.

Iranian officials said at least 20 civilians were killed in the strikes.

Amnesty said it had spoken to a local journalist, whom the organisation named "Kiana", who said that the scene was "horrific" and that between 15 and 20 apartment buildings had been damaged in the blasts.

Residential buildings were reduced to rubble near Niloufar Square. (AFP)

She told the organisation that a father and son working in a bakery were believed to be among the dead.

The second strike was on the Resalat neighbourhood in eastern Tehran, where Iranian officials said at least 16 people were killed, including 12 members of the same family, on the afternoon of March 9.

The strike there appeared to target a building belonging to the Basij, the Iranian regime's notorious paramilitary branch of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Amnesty's investigation revealed another three buildings were badly damaged, but the organisation could only verify one as being a residential block.

One source it spoke to insisted the residents of the building, known as Number 12, were all civilians, and said he had seen horrific injuries and bodies blown to pieces.

Despite threats from Trump, Iran's regime is 'at war with its own people' Three Iranians share their insights on life under the regime, as the war passes its fifth month.

At the time, the Israeli military had announced it was hitting Basij targets across the Iranian capital.

The third attack scrutinised by Amnesty occurred on March 13 in Javadieh, southern Tehran, where at least five people were killed.

The group described it as a "low-income neighbourhood characterised by aging infrastructure and small, closely packed homes and other civilian structures".

Again, a police station appeared to be the target. But Iranian state media reported a number of other buildings were either destroyed or seriously damaged, including an apartment block and nearby businesses.

Amnesty said it had reviewed a photograph published by state media and believed it showed components of an American guided missile system used by the US and Israeli militaries.

Effects extend 'well beyond' targets

The United States and Israel are yet to respond to Amnesty's report but have previously defended their military actions as lawful.

Both countries have said they do not target civilians.

Amnesty said the control the Iranian regime has over the country's police force may have made the police stations lawful military targets — despite police generally being considered civilian in many circumstances.

It also said the Basij, being paramilitary, may also have qualified "as a military objective under international humanitarian law".

But it argued its analysis of the three strikes raised "serious concerns" about breaches of international law, "particularly the principles of distinction and precautions in attack."

Loading...

In Niloufar, Amnesty argued the presence of civilians was predictable.

"Even if the police station could qualify as a military objective … the timing and location, the presence of civilians in surrounding residential buildings, restaurants and public spaces required the attacking forces to take all feasible precautions to avoid or minimise incidental death of or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects," it said.

"The extensive blast damage affecting numerous apartment blocks, a school, and commercial premises, coupled with reports of significant civilian casualties, suggests the use of explosive weapons with wide area effects.

" The use in a densely populated area of a weapon whose effects extend well beyond the targeted object raises serious concerns regarding the respect of the principles of distinction and precaution. "

Israel undertaking genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, Amnesty International claims A new 300-page report alleges Israel has and continues to undertake acts of genocide against Palestinian people in Gaza.

In Javadieh, Amnesty said the concerns around harm to civilians should have been considered.

"The reported blast radius, extending up to 50 metres, and the scale of damage to homes and commercial properties indicate that the effects of the attack were not limited to the intended target," it said.

In Resalat, the organisation said it was likely a building other than the Basij compound was hit in a separate strike.

"Investigations should clarify whether any residential buildings that were struck were intentionally targeted, or whether they were struck recklessly despite indications that they were civilian objects," Amnesty said.

"If so, those attacks may amount to war crimes."

Hundreds of civilians have been killed since the Iran war began on February 28, with estimates ranging from 1,700 to more than 3,400.

Mr Witheford said Iran had also contributed to civilian deaths during the war, both through attacking other countries and executing its own people.

"The laws of war apply to the Iranian military as well, and they have dropped the ball in this case as well," he said.

Mr Witheford said Amnesty approached both the Israeli and United States militaries for input on its report and did not receive a response.

World.title: Football league says Swans scandal comments 'clearly insensitive'
World.content:
A country football league has distanced itself from "insensitive" and "unacceptable" comments made at a recent awards event at which the master of ceremonies joked about the Sydney Swans scandal.

But the league also said that, "in his defence", the man was attempting "to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve".

In video posted online, the MC at the Whyalla Football League's event made light-hearted reference to the Swans scandal, citing it in the context of local club South Whyalla's upcoming match.

The man, Jock Sleep, suggested the local club draw inspiration from Sydney's win over Brisbane in Saturday's AFL qualifying final, linking that performance to the scandal engulfing the Swans.

"My advice to the Souths' coach … [is] maybe we can manufacture a good old-fashioned scandal just to get that team going," the MC said.

"It worked for the Sydney Swans. I'm just talking a scandal — not a real big one."

Last week, Victoria Police detectives spoke with four Sydney Swans players as part of their sexual assault investigation linked to the club.

A still from the video shared online. (Facebook)

The man's remarks at the Whyalla awards night were strongly condemned by Australian Femicide Watch's Sherele Moody, who shared video on her social media pages and described the comments as "terrible".

"The crowd at the awards night laughed along with him. There was no attempt to shut down the conversation by the organisers," she wrote.

In a statement, Whyalla Football League president Keith Sichler said Mr Sleep was a "well-known local identity" and local football historian.

"His comments and joke were clearly insensitive and not indicative of current attitudes. In his defence, it was merely an attempt to show how certain events can galvanise a team's resolve with the intent of improving their performance. Nothing more," Mr Sichler said.

"Nonetheless, references of this nature are unacceptable and inconsistent with the inclusive and respectful environment we expect across our League.

"The WFL has spoken with him, and he understands the impact of his remarks and has expressed regret for any harm caused."

The ABC has reached out directly to Mr Sleep for comment.

Last week, the Swans said five players would remain stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August, regardless of how an ongoing police investigation unfolded.

Victoria Police has interviewed four Sydney men as part of an investigation into sexual assault allegations during a post-AFL match party at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel.

World.title: Thieves steal two paintings from Renoir Museum worth 9 million euros
World.content:
Thieves have stolen two paintings from the Renoir Museum in France via a hole made in a garden fence.

The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, said a group of "well-equipped" and "well-informed" thieves broke into the museum dedicated to French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, early Tuesday, local time.

They sliced through a fence and entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Mr Masson said.

Coco Lisant (1905) by Renoir, one of the paintings reportedly stolen. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

The museum had 12 works by Renoir in total, four were stolen, but two canvases were dropped during the police chase and found in the museum garden.

Local French newspaper Nice-Matin reported the paintings as Portrait of Madame Pichon (1895), Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910), Coco Lisant (1905) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).

The mayor confirmed Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano and Jeune fille au puits were the two artworks still missing.

Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (left) and Portrait of Madame Pichon (right) by Renoir. (Wikimedia Commons: Pierre-Auguste Renoir)

Mr Masson's office estimated the value of the stolen works at 9 million euros ($14.5 million).

"Spotted thanks to the town's video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran," Mr Masson said.

Mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer Bryan Masson makes a statement outside the Musee Renoir after four paintings were stolen. (AFP: Valery Hache)

"The museum alarm went off at 5:48am. At 5:53am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene.

"Since this morning, both the municipal and national police have been deployed to the site.

" The perpetrators are being actively sought, and the investigation is ongoing. "

The museum was closed Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.

The mayor said it took five minutes for authorities to respond. (AFP: Valery Hache)

The Renoir Museum was opened in 1960 in the painter's last home before his death in 1919.

Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes, and nudes painted by the artist.

Spate of art heists in Europe

The theft comes less than a year after jewels valued at around 88 million euros ($141 million) were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris.

The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items still have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.

How the Louvre jewellery heist was pulled off Here are the details on the items stolen in the Louvre heist that unfolded in broad daylight in Paris.

In August, three century-old paintings, including a Renoir, stolen by an organised gang from an Italian museum during a three-minute heist were recovered.

The artworks included Fish by Auguste Renoir, Paul Cézanne's Still Life with Cherries, and Odalisque on the Terrace by Henri Matisse.

Days after their recovery, another four paintings were stolen from another Italian museum.

Artworks by 15th century painter Antonello da Messina were taken from the Museo Regionale di Messina — the pieces some of the only surviving work by the Renaissance painter to have remained in his native city.

ABC/AFP/AP

World.title: Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank
World.content:
WorldEuropeIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Israel targets UK in response to sanctions on settlements in West Bank David Crowe September 9, 2026 — 3:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Israel has slammed a move by a dozen countries to impose trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, launching a furious diplomatic response after Britain accused it of allowing “ethnic cleansing” in the contested lands. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar rebuked the British government for what he called its “morally distorted” decision to punish the country and the settlers, declaring that Israel had to respond to the “hostile” moves. The British Consulate in East Jerusalem. AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean The dispute also intensified arguments within Israel over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the lead-up to the country’s elections on October 27, with a key political rival accusing him of being taken by surprise by the international action. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband led the sanctions push by blaming Israel for allowing illegal settlements in the West Bank and failing to stop “ethnic cleansing” and violence against Palestinian communities losing their land.



While Israel targeted Britain with its response, including the closure of the consulate in Jerusalem, countries ranging from Canada to Denmark, France and Sweden also backed the trade moves over the settlements. Miliband said terrorist group Hamas should play no role in the future governance of Gaza, and he declared in parliament that Israel had the right to stop terrorism, protect its people and defend its territory. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband blamed Israel for allowing illegal settlements in the West Bank. Getty Images He argued, however, that this did not justify the extent of the destruction in Gaza, where he said more than 70,000 people had been killed, and he said the people of Gaza were suffering an avoidable catastrophe. “International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars - including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians,” he said.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Penny Wong prepares new sanctions against Israel but no trade ban “Serious and intentional violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes.” Miliband backed a United Nations inquiry into Gaza and cited genocides in the past in Rwanda and other countries, although he did not state explicitly that Israel was engaged in genocide. On the settlements in the West Bank, an area home to 3.4 million Palestinians but claimed by some Israeli settlers, he accused the Israel Defence Forces of protecting illegal settlers who intimidated local communities. “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank – perpetrated by settler terrorists,” he said.



The British sanctions are to be imposed in the coming months on companies and individuals providing services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” Miliband said. The new measures include a ban on advertising settlements. The UK’s Chief Rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, called the sanctions a “dark day for British Jews” and likened them to “gesture politics”. The Greens said they did not go far enough, while the Conservative Party opposed them. The Israeli foreign minister invoked one of the historic steps toward the creation of Israel, the Balfour Declaration by the British government in 1917, to argue that the Jewish people had rights to Judea and Samaria, the Israeli names for some of the contested lands. “The Israeli public overwhelmingly supports the communities in Judea and Samaria, and overwhelmingly opposes the establishment of a Palestinian terror state in the heart of our land,” Sa’ar said.



“This is something that the Labour government is attempting, through measures that are doomed to fail, to force upon Israel. It will not work. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, drawing sharp rebukes “We did not return to our land after 2000 years only to lose it under pressure from jihadists, Islamists, anti-Semites, far-leftists and wokes. “Not only will you fail to harm us, you will harm yourselves and your own influence.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled the action on Gaza and the West Bank in one of his first remarks as leader, saying in early July the government had to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government.



Miliband prepared for the reaction from the Israeli government by citing senior Jewish figures who criticised the settlements. Former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert has called the settlements a “violent and criminal effort to ethnically cleanse territories” in the West Bank. Former Israeli army officer and health minister Ephraim Sneh has also called the settlements “ethnic cleansing”. One of Netanhayu’s key rivals in the coming election, Yesh Atid party leader Yair Lapid, rejected the British decision and said it would strengthen extremist voices inside Israel and encourage Hamas terrorists. “The British government’s decision to impose boycotts and sanctions on Israel is fundamentally flawed and dangerous policy, implemented at the wrong time and for the wrong reasons,” Lapid said in a statement.



At the same time, he accused Netanyahu of doing too little to counter the moves by countries acting alongside Britain to sanction the settlements. “For a whole week, the government has been preparing us for sanctions from Britain, and then it turns out that another 10 [sic] important countries have joined it and no one knew,” he said. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Could this grieving political novice defeat Netanyahu? The polls say yes “Didn’t they wake him up?” This appeared to be a reference to Netanyahu. The dispute over Netanyahu’s ability to anticipate events came after major investigations by Israeli media, including The Times of Israel, claimed the prime minister was warned of imminent violence from Hamas before the attack on October 7, 2023.



Britain was joined by 11 countries in the sanctions on settlements. Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden said they were considering or going ahead with restrictions on trade with settlements that were illegal under international law. The 12 countries all go further than Australia, given that Foreign Minister Penny Wong has signalled plans for “targeted measures” but has rejected a “blanket-style import ban” on goods produced in the settlements. World.title: The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school Danny Russell Updated September 8, 2026 — 10:34pm ,first published 6:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the stories told about racing patriarch Paddy Payne, few better encapsulated the loving, chaotic nature of his life than the day he dropped off youngest daughter Michelle for her first day of secondary school. It was one of his forgetful moments – a memory lapse that could be brought on by running farms, training horses and raising 10 rowdy kids. A moment that would happen almost 30 years before his peaceful death at home on Tuesday at the age of 90. Paddy Payne, father of 2015 Melbourne Cup winning jockey Michelle Payne, at his family home where he raised his 10 children in Miners Rest. Jesse Marlow The year was 1998, and Michelle, not long turned 13, was following in her sisters’ footsteps. They, too, had gone to Ballarat’s Loreto College. But soon after her father drove in from Miners Rest and dropped her at the school gates, Michelle was hit by a confronting reality: no one could find her name on the classroom lists.



Related Article CBD The next big change coming for pregnant Michelle Payne Confused, she went to the front office with a friend. There she was told she hadn’t been enrolled. “I started to get a bit sad and was nearly crying, and they’re like, ‘don’t cry, it’s okay. We’ll call your dad’,” Michelle told The Age last year. “And they ring dad, who is home by this stage after dropping us off, and they said, ‘Oh, we’re just here with your daughter, Mr Payne, we just have a problem: You haven’t enrolled her’. “And he was like, ‘Ah, haven’t I?’ Because I could hear him. He’s always louder over the phone speaker. And he goes, ‘Oh, sorry about that’.



“They’re like, ‘Oh, that’s alright. We’ll try and find her a spot’. So they found me a classroom. Thank God they understood, you know, because he was doing his best – a single parent raising 10 kids.” Born in Hawera in South Taranaki, New Zealand, Payne’s best turned out to be pretty good. His life was upended in 1986 when his wife, Mary, was killed in a car accident near Ballarat. Initially, there was talk of farming out the youngest children to other families to help ease the burden. Michelle was just six months old. But the patriarch wanted to keep the family together and decided to raise the children on his own. “My dad always talked about her to me, always told me what a beautiful lady she was,” Michelle recalled in an interview when she was 24.



“It was probably hard for the older kids who remembered her to talk about her. They had their memories they kept to themselves. Dad used to tell me every day how lucky he was. I think it was good for him to get it out, but it was good for me too.” Under Payne’s guidance, the family would go on to leave an indelible mark on the sport of racing. Maree, Cathy and Bernadette Payne at Flemington. Neil Newitt Eight of the 10 kids would become jockeys – Brigid, Bernadette, Therese, Patrick, Andrew, Maree, Cathy and Michelle. Only Margaret and Stevie would not ride in a race. Patrick, Andrew and Michelle would later become trainers like their father.



“He passed away peacefully in his sleep, early this morning at home, he got to have his dying wish,” daughter Therese said in a family statement on Thursday. “We feel he had a great life, and we were happy he was comfortable. We hope he’s joined our mum and brother and sisters.” The Paynes lost son Michael in 1985, three days after he was born. Eldest sister Brigid died in 2007 from a heart attack, six months after a bad track work fall, while the family lost second-eldest daughter Bernadette in March last year. Mercifully, there were high points in between. Patrick Jr won the 2002 Cox Plate on Northerly and Michelle would create history by becoming the first woman to ride the winner of the Melbourne Cup in 2015.



Michelle’s trailblazing exploits would be captured in the film Ride Like a Girl. Her father was portrayed by the late, great Kiwi actor Sam Neill, while his youngest son Stevie would play himself, the strapper of Prince Of Penzance. Michelle rode her first winner as a 15-year-old on her father’s horse Reigning in front of her cheering schoolmates at Ballarat. Soon after the victory, her father suggested she chuck it in and go back to school. Michelle Payne with brother Stevie and 2015 Melbourne Cup winner Prince Of Penzance. Getty Images “For the first six months, Dad was saying, ‘You just don’t seem to have it. All the other kids showed a little bit of potential...’,” Michelle said. “I remembered him telling the other kids that they weren’t any good either, telling Maree she could only sit one leg either side and move her little fingers, that was all she could do.



“I knew it wasn’t just me, but it made me so angry. It made me more determined to try harder and prove him wrong.” In some ways, she did prove him wrong. Payne was always a big supporter of female jockeys and knew they would one day win the Melbourne Cup. He just didn’t dream it would be one of his daughters. Patrick and Michelle Payne. Getty Images Apart from his lifelong love of horses, Payne was also a dairy farmer. He spent his final years at the family property at Miners Rest near Ballarat. Michelle and Stevie lived nearby. His last runner was Nip at Kilmore on March 6 this year, 10 days before his 90th birthday, while his final winner was Rosalia at Ballarat in August 2024 when he was 88.



His filly Miner’s Miss, ridden by Michelle, finished third in the 2018 VRC Oaks. It gave the entire family a thrill. “I worked my whole life with him and started my apprenticeship with him and I can’t remember him having a runner in a group 1, let alone riding for him in one,” Payne told The Age before the race. “Riding for him in a group 1 is so special.” While Payne won races over the jumps in New Zealand, the galloper that would help set him up for life was Our Paddy Boy, a horse he bought in New Zealand for $1300 in the late 1970s who would go on to win the 1980 group 1 Ellerslie Sires’ Produce Stakes (1400m). Payne sold Our Paddy Boy to Robert Sangster for $300,000, a transaction that would bankroll the family’s movie to Australia. They intended to come for two years and never left. As the Payne family mourned the loss of their father on Thursday, the tributes poured in from the racing world.



Racing Victoria chief executive Aaron Morrison called him “the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing”. “Paddy will be remembered as a great horseman and a loving father,” Morrison said. “His positive influence on female jockey participation cannot be undersold, having encouraged his daughters to ride at a time when female jockeys were fighting for acceptance.” Victorian Jockeys’ Association chief executive Matt Hyland said the state’s riding ranks were richer for the Payne family’s contributions, and “for that we must say thank you to Paddy”. Australian Trainers’ Association chief executive Stephen Bell said Payne held a trainer’s licence in Victoria for more than 40 years after earlier success in New Zealand. “His role in nurturing a family that has contributed so much to racing is legendary and something that we all respect and are thankful for,” Bell said.



Ballarat Turf Club chairman Bill Gribble said Payne’s contribution to racing extended well beyond the racetrack. “Paddy was the patriarch one of Australian racing’s most remarkable families, and his influence, horsemanship and dedication to the industry will leave a lasting legacy,” Gribble said. World.title: Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’ Shane Wright September 8, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost of the age pension to taxpayers will fall even as more than 9 million people reach retirement age over the next 40 years, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal on Wednesday amid accusations that the next election will be an existential fight for the future of superannuation. As the Liberal Party signalled it was looking at allowing young people to access their super to get out of the rental market, Chalmers will argue Australia is defying a global trend in age pension cost blowouts because of the superannuation system. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will release data showing the cost to the budget of the age pension is falling – due to superannuation. Alex Ellinghausen One Nation this week revealed that if it formed government, renters and people with a mortgage could take a quarter of their 12 per cent super guarantee as income for up to three years in a move it said would deliver $44 a week to someone on the median wage. It has since struggled to explain how the policy would work, denied it would add to inflation while reducing retirement incomes, and prompted One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce to declare he was “not Jesus Christ” when pressed by ABC’s 7.30 to outline key elements of his party’s plan.



Chalmers, in a speech to the Super Members Council on Wednesday, will reveal findings of the upcoming intergenerational report that is due to be delivered on September 21. The report, instigated by Peter Costello in 2002, outlines key pressures on the budget over the coming four decades. Related Article Analysis

Superannuation One Nation’s super raid: inflationary today, impoverishing tomorrow According to Chalmers, the latest intergenerational report will show that by 2066, there will be about 9 million people over the age pension age of 67. But the number of people on the pension is expected to fall from 66 per cent last year to 52 per cent. Budget spending on the pension is expected to fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP last year to 1.8 per cent by the mid-2060s. By contrast, pension spending is expected to reach 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand and 6 per cent in the US.



“That is phenomenal in an ageing society, and it’s essential,” Chalmers will say. “Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence. “Having super at the core of the best retirement incomes system in the world means pension spending as a share of the economy will be the lowest in the OECD, but even as those costs moderate, retirees will have more economic security, not less.” Chalmers will reveal that the median retirement age super balance will approach $450,000 by the mid-2030s. That would be more than double the current estimated $200,000 and well up on the $115,000 of 2015. In Costello’s first intergenerational report, the age pension was forecast to climb to 4.6 per cent of GDP by 2046-47 and continue to increase. At the time, the superannuation guarantee levy was legislated to rise to 9 per cent.



The guarantee reached 12 per cent last financial year. In Chalmers’ 2023 intergenerational report, Treasury expected the age pension to cost 2 per cent of GDP by the early 2060s. On Tuesday, the Australian Financial Review revealed that the Liberal Party under Sussan Ley costed a policy almost identical to that unveiled by Hanson. Under the Liberal proposal, while a worker could withdraw three percentage points of their super, there was no time limit. And rather than coming through a person’s super fund as proposed by One Nation, payments would come directly from a person’s employer. The extra pay would be taxed at a person’s marginal rate. This would deliver an extra $1 billion in personal income tax to the government every year as superannuation is taxed at a concessional rate.



Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said the Coalition was concerned that more people would enter retirement as renters. Related Article Superannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy “If we are going to become almost a majority nation of retired renters, then we need to look very carefully at how these things are calibrated,” he said. But Chalmers will argue both the Coalition and One Nation were intent on dismantling superannuation in a move that would hurt the budget and the retirement incomes of older Australians. “We’re witnessing now the biggest threat to compulsory super, with preservation at its core, in the four decades since it began.



“The next election will be super’s existential moment. It will help determine whether we make the most of our intergenerational advantages or trash them.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Stayin’ alive on that big dipper
World.content:
The Brothers Gibb (C8) sure got around back in the day, going by this latest encounter. Les Herbert of Concord recalls that “in 1963, my brother Paul, then aged 14 was a friend of Bandstand regular Trevor Gordon who invited him to Luna Park where they spent the day with a couple of other 14-year-olds, Gibb twins, Maurice and Robin. He reminisced on that story over many years. On a sad note, not one of the four from that day made the age of 65.”

“Robyn Cashman suggests a Cathy Wilcox book would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list,” notes Maralyn Lawson of Greenwich. ” A wonderful idea. Europe Since Versailles : A History in One Hundred Cartoons with a Narrative Text (1940) by the New Zealand-born political cartoonist David Low was brilliant teaching resource. Like Wilcox, Low encapsulated dire circumstances with honesty, wit and a depth of understanding which clarified complexity and human failing without rancour.”

“Don’t know about a book,” says Barry Riley of Woy Woy. “But surely, there’s an art gallery somewhere dedicated to Cathy Wilcox’s work.”

Merilyn McClung of Forestville rejoins the name (change) game: “I suggest that north of the 40th parallel in the US be renamed (C8) Canada South and the remainder North Mexico. That will rid the world of this troublesome president.” Grand idea. Now you just have to talk those two nations into taking on a $US40 trillion ($55.3 trillion) debt.

“Being retired and having time on my hands and needing a good laugh, I thought I might attend the ICAC inquiry (C8),” says Paul Duncan of Leura. “But then I realised I’d better not in case I contracted the memory loss, which seems to be contagious, and could not find my way home.” Jeff McNamara of Ulverstone (Tas) adds: “Seems Ray Hadley (as a witness in the Alan Jones trial) has also been infected with Amnesia testium following outbreaks in the ICAC inquiries. Better get the N95 face masks out if you’re in Sydney at the moment.”

The owner of Queen’s Wharf has taken Brisbane City Council to court in a bid to reduce a multimillion-dollar unpaid rates bill.

Deputy Mayor Fiona Cunningham told City Hall on Tuesday Destination Brisbane Consortium had commenced proceedings in the Supreme Court of Queensland against the local government and the state valuer-general.

It is disputing its land valuations and growing debt, having not paid rates since opening.

The Queen’s Wharf complex is owned by Destination Brisbane Consortium, which is challenging council over its rates bill of some $30 million. Courtney Kruk

A spokesperson for the lord mayor’s office said the amount owed was in the realm of $30 million.

The Israeli foreign minister invoked one of the historic steps toward the creation of Israel, the Balfour Declaration by the British government in 1917, to argue that the Jewish people had rights to Judea and Samaria, the Israeli names for some of the contested lands. “The Israeli public overwhelmingly supports the communities in Judea and Samaria, and overwhelmingly opposes the establishment of a Palestinian terror state in the heart of our land,” Sa’ar said.



“This is something that the Labour government is attempting, through measures that are doomed to fail, to force upon Israel. It will not work. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, drawing sharp rebukes “We did not return to our land after 2000 years only to lose it under pressure from jihadists, Islamists, anti-Semites, far-leftists and wokes. “Not only will you fail to harm us, you will harm yourselves and your own influence.” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled the action on Gaza and the West Bank in one of his first remarks as leader, saying in early July the government had to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government.



Miliband prepared for the reaction from the Israeli government by citing senior Jewish figures who criticised the settlements. Former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert has called the settlements a “violent and criminal effort to ethnically cleanse territories” in the West Bank. Former Israeli army officer and health minister Ephraim Sneh has also called the settlements “ethnic cleansing”. One of Netanhayu’s key rivals in the coming election, Yesh Atid party leader Yair Lapid, rejected the British decision and said it would strengthen extremist voices inside Israel and encourage Hamas terrorists. “The British government’s decision to impose boycotts and sanctions on Israel is fundamentally flawed and dangerous policy, implemented at the wrong time and for the wrong reasons,” Lapid said in a statement.



At the same time, he accused Netanyahu of doing too little to counter the moves by countries acting alongside Britain to sanction the settlements. “For a whole week, the government has been preparing us for sanctions from Britain, and then it turns out that another 10 [sic] important countries have joined it and no one knew,” he said. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Could this grieving political novice defeat Netanyahu? The polls say yes “Didn’t they wake him up?” This appeared to be a reference to Netanyahu. The dispute over Netanyahu’s ability to anticipate events came after major investigations by Israeli media, including The Times of Israel, claimed the prime minister was warned of imminent violence from Hamas before the attack on October 7, 2023.



Britain was joined by 11 countries in the sanctions on settlements. Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden said they were considering or going ahead with restrictions on trade with settlements that were illegal under international law. The 12 countries all go further than Australia, given that Foreign Minister Penny Wong has signalled plans for “targeted measures” but has rejected a “blanket-style import ban” on goods produced in the settlements.
