World.title: The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing The loving memory of Michelle Payne’s father that almost made her cry at school Danny Russell Updated September 8, 2026 — 10:34pm ,first published 6:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Of all the stories told about racing patriarch Paddy Payne, few better encapsulated the loving, chaotic nature of his life than the day he dropped off youngest daughter Michelle for her first day of secondary school. It was one of his forgetful moments – a memory lapse that could be brought on by running farms, training horses and raising 10 rowdy kids. A moment that would happen almost 30 years before his peaceful death at home on Tuesday at the age of 90. Paddy Payne, father of 2015 Melbourne Cup winning jockey Michelle Payne, at his family home where he raised his 10 children in Miners Rest. Jesse Marlow The year was 1998, and Michelle, not long turned 13, was following in her sisters’ footsteps. They, too, had gone to Ballarat’s Loreto College. But soon after her father drove in from Miners Rest and dropped her at the school gates, Michelle was hit by a confronting reality: no one could find her name on the classroom lists.



Related Article CBD The next big change coming for pregnant Michelle Payne Confused, she went to the front office with a friend. There she was told she hadn’t been enrolled. “I started to get a bit sad and was nearly crying, and they’re like, ‘don’t cry, it’s okay. We’ll call your dad’,” Michelle told The Age last year. “And they ring dad, who is home by this stage after dropping us off, and they said, ‘Oh, we’re just here with your daughter, Mr Payne, we just have a problem: You haven’t enrolled her’. “And he was like, ‘Ah, haven’t I?’ Because I could hear him. He’s always louder over the phone speaker. And he goes, ‘Oh, sorry about that’.



“They’re like, ‘Oh, that’s alright. We’ll try and find her a spot’. So they found me a classroom. Thank God they understood, you know, because he was doing his best – a single parent raising 10 kids.” Born in Hawera in South Taranaki, New Zealand, Payne’s best turned out to be pretty good. His life was upended in 1986 when his wife, Mary, was killed in a car accident near Ballarat. Initially, there was talk of farming out the youngest children to other families to help ease the burden. Michelle was just six months old. But the patriarch wanted to keep the family together and decided to raise the children on his own. “My dad always talked about her to me, always told me what a beautiful lady she was,” Michelle recalled in an interview when she was 24.



“It was probably hard for the older kids who remembered her to talk about her. They had their memories they kept to themselves. Dad used to tell me every day how lucky he was. I think it was good for him to get it out, but it was good for me too.” Under Payne’s guidance, the family would go on to leave an indelible mark on the sport of racing. Maree, Cathy and Bernadette Payne at Flemington. Neil Newitt Eight of the 10 kids would become jockeys – Brigid, Bernadette, Therese, Patrick, Andrew, Maree, Cathy and Michelle. Only Margaret and Stevie would not ride in a race. Patrick, Andrew and Michelle would later become trainers like their father.



“He passed away peacefully in his sleep, early this morning at home, he got to have his dying wish,” daughter Therese said in a family statement on Thursday. “We feel he had a great life, and we were happy he was comfortable. We hope he’s joined our mum and brother and sisters.” The Paynes lost son Michael in 1985, three days after he was born. Eldest sister Brigid died in 2007 from a heart attack, six months after a bad track work fall, while the family lost second-eldest daughter Bernadette in March last year. Mercifully, there were high points in between. Patrick Jr won the 2002 Cox Plate on Northerly and Michelle would create history by becoming the first woman to ride the winner of the Melbourne Cup in 2015.



Michelle’s trailblazing exploits would be captured in the film Ride Like a Girl. Her father was portrayed by the late, great Kiwi actor Sam Neill, while his youngest son Stevie would play himself, the strapper of Prince Of Penzance. Michelle rode her first winner as a 15-year-old on her father’s horse Reigning in front of her cheering schoolmates at Ballarat. Soon after the victory, her father suggested she chuck it in and go back to school. Michelle Payne with brother Stevie and 2015 Melbourne Cup winner Prince Of Penzance. Getty Images “For the first six months, Dad was saying, ‘You just don’t seem to have it. All the other kids showed a little bit of potential...’,” Michelle said. “I remembered him telling the other kids that they weren’t any good either, telling Maree she could only sit one leg either side and move her little fingers, that was all she could do.



“I knew it wasn’t just me, but it made me so angry. It made me more determined to try harder and prove him wrong.” In some ways, she did prove him wrong. Payne was always a big supporter of female jockeys and knew they would one day win the Melbourne Cup. He just didn’t dream it would be one of his daughters. Patrick and Michelle Payne. Getty Images Apart from his lifelong love of horses, Payne was also a dairy farmer. He spent his final years at the family property at Miners Rest near Ballarat. Michelle and Stevie lived nearby. His last runner was Nip at Kilmore on March 6 this year, 10 days before his 90th birthday, while his final winner was Rosalia at Ballarat in August 2024 when he was 88.



His filly Miner’s Miss, ridden by Michelle, finished third in the 2018 VRC Oaks. It gave the entire family a thrill. “I worked my whole life with him and started my apprenticeship with him and I can’t remember him having a runner in a group 1, let alone riding for him in one,” Payne told The Age before the race. “Riding for him in a group 1 is so special.” While Payne won races over the jumps in New Zealand, the galloper that would help set him up for life was Our Paddy Boy, a horse he bought in New Zealand for $1300 in the late 1970s who would go on to win the 1980 group 1 Ellerslie Sires’ Produce Stakes (1400m). Payne sold Our Paddy Boy to Robert Sangster for $300,000, a transaction that would bankroll the family’s movie to Australia. They intended to come for two years and never left. As the Payne family mourned the loss of their father on Thursday, the tributes poured in from the racing world.



Racing Victoria chief executive Aaron Morrison called him “the doyen of a family that has greatly enriched Australian racing”. “Paddy will be remembered as a great horseman and a loving father,” Morrison said. “His positive influence on female jockey participation cannot be undersold, having encouraged his daughters to ride at a time when female jockeys were fighting for acceptance.” Victorian Jockeys’ Association chief executive Matt Hyland said the state’s riding ranks were richer for the Payne family’s contributions, and “for that we must say thank you to Paddy”. Australian Trainers’ Association chief executive Stephen Bell said Payne held a trainer’s licence in Victoria for more than 40 years after earlier success in New Zealand. “His role in nurturing a family that has contributed so much to racing is legendary and something that we all respect and are thankful for,” Bell said.



Ballarat Turf Club chairman Bill Gribble said Payne’s contribution to racing extended well beyond the racetrack. “Paddy was the patriarch one of Australian racing’s most remarkable families, and his influence, horsemanship and dedication to the industry will leave a lasting legacy,” Gribble said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’
World.content:
PoliticsFederalSuperannuation Super-sized political battle: Chalmers issues warning on ‘existential threat’ Shane Wright September 8, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cost of the age pension to taxpayers will fall even as more than 9 million people reach retirement age over the next 40 years, Treasurer Jim Chalmers will reveal on Wednesday amid accusations that the next election will be an existential fight for the future of superannuation. As the Liberal Party signalled it was looking at allowing young people to access their super to get out of the rental market, Chalmers will argue Australia is defying a global trend in age pension cost blowouts because of the superannuation system. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will release data showing the cost to the budget of the age pension is falling – due to superannuation. Alex Ellinghausen One Nation this week revealed that if it formed government, renters and people with a mortgage could take a quarter of their 12 per cent super guarantee as income for up to three years in a move it said would deliver $44 a week to someone on the median wage. It has since struggled to explain how the policy would work, denied it would add to inflation while reducing retirement incomes, and prompted One Nation’s treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce to declare he was “not Jesus Christ” when pressed by ABC’s 7.30 to outline key elements of his party’s plan.



Chalmers, in a speech to the Super Members Council on Wednesday, will reveal findings of the upcoming intergenerational report that is due to be delivered on September 21. The report, instigated by Peter Costello in 2002, outlines key pressures on the budget over the coming four decades. Related Article Analysis

Superannuation One Nation’s super raid: inflationary today, impoverishing tomorrow According to Chalmers, the latest intergenerational report will show that by 2066, there will be about 9 million people over the age pension age of 67. But the number of people on the pension is expected to fall from 66 per cent last year to 52 per cent. Budget spending on the pension is expected to fall from 2.3 per cent of GDP last year to 1.8 per cent by the mid-2060s. By contrast, pension spending is expected to reach 10 per cent by 2060 in the UK, 8 per cent in Canada, 7 per cent in New Zealand and 6 per cent in the US.



“That is phenomenal in an ageing society, and it’s essential,” Chalmers will say. “Super takes serious pressure off social security outlays and makes the budget much more sustainable as a consequence. “Having super at the core of the best retirement incomes system in the world means pension spending as a share of the economy will be the lowest in the OECD, but even as those costs moderate, retirees will have more economic security, not less.” Chalmers will reveal that the median retirement age super balance will approach $450,000 by the mid-2030s. That would be more than double the current estimated $200,000 and well up on the $115,000 of 2015. In Costello’s first intergenerational report, the age pension was forecast to climb to 4.6 per cent of GDP by 2046-47 and continue to increase. At the time, the superannuation guarantee levy was legislated to rise to 9 per cent.



The guarantee reached 12 per cent last financial year. In Chalmers’ 2023 intergenerational report, Treasury expected the age pension to cost 2 per cent of GDP by the early 2060s. On Tuesday, the Australian Financial Review revealed that the Liberal Party under Sussan Ley costed a policy almost identical to that unveiled by Hanson. Under the Liberal proposal, while a worker could withdraw three percentage points of their super, there was no time limit. And rather than coming through a person’s super fund as proposed by One Nation, payments would come directly from a person’s employer. The extra pay would be taxed at a person’s marginal rate. This would deliver an extra $1 billion in personal income tax to the government every year as superannuation is taxed at a concessional rate.



Opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg said the Coalition was concerned that more people would enter retirement as renters. Related Article Superannuation Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy “If we are going to become almost a majority nation of retired renters, then we need to look very carefully at how these things are calibrated,” he said. But Chalmers will argue both the Coalition and One Nation were intent on dismantling superannuation in a move that would hurt the budget and the retirement incomes of older Australians. “We’re witnessing now the biggest threat to compulsory super, with preservation at its core, in the four decades since it began.



“The next election will be super’s existential moment. It will help determine whether we make the most of our intergenerational advantages or trash them.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Stayin’ alive on that big dipper
World.content:
The Brothers Gibb (C8) sure got around back in the day, going by this latest encounter. Les Herbert of Concord recalls that “in 1963, my brother Paul, then aged 14 was a friend of Bandstand regular Trevor Gordon who invited him to Luna Park where they spent the day with a couple of other 14-year-olds, Gibb twins, Maurice and Robin. He reminisced on that story over many years. On a sad note, not one of the four from that day made the age of 65.”

“Robyn Cashman suggests a Cathy Wilcox book would make a great addition to every school’s modern history reading list,” notes Maralyn Lawson of Greenwich. ” A wonderful idea. Europe Since Versailles : A History in One Hundred Cartoons with a Narrative Text (1940) by the New Zealand-born political cartoonist David Low was brilliant teaching resource. Like Wilcox, Low encapsulated dire circumstances with honesty, wit and a depth of understanding which clarified complexity and human failing without rancour.”

“Don’t know about a book,” says Barry Riley of Woy Woy. “But surely, there’s an art gallery somewhere dedicated to Cathy Wilcox’s work.”

Merilyn McClung of Forestville rejoins the name (change) game: “I suggest that north of the 40th parallel in the US be renamed (C8) Canada South and the remainder North Mexico. That will rid the world of this troublesome president.” Grand idea. Now you just have to talk those two nations into taking on a $US40 trillion ($55.3 trillion) debt.

“Being retired and having time on my hands and needing a good laugh, I thought I might attend the ICAC inquiry (C8),” says Paul Duncan of Leura. “But then I realised I’d better not in case I contracted the memory loss, which seems to be contagious, and could not find my way home.” Jeff McNamara of Ulverstone (Tas) adds: “Seems Ray Hadley (as a witness in the Alan Jones trial) has also been infected with Amnesia testium following outbreaks in the ICAC inquiries. Better get the N95 face masks out if you’re in Sydney at the moment.”

World.title: Suburbs where house prices are rising and falling fastest
World.content:
Depending on where you live in the country, house values in your suburb could have increased by 5 percent in the past three months, or townhouse values could have slipped more than 11 percent.

New data from Cotality shows almost 80 percent of New Zealand's suburbs recorded falling standalone house values in the three months to September, and just under 75 percent experienced a drop in townhouse values.

But in some suburbs, there were double-digit drops for townhouses, as increased supply in the market met sluggish demand.

Cotality tracked 1422 suburbs in its latest update and said 750 recorded falls of more than 1 percent. About 300 suburbs had prices that were flat or increasing.

For townhouses, 74 percent of suburbs had value drops and 22 suburbs recorded falls of more than 5 percent.

When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Cotality chief property economist Kelvin Davidson described it as "broad-based sluggishness".

Sales activity had been slow, he said, and the stock of available listings was high so buyers had the upper hand in negotiations.

He said regions where property values were more affordable were the strongest performers when it came to the value of standalone houses.

Median values rose by 2 percent or more since June in areas including Pukenui, up 5.1 percent, Waimamaku, up 2.9 percent, Makarewa, up 2.7 percent and Kennington, up 2.5 percent.

Blackball on the West Coast was up 2.3 percent and St Arnaud in Tasman was up 2.1 percent. Townhouses increased in value most quickly in Paeroa, Castlecliff and Koutu, Rotorua.

Davidson said regional areas were generally experiencing more value growth than Auckland and Wellington.

Townhouses had dropped the most in areas such as Beachlands, where they were down 11.2 percent, Mangere, where they were down 9.9 percent, Wiri, down 9.8 percent, Kingsland, down 9.1 percent and Kelburn, down 10.7 percent.

"In general, our data is not showing that townhouse values are dramatically underperforming their standalone counterparts," Davidson said.

"But some particular terraced properties in these specific suburbs may be lagging due to characteristics such as unpopular floor/storey layouts or a lack of parking. Anecdotally, sales incentives are becoming more popular too, or unsold stock is sometimes being put out to rent."

He said he was hearing about townhouses in the middle of three being trickier to sell, or those without parking or access. "It might be the same floor space spread over three storeys rather than two storeys so the internal layout could be a bit difficult.

"We hear of sales incentives going on for townhouses where you keep the list price the same but pay the buyer's mortgage for the first year or something.

"These sorts of things are not going to be picked up in sales records."

He said in Auckland there had been a large increase in supply of townhouses but that was increasing supply of property overall for a fixed level of demand.

"People are still buying townhouses, first-home buyers have been pretty keen on them. That is the new stock, so you're getting around loan-to-value ratios and debt-to-income ratios."

Herne Bay still had the country's most expensive houses, at a median $3.03 million and Stonefields had the highest townhouse median, at $1.3 m.

Davidson said he expected the subdued conditions in the market to persist.

"With elevated economic uncertainty, higher mortgage rates, and a labour market recovery delayed until 2027, activity could stay subdued for at least another six months. However, improved affordability should help limit further downside risk.

"Even in parts of Canterbury, parts of Southland, it's not as if things are really screaming away. Even in so-called resilient markets, (the growth is still low by past standards, but it just looks quite strong compared to Auckland or Wellington) … it's just really difficult at the moment to see what turns this around. There's a real sort of holding pattern vibe to the housing market at the moment with buyers. Buyers do have the power in a lot of areas, but we're not seeing sort of mass layoffs or anything, so people with houses, with mortgages, are generally keeping their job.

"It's the new people coming into the labour force that are struggling to find work, but they won't have a mortgage probably."

He said it could be another six months of "going nowhere".

World.title: Government to implement findings from mental health hotline review
World.content:
The government has accepted all the recommendations from a report into the telehealth service for mental health.

The review found too many people who tried to call for help didn't get through.

"Too many people approaching these services do not get their calls answered, a proportion of whom may be experiencing acute distress," the independent report said.

It also found the telehealth services weren't adequately integrated with the wider mental health and addiction system.

Minister for Mental Health Matt Doocey said the government was "acting swiftly to implement the findings of the review".

"The review provides reassurance that core safety systems are in place, including triage, risk assessment, escalation processes, and clinical governance," he said.

"But it also makes clear there is more work to do. Too many people are not getting through quickly enough, and we do not always have enough visibility of what happens after someone is referred or escalated to another service."

He outlined three initiatives intended to address the report's findings.

First was to expand peer support via the 1737 hotline, which previously operated between 2pm and 10pm, to 9am to midnight.

It would also commission a pilot to attempt proactive follow-up calls to people who had contacted 1737 in distress.

The third initiative would set up a 24/7 suicide prevention crisis line within the telehealth system.

"We are clear, and there are no exceptions to the rule; when someone reaches out for help, they should be able to access the support they need without waiting too long," Doocey said.

Where to get help:

Need to Talk? Free call or text 1737 any time to speak to a trained counsellor, for any reason.

Lifeline: 0800 543 354 or text HELP to 4357.

Suicide Crisis Helpline: 0508 828 865 / 0508 TAUTOKO. This is a service for people who may be thinking about suicide, or those who are concerned about family or friends.

Depression Helpline: 0800 111 757 or text 4202.

Samaritans: 0800 726 666.

Youthline: 0800 376 633 or text 234 or email talk@youthline.co.nz.

What's Up: 0800 WHATSUP / 0800 9428 787. This is free counselling for 5 to 19-year-olds.

Asian Family Services: 0800 862 342 or text 832. Languages spoken: Mandarin, Cantonese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, Japanese, Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, and English.
