World.title: Coroner calls on MBIE to ban tankless diving device after accidental drowning
World.content:
The day before he died, Shengwei Cao pulled out his new tankless diving device - a Wolach 919 - and tested it in the bathtub.

By 11.30am on 5 March, 2023, the device, sometimes known as a hookah type system, was on the surface of the water off the coast of Mana Island, pumping air through an umbilical hose to Cao, who was diving below.

About an hour later, a couple of boaties - alerted to a missing diver - pulled the 58-year-old's body from the water.

He was declared dead onshore shortly after.

In findings published on Wednesday, Coroner Amelia Steel ruled Cao's death an accidental drowning, with decompression complications a contributing factor.

She recommended the Wolach 919 be banned from importation into the country and that the Ministry of Business, Innovation, and Employment (MBIE) launch an awareness campaign about such devices and a broader product review of risks and regulations.

In her report, Steel said Cao, a painter from Lower Hutt, had been free diving for at least five years.

He usually dived in shallow water close to the shore, and only when the weather was good, she said. Occasionally he would take pills for seasickness.

Steel said Cao wasn't trained in scuba diving but hoped to learn and had discussed its differences with friends.

An advertising image shows the Wolach 919. Supplied / Alibaba.com

His online purchase of the Wolach 919 would enable him to dive deeper, she said, and he tested it in the bathtub on 4 March, 2023.

The next day, the 58-year-old met up with six other friends and began diving off Mana Island around 11.30am.

"Mr Cao was using the Wolach to free dive for the first time, while the other people were scuba diving."

The Wolach was attached to a buoy.

After several dives, Cao returned to the boat, complaining of seasickness and that the Wolach wasn't working. Steel said he needed help getting out of the water, which was unusual.

But 10 minutes later, feeling better, he was back in the water.

However, not long after, his friends requested to dive elsewhere and unable to get Cao's attention, they left him alone, Steel said. The skipper noted the 58-year-old's breathing bubbles on the surface as they went.

When the skipper returned to the site, the rocky shore prevented him from approaching Cao. He headed back to the main group and alerted a passing boat to a missing diver.

The boaties found Cao's body still attached to the buoy, in water about five metres deep, Steel said.

The breathing tube and pump, which went from the surface of the water to Cao, were also attached to the buoy she said.

"However, the mouthpiece attached to the breathing tube was to the side of Mr Cao's head, rather than in his mouth."

A short time later on shore, Cao was declared dead by emergency services.

Steel said a specialist from the Police National Dive Squad tested Cao's gear in a diving pool and among several findings noted the Wolach design left the diver with an inconsistent air supply, particularly at depths of around 4.5 to 5 metres.

The specialist considered it to be a "dangerous system" leaving the diver in an unsafe position without immediately available air.

The specialist found Cao's use of the Wolach, continuing to dive when unwell, and diving alone were all factors in his death, Steel said.

'Avoidable tragedy'

Water Safety New Zealand said Cao's death was an avoidable tragedy that demonstrated the risks of diving alone.

In 2025, more than 55 percent of the 79 drownings were people undertaking water activities by themselves, it said.

Supplied / Water Safety New Zealand

The organisation's kaihautū Māori Rob Hewitt said the coroner's findings read like a "tragic list of everything you must never do" when heading out underwater.

"Diving in open water is absolutely not the place to try new equipment," he said.

Hewitt told RNZ Cao's death hit home. Hewitt survived four days at sea in 2006 after a routine dive trip off Mana Island went wrong.

"When I first ... saw the coroner's report and saw where it was, it sort of touched my heart and woke up a few thoughts of when I was lost out at sea."

He said New Zealand men needed to understand they weren't bulletproof.

"When the unexpected happens you need someone close to you who can immediately give you some help. Tragically this was not the case for Mr Cao."

He said training, ensuring equipment was fit for purpose and diving with a buddy were critical.

MBIE considering findings

MBIE's manager of consumer services Simon Gallagher said the agency was considering the coroner's findings and recommendations and was committed to assessing any appropriate actions.

He noted the Wolach 919 was not currently available for sale in the country, but recognised the importance of understanding and addressing potential risks with such tankless diving products.

World.title: Rotorua triple homicide: Police stand guard at scene overnight
World.content:
Police have been standing guard overnight at the scene of a triple homicide in Rotorua.

Emergency services arrived at the home on High Street in Glenholme shortly before 10.30pm on Monday, where they found the bodies of two young children along with a critically injured woman who died at the scene.

Police began a homicide investigation and a man aged in his early 20s appeared in the Rotorua District Court on Tuesday, charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship.

The man and the victims were granted interim name suppression and he was remanded in custody until next month.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell said she was heartbroken to hear of the deaths, which had been tragic for the community.

"As the investigation continues, our thoughts are with the victims and of course their loved ones," she said.

"I really want to acknowledge the emergency services and frontline staff who have had to respond to this horrific tragedy."

Tapsell said the Glenholme area was home to many elderly people who had lived there for a long time.

A 79-year-old man who had lived on the street his whole life said he was in shock since learning what had happened.

The people living in the house seemed to have recently moved in, he said, and he had seen new children around the street.

World.title: Hospitals were overflowing well before flu cases peaked, data reveals
World.content:
Hospitals were overflowing well before flu cases reached their peak, newly released data shows.

Health NZ released a snapshot of the occupancy rates of eight hospitals at 8am over eight days in mid August.

It showed most had more patients than staffed beds.

Christchurch Hospital was worst hit - with nearly a fifth more patients than beds most days.

Whangārei was usually at about 110 percent capacity, with Waikato just under.

Auckland and Wellington were regularly over 100 percent, with North Shore and Waitākere between 103 and 93 percent.

The figures covered 7 to 14 August, excluding the weekend.

Flu hospitalisations were increasing that week but have grown to record numbers since then, prompting many hospitals to cut elective surgeries and set up dedicated flu wards.

Health NZ said emergency department presentations began to drop off in the second half of August but were still very high. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Health NZ said hospital occupancy was measured as the percentage of staffed bed capacity at a point in time and could fluctuate throughout the day.

When hospitals were over 100 percent occupancy, they used so-called flex beds - beds which were available only for very busy times and were not included in official occupancy counts.

The figures in this story are several weeks old because it took that long for Health NZ to provide them.

Health NZ said it could not give an update on hospital occupancy on Tuesday.

However it said, nationally, emergency department presentations began to drop off in the second half of August but were still very high.

It could not immediately give data for ED presentations for individual hospitals, a spokesperson said.

Emergency department doctors and nurses have told RNZ there was a lot of variation from hospital to hospital.

RNZ requested the hospital occupancy rates after it was revealed last month some ambulance patients in the North Shore rohe were being diverted to Whangārei Hospital.

It asked for the rates for those two hospitals, as well as for Waitakere, Auckland City, Waikato, Wellington, Christchurch and Dunedin.

Health NZ said it could not give the rates straight away and put the request through its Official Information Act process which took three weeks.

Of the hospitals in the request, only Dunedin Hospital never hit 100 percent.

World.title: Drug funding: 'We are way behind where we need to be globally'
World.content:
A public health professor is backing the call for more drug funding, but says any cost-benefit analysis must include Pharmac's negotiating power.

It follows an economic study commissioned by Business NZ that found every additional dollar spent on medicines delivers an almost $2 economic return.

The report said New Zealand spent 4.9 percent of its health budget on drugs compared to 12.2 percent in Australia.

Three drug companies - AbbVie, GSK, and Roche helped fund the study and gave expertise - but BERL consultancy says the report findings are entirely its own.

Bond University Business School executive dean Robin Gauld said New Zealand did not spend enough on pharmaceutical goods.

"We are way behind where we need to be globally."

He said the country did not have the same access to modern drugs, especially advanced cancer drugs or those for rare conditions, and maintained any analysis that helped decision makers expand funding was valuable.

However, he said the report did not include Pharmac's role in keeping drug prices low.

Gauld said New Zealand paid about half the price that Australia did for the most commonly prescribed drugs, thanks to the state drug buyer.

"If New Zealand was paying Australia's prices, we may be up nearer to the percentage of dollars being spent on drugs within the overall health budget.

"Australia will be spending a bit more of a percentage in any case, and that means that all of these extra cancer drugs and so forth are available."

Pharmac director of strategy, policy and performance Michael Johnson said the agency acknowledged the Business New Zealand report, and concerns about New Zealand's level of medicines spending compared to other OECD countries.

"Funding allocation for medicines is decided by the Government through the annual Budget process, with Pharmac responsible for deciding which medicines are publicly funded within the available budget to deliver the greatest health benefit for New Zealanders," he said in a statement.

In recent years, the Government had provided significant increases to the medicines budget, he said.

"Pharmac continues to explore how it might update its assessment approach to include the wider societal benefits of funding medicines."

Gauld said New Zealand's lack of investment in drugs was symptomatic of a broader under-investment in healthcare and pointed to recent reports of wait times in cardiology and [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/health/1197171/patients-going-blind-36-000-overdue-for-tests-amid-high-demand ophthalmology of a system that was not working.

He said the health system had been unacceptable for several years.

"I thought about the 36,000 people who haven't been able to see an eye specialist, I just can't imagine 36,000 cars sitting up and down the roads of New Zealand with flat tyres, burnt out, unable to be moved because the roads are so bad.

"And that's the analogy with our healthcare system. People are just being left behind."

He said it was a political scandal.

"It's absolutely appalling that in a so-called first-world country, our successive political leaders - across all political parties that have been in power - have abjectly failed the country.

"The drug spend is sort of a micro-system within the broader health spend and health policy of the country."

Gauld said there was a real need for "genuine cross-party consensus" on health that was designed to endure the election cycle.

The Ministry of Health directed questions to the minister's office.

World.title: Police officers made 'split second tactical decisions' in fatal shooting of Kaoss Price, High Court told
World.content:
Lawyers for the Crown have told the High Court in Wellington officers involved in the fatal shooting of Kaoss Price in 2022 made "split second tactical decisions".

Counsel are testifying on the second day of proceedings in a Judicial Review of the decision not to charge the officer who fired the fatal shot.

The Independent Police Conduct Authority's investigation found the officer who fired the fatal shot used excessive force, but did not recommend prosecuting the officer.

Split second decisions

Crown Counsel Peter Gunn said three and a half minutes elapsed between officers attempting to pull over a car driving ahead of Price, his accelerating away and side swiping a police dog van before being shot while trying to hi-jack another car.

Price had been released from prison earlier that year and Gunn told the court a prior search of a vehicle linked to Price had recovered four firearms - including a loaded shotgun.

"Mr Price had been well known to police. He had numerous criminal convictions which included theft, car conversion, assault and driving offences," Gunn said.

Officers armed at the beginning of their shift

On the night of the incident the two officers involved had chosen to wear their Glock pistols at the beginning of their shift which they put down to their awareness of a warrant for Price and concerns over two other individuals in the area.

At about 9.30pm on 16 April, Price's VW Golf was seen driving closely behind another BMW vehicle.

"They both knew that Mr Price was a repeat offender, was known to carry firearms and knives and was also the subject of an arrest warrant," Gunn told the court.

Gunn told the court when the officers signalled to pull the BMW over the VW Price was driving then turned off its head lights and accelerated away.

He said the VW turned and drove towards the officers' vehicle at high speed and on the wrong side of the road.

In interviews Officer A said he felt Price was "hunting" the officers.

"I thought I was going to die. I thought my name was going to be on the plaque at the police college," the officer said.

The officers described feeling their vehicle (a dog van) shudder as the VW narrowly passed and turned in front of oncoming traffic before heading back.

"Both officers felt the vehicle collide with the dog van and scrape along the vehicle. During the Collision Officer A drew his pistol and fired two shots through the open window at the passing vehicle," Gunn said.

The officers heard the VW's engine revving and gears grinding and feared the VW would be put into reverse.

Price climbed out of the VW and ran away from the officers, down the road, trying the handles of vehicles as he went while Officer A fired more shots.

Price then forced his way into an occupied Hyundai and struggled with the driver to gain control of the vehicle.

Gunn said Officer A told interviewing officers he had only moments to decide his course of action.

"I needed to help those two people [occupants of the vehicle]. There was no time to sit back and discuss what I was going to do. I had to make a decision," the officer told investigators.

Officer A arrived at the car and ordered Price to get out of the car, he did not comply, and the officer shot Price in the chest through the window.

A second officer then tasered Price and he was removed from the car and given first aid. He died at the scene.

Lawyers argue investigation failed Bill of Right's obligations

Yesterday, lawyer for Price's family, Max Harris, said the IPCA's investigation had failed in its obligations under the Bill of Rights to be independent, impartial, prompt, thorough and transparent - and the process had undermined the effectiveness and the credibility of the investigation.

Gunn said it was inaccurate for lawyers for Price's family to suggest to suggest that the IPCA was not acting independently of police.

"If a police investigation misfires then the Section 8 [Bill of Rights] obligation may be made by the IPCA. [Here] we have an IPCA investigation report which has not been challenged," Gunn said.

He said police had drawn investigating officers from other parts of the country and delays in interviewing the officer were related to public holidays near the incident and police's commitment to head the investigation with staff not close to the officers involved.

In response to the family's lawyers' criticism of the IPCA - stemming from the authority's handling of disgraced former Police Commissioner Jevon McSkimmings - Gunn told the court the investigation into Price's shooting showed no similar evidence of collusion or influence from police to conceal the nature of the events.

Gunn also took aim at criticism of the police interviews and said officers who called Officer A "mate" fourteen times during his nearly seven hour interview were "building rapport" with the officer.

"What they are attempting to do is find common ground. When you show empathy people open up," Gunn said.

Gunn said that police actions following the shooting demonstrated they were aware a charge of homicide was a real possibility.

"[The officer] was tested for firearm residue, performed a drug and alcohol test and his uniform was seized before he was allowed to go home," Gunn said.

Gunn told the court that a senior officer cautioned Officer A as to his rights as was necessary when a person was detained, or questioned as a suspect.

"At the time, in the absence of an explanation and the circumstances - as I understood them to be - I thought there was a strong possibility of a homicide charge and a Bill of Rights caution was appropriate," The officer told investigators.

Gunn said the police's actions towards the officers involved highlighted seriousness with which they approached the incident and their "open mind" towards the potential prosecution of the officers involved.

Police letter to family 'unhelpful' - Justice Heine

Counsel for the Crown, Peter Marshall defended the letter sent to Price's family informing them of the circumstances of his death, police intelligence regarding his offending and a single sentence as to why his shooting would not be prosecuted which read:

"Based on an assessment of the circumstance and the law relating [to] self defence and the defence of another (Section 48 of the Crimes Act), police has determined there is insufficient evidence to support criminal prosecution of the officers involved in this incident."

"Decisions are made by public prosecutors in the public interest. They are not ever made in the interest of victims," Marshall said.

Justice Victoria Heine said the language used to convey the decision was "economical" and "not particularly helpful" to the family.

But Marshall said it was not up to prosecutors to "evaluate the evidence" for the benefit of the family.

He went on to tell the court that a homicide charge against Officer A could be defended on the grounds that the officers actions arose from the belief that Price intended to kill the officers or harm others.

"It's not whether [Price] intended to do that but whether you could prove the officer did not hold that belief," Marshall said.

'There was time to make a tactical assessment to disengage'

In summing up, lawyer for the family Christopher Stevenson contrasted Price with the case concerning Stephen Wallace, who was shot as he advanced on officers with a weapon in 2000.

"By the time Mr Price had climbed out of the vehicle he'd been shot at twice, he was then running away and Officer A made that choice to follow him to the vehicle [where he was shot].

"There was time to make a tactical assessment to disengage but that didn't happen," Stevenson said.

He said the officer had conceded that he had seen Price's empty hands as he attempted to enter nearby vehicles.

He said because the ICPA could not instigate prosecution it could not cure the deficiencies in the police investigation.

He argued that Counsel for the Crown's point that Officer A being cautioned as to his rights could be seen as an indication that police saw a real potential for charges being laid against the officer but said that wasn't reflected in a decision to treat the officer as a witness.

"The unarmed man fleeing police - and then he was shot - that does require [the officer] to be treated as a suspect," Stevenson said.

World.title: Two people arrested after hours long stand-off with Nelson police
World.content:
Two people have been arrested after an hours long stand-off with police in Nelson.

Senior Sergeant Mark Surman said police were at an address in Toi Toi regarding an unrelated incident when a man became enraged, threatened police, then locked himself inside a residence and refused to leave.

Armed police were at the scene as a precaution and cordons were put in place along Emano Street from Murphy Street to Toi Toi Street.

A neighbour who entered the property during the stand-off was also arrested.

Both were taken into custody about 6.25pm and cordons were lifted at 7pm.

Police want to reassure the public that there was no threat to public safety.

World.title: Crook elbows and big dreams propelling unheralded Knights for NRL finals
World.content:
Newcastle forward Francis Manuleleua might be less than two weeks off dislocating his right elbow but at the end of an interview he'll still shake your hand and shake it hard.

"Nah, let's go for it G," Manuleleua said when offered the chance to forgo a handshake, just in case.

"It's gotta be strong."

The 22-year-old's right arm bent in a way that right arms are not supposed to bend in the Knights loss to the Warriors a fortnight back.

Manuleleua suffered a dislocated elbow against New Zealand two weeks ago. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

It looked gruesome — Manuleleua was straight on the green whistle and phrases like "bony deformity" were used in analysis of the video.

But with Newcastle already without key men Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti due to injury and suspension ahead of Friday's sudden-death semifinal against South Sydney and after being cleared of a fracture, Manuleleua will push to play.

He was named on Tuesday for what would be his NRL finals debut and is one of an unheralded mix of youngsters and journeymen in the Knights forwards who will be tasked with taking down the Rabbitohs.

In terms of star power it's a no-contest. Every player in the South Sydney starting pack has played either Test or Origin football except for Tallis Duncan, who might not have to wait long to join them.

Duncan pushing for maiden World Cup berth Australia are facing a shortage of backrowers for this year's Rugby League World Cup but South Sydney tyro Tallis Duncan could prove to be the answer.

Manuleleua has a mere 11 NRL matches to his credit and fellow second rower Jermaine McEwen is wrapping up his first full season as an every week player.

The baby of the side is starting prop Cody Hopwood, still just 20, although at 196cm and 105kgs that's a damn big baby.

He's great mates with eight-gamer Lachlan Crouch, who received his first Knights cap from Paul Harragon himself upon his NRL debut earlier this year.

Both the rookies played their juniors in Maitland, as did the more seasoned Thomas Cant and Pasami Saulo who both fit the image of the honest toiler.

Cant has played almost 40 NRL matches since his debut in 2023 and is yet to score a try but that pales compared to Saulo — he's about to finish his ninth season in the league without a single four-pointer to show for it.

Injuries have ripped through the Knights pack in recent weeks. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Newcastle will lean heavily on the experience of 300-gamer Tyson Frizell and the underrated Matt Croker at lock as they match it with a South Sydney pack that is both fully loaded and battle-hardened.

Cameron Murray, Junior Tatola, David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi all have 150 NRL games or more to their credit and all but Fifita have been through multiple finals campaigns.

Even Duncan, by far their least experienced starting forward, has made more first grade appearances than Manuleleua, Crouch, Hopwood and McEwen combined.

Given he's marking up on the reborn Fifita, Manuleleua might be facing the biggest task of all and certainly the hardest test of an NRL career that began just a few months ago. He can't wait for it.

"He's a big, powerful boy and there's a job to do. But I'm keen for the challenge," said Manuleleua.

"They've got a lot of strengths on their edge with Fifita, Latrell Mitchell and Jack Wighton and a great ball-player in Cody Walker, so it's a good challenge for us edges.

"But that's the kind of footy we want to play anyway. We want to go after that challenge, go after them and see what happens."

Despite making his NRL debut in Round 3, a steady start is leading to a big finish for Manuleleua.

It wasn't until Round 20 that he became a regular starter following Lucas going down with an ankle injury.

But with six line breaks, two tries, five try assists and 23 tackle busts in the six games since, Manuleleua has proven to be one of the finds of the season.

He's a big, explosive man who can do big, explosive things and has it in him to be a wrecking machine but he's also fresh enough that so much of this is still new.

The match against the Warriors, for example, was the first time the Papatoetoe junior got to play back in New Zealand and over 25 family members and countless friends packed out the stands to see him.

Manuleleua scored a try on his return to New Zealand last week. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters )

"It's pretty surreal. I still can't believe it. I didn't think I'd be playing finals footy this early in my career," said Manuleleua.

"It was gun, that game against the Warriors. They (my family) were loud as hell, Warriors had 25,000 fans but I could still hear my family and it was the first time I played an NRL game in front of them at home.

"It was bittersweet because we couldn't win the game but they were just happy I scored a try."

Manuleleua's clash with Fifita might be the most difficult job but it's not the biggest — that belongs to Hopwood, who will start at prop.

He did the same in the club's most recent clash with South Sydney in Round 19, when Hopwood and Crouch got in the mix with the Rabbitohs amid a torrid physical battle.

The two Maitland boys are popular members of the Knights squad given they have a special brand of front-row charm, as Manuleleua explains.

"They're intentionally funny. They'll do something weird but it'll be funny," said Manuleleua.

"When it comes to the game they look like monsters but they're kind at heart, they're good people."

Hopwood doesn't have time to think about what Manuleleua is talking about given he's about to play the biggest game of his life.

Hopwood will start in the front row for an NRL final at just 20 years of age. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

"I have no idea what that means. I don't think I want to know either," said Hopwood.

"Whenever you're out and about people are wishing you luck for Friday night, the town's flying and we're all excited.

"I'm really confident, I'm in a good spot mentally and physically. Attack it front on, that's probably the best way to go. Just go hard and try to go for longer."

Hopwood was a highly rated junior, representing New South Wales Under 19s twice, but despite making his NRL debut in the final round of last season he never thought he'd play as much first grade in 2026 as he has.

"Not at all, but I've had some really good people around me that have helped with the transition," said Hopwood.

"I thought I might only play two or three games this year, so it's all come pretty quick.

"I'm feeling really supported and I don't want to let anyone down, I want to repay that faith."

Hopwood did not expect to play more than one or two NRL games this year. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar )

Hopwood's done a fine job with it so far, starting seven of his 14 games this season, and seems the type who never learned to take a backward step.

Whether that will be enough against players like Koloamatangi and Murray remains to be seen but Hopwood isn't thinking about the odds stacked against him or his side.

Like any good Novocastrian, he has dreamed of making a difference for the Knights his whole life and was there as a 17-year old in the crowd for their last finals win three years ago.

Dom Young roaring down the sideline for a length-of-the-field try is a memory that will never leave him and now all he wants is to give Knights fans another moment that lasts forever.

"I remember thinking how much I'd love to be a part of something like that and I get to live it on Friday night," said Hopwood.

"How good is that?"

World.title: Popovic knocked back four-year Socceroos contract extension
World.content:
Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

Popovic instead signed a six-month extension during the World Cup to take the team through to the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia, which begins in January.

"It was my choice to go until the Asian Cup. Although I was offered a four-year deal, I decided to go to the Asian Cup," Popovic told journalists on Tuesday.

"And I think that is something that I think is good.

"It gives the FA the opportunity if they want to go in a different decision they can, and I'm very comfortable with the decision that's been made."

FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' Football's major governing bodies continue to fight over the failed plan by FIFA president Gianni Infantino to sell off the rights for the World Cup, with the global governing body accusing European body UEFA of a "smear campaign" against the president.

Popovic led the Socceroos to the round of 32 knockout stage of the World Cup in the United States, where the team lost to Egypt in a penalty shoot-out heartbreaker.

His side won its opening match against Türkiye, lost to the United States and drew with Paraguay before the fateful match against Egypt ended the Socceroos' dream run.

He led the youngest side at the World Cup of all 48 nations with an average of 25 years and 155 days.

Some of the Socceroos stars of the tournament have since signed transfer contracts worth up to $33 million, including Lucas Herrington (Hull City), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting Lisbon), Alessandro Circati (Benfica), Patrick Beach (Troyes) and Paul Okon-Engstler (Köln).

When asked directly whether he wanted to continue coaching the Socceroos, Popovic declined to give a direct answer, instead elaborating on his focus on fostering young talent.

"I love coaching the Socceroos," he said.

"When we qualified there was obviously 12 months before the World Cup.

"I ended up signing [his six-month contract] the last week before the first [World Cup] match, and we started this evolution of the team for 12 months without knowing whether I'd be there or not.

"I've never shied away from the expectation of results.

"But I've always had an eye on the future, and I think that was reflected in the squad we chose, the players we played and how much the team changed in 12 months."

Socceroos' World Cup story ends in heartbreak The Socceroos exited the World Cup in the cruellest possible manner, on penalties to Egypt. But the roots of the defeat could be found in the 120 minutes of play, which clearly showed where Australia must improve.

He said he was happy to make those decisions without the security of a long-term contract.

"I had no concerns about whether I signed or not and if I hadn't signed I would have been happy with what I had done and what I have left behind," he said.

"The same will be after the Asian Cup.

"I know the legacy that I will leave behind.

"And if it's someone else that takes it forward, that's fine; if it's me, great, if we agree to do this together," he said.

Popovic's decision to not take up the four-year contract offer gives him the option of pursuing a club contract now that he's been able to shop his talents through the World Cup window.

In his first press conference since returning from the World Cup, Popovic reflected on the decisions he made at the tournament and said there was little he would change.

He drew criticism from commentators for the goalkeeper substitution minutes before the penalty shoot-out against Egypt, which the Socceroos ultimately lost 4-2 when Harry Souttar and Lucas Herrington missed penalties.

Popovic introduced captain Matt Ryan, who hadn't played a minute in the World Cup, for Patrick Beach, who had been outstanding, conceding just three goals in four matches.

He said he would make the same decision again.

"There are many reasons why Matty came in," he said.

"Matty has experience; Matty saved two penalties for us in the qualifiers; Matty saved penalties for [his Spanish club team] Levante.

"Patrick Beach has not saved one penalty in any shoot-out, pretty much.

"In that moment it was very clear to me that Matty should come in.

"And like I said the next day I would have done the same thing."

The Socceroos play their first Asian Cup match against Singapore on January 9, where Popovic said he would continue his youth policy.

There will be a lot of young players probably at the Asian Cup, and that will be done without losing any expectation that I believe that we should be challenging for the Asian Cup," he said.

"Once you're there, you want to win it.

"I think that should happen for Australia."

The team has two friendlies later this month against the might of five-time world champions Brazil in Townsville and Brisbane.

Popovic said the team would have a chance to play another round of matches during the November friendly window, most likely in the Middle East.

World.title: Cricket Australia agrees to bring private investment to Big Bash
World.content:
Cricket Australia has agreed to bring private investment into the Big Bash League, starting with the sale of the Melbourne Renegades.

The Cricket Australia (CA) board made the announcement on Tuesday, with the sale process of the Renegades to be the first venture into bringing private investment into the franchise T20 league.

Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation The Big Bash League is set to look like it never has before as Cricket Australia prepares to welcome private ownership to the competition.

CA is hoping the Renegades will play under new ownership for the 2027/28 Big Bash season.

Depending on the success of the Renegades sale, CA said in a statement on Tuesday that it would "consider taking other clubs to market under a self-determination model that gives each State member the ability to assess the optimal pathway for its own club and community".

CA chair Mike Baird said the decision was a major moment for cricket in Australia.

"Beginning the sales process for the Renegades allows us to take the first step in a self-determination model for our members and represents a defining moment for the game," he said.

"Importantly, CA and its members will maintain control over the most significant aspects of Australian Cricket operations, including international scheduling, player availability, the Big Bash Leagues' salary caps, branding proposals as well as the reserve price for a licence to operate that must be achieved, and approval of investors."

The move to bring private investment into the Big Bash Leagues has been debated for months.

CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said in May that private investment was "inevitable", and privatisation was thrust into the spotlight when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Renegades in June.

Baird said inviting private investment would allow cricket to grow at every level of the game.

"Cricket Australia and its state members are united in our commitment to investing in and growing the BBL and WBBL, and to advancing the interests of cricket at every level," he said.

"By opening the door to private investment in the Big Bash Leagues, Cricket Australia is taking a deliberate step to strengthen and secure the long-term future of the game, accelerate growth and ensuring we can keep investing in community cricket and grassroots participation, domestic and international pathways and the elite level.

"This is a significant decision that has involved an enormous amount of analysis, discussion and collaboration over many months. I'd like to thank all involved as we move to what we believe is the best way to secure cricket's future in this country, strengthen the Big Bash and protect our standing on the global stage."

World.title: Lion turns down monster offer, premiership Bulldog calls time
World.content:
Brisbane Lions premiership hero Zac Bailey has re-signed with the reigning premiers, ending a long-running saga about whether he would move to Adelaide.

In an added subplot to this Saturday night's semifinal between the Lions and the Crows at the Gabba, Bailey has turned down a monster offer from Adelaide.

The restricted free agent has penned a new eight-year deal to remain with the Lions until the end of 2034.

A two-time All-Australian, Bailey has enjoyed another outstanding season with 31 goals and averaged a career-high 21.7 disposals.

The 26-year-old's call comes as the Lions prepare to farewell star veteran Lachie Neale, who is expected to move to Collingwood during the trade period.

Bailey's signature comes just three days after the Lions were unexpectedly smashed by Sydney in the qualifying final at the SCG.

Western Bulldogs AFL premiership hero Tom Liberatore retires

Western Bulldogs stalwart and premiership hero Tom Liberatore has retired, drawing a stellar AFL career to a close.

Liberatore, 34, has been a heart-and-soul player for the Bulldogs since he was drafted as a father-son selection in 2010, including playing a pivotal role in the breakthrough 2016 premiership.

Loading Instagram content

But the son of club great and Brownlow medallist Tony Liberatore battled with injury and concussion in recent years, playing just 11 AFL matches this year.

Liberatore retires with 268 AFL games, 93 goals, a premiership and a Charles Sutton Medal as the Bulldogs' 2014 best and fairest to his name.

"This club and its community have been such a huge part of my life," Liberatore said in a club statement.

"I'm so fortunate to have lived out my dream for 16 years, from watching my old man play for the club to being part of a premiership that meant so much to all of our fans and to the western suburbs, it's been a real privilege.

"I still love being here and competing each week but it's time for me to step aside, spend more time with my family and friends and support this great club from the stands.

"I've built lifelong friendships with many teammates through the years, that's what means the most to me.

"I'm really proud of where the club is going and excited about what the group is capable of moving forward. I'm looking forward to watching on with a beer in hand."

Liberatore's retirement means captain Marcus Bontempelli is the only surviving Bulldog from the 2016 premiership team.

Marshall demands trade from Saints, Duursma wants to leave Roos

Meanwhile, Rowan Marshall is demanding a trade from St Kilda, a year after Geelong tried to lure the experienced ruckman.

Rowan Marshall wants to be traded away from St Kilda. (AAP: Morgan Hancock)

Marshall is contracted at the Saints until the end of next season, with the Cats and Essendon his strongest suitors.

He tried to leave for Geelong at the end of last season but has not yet nominated his preferred new club.

Cats coach Chris Scott was tight-lipped on his club's prospects of signing the 30-year-old.

"If I was [interested], I wouldn't tell you," Scott told reporters on Tuesday.

"It's an unfortunate situation. I think everyone would like us all to be a bit more open, but I think it's got to the stage now [where] the communication should be driven by the players themselves.

"I don't think it's our place to sort of speak on their behalf, so it's probably a question better directed at him."

Scott said the fact Marshall remained contracted at the Saints complicated matters.

Marshall played 21 games this season for the Saints, who opted for ex-Carlton recruit Tom de Koning as the club's first-choice ruck.

St Kilda said it would consider its options ahead of the trade period, which opens on October 5.

"Marshall has not nominated a preferred destination at this stage, with the club making clear that any trade will need to be in the best interests of the St Kilda Football Club," the statement said.

Meanwhile, the fourth pick from the 2023 draft, Zane Duursma, has told North Melbourne he wants to move to Melbourne.

Loading...

The Demons have long been linked to the 21-year-old, who has played 38 games for the Kangaroos in three seasons.

Duursma has resisted signing a fresh three-year contract offer from the Roos, who last week sacked veteran coach Alastair Clarkson.

The Demons are understood to have separately told former captain Jack Viney that he is welcome to explore a trade after an injury-cruelled season.

Viney, 32, played only one game — in Melbourne's wildcard finals loss to Carlton — after having pre-season Achilles surgery and then suffering back and toe injuries.

Viney, a premiership player in 2021, is contracted until the end of 2028.

AAP

World.title: Dutchman who knocked de Minaur out of US Open stages epic comeback
World.content:
Dutch tennis player Botic van de Zandschulp saved match point to avoid losing in straight sets, before staging a huge comeback to advance to the US Open quarterfinals.

The 30-year-old, who downed Australian Alex de Minaur in a second-round upset at Flushing Meadows, was on the brink of defeat against Frenchman Arthur Gea but recovered to make it to a grand slam quarterfinal for the second time in his career.

Gea, who got into the main draw tournament when 2022 runner-up Casper Ruud pulled out with a back injury, was trying to become the first lucky loser to make a men's singles grand slam quarterfinal.

After winning the opening two sets, Gea had match point in the third-set tiebreaker, but van de Zandschulp saved that, then staged his comeback to claim a 3-6, 6-7(0), 7-6(7), 7-6(3), 6-4 victory in 5 hours, 13 minutes.

It was the fourth-longest match in US Open history.

"I think this is probably better than the first quarterfinal I made here," van de Zandschulp said, referring to his other US Open quarterfinal appearance in 2021.

"It hasn't sunk in yet, but I think tomorrow it's going to be a great feeling."

Zverev through to quarterfinals in straight sets

Men's top seed Alexander Zverev has marched into the quarterfinals at Flushing Meadows with a 6-2 6-2 7-6(3) straight-sets win over Italian Luciano Darderi.

Germany's Alexander Zverev defeated Italy's Luciano Darderi in their round of 16 match at the US Open. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

It is a second consecutive straight-sets win for the German, after opening his grand slam with back-to-back five-setters in New York.

Zverev, who claimed his maiden grand slam title at this year's French Open, was expecting a much later night in New York, but was able to wrap up his victory before midnight, local time.

"I think after 10 hours on court, I just maybe found my rhythm a little bit better, which is helpful because the first two matches were really not great level," Zverev said.

"I think I'm going in the right direction, moving forward in the right direction."

Zverev will face van de Zandschulp in the quarterfinals.

Number 28 seed Alexander Blockx beat 24th seed Francisco Cerundolo 6-3, 4-6, 7-5, 7-5 to become the first man from Belgium to reach the US Open quarterfinals, where he will play Karen Khachanov.

Khachanov also needed five sets to advance to the quarterfinal stage, downing American 14th seed Learner Tien 7-5, 4-6, 6-7(6), 6-1, 6-4.

ABC/AP/Reuters

World.title: Aussie Maya Joint caught up in handshake snub at US Open
World.content:
Maya Joint's US Open has come to an end with defeat in the third round of the women's doubles in New York, but the Aussie's exit came with an unexpected controversy.

Joint and partner Hao-Ching Chan, who eliminated Serena and Venus Williams in the opening round of the grand slam, lost their third round match in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, to Su-wei Hsieh and Jelena Ostapenko.

But the controversy came after match point, when Chan and Hsieh, both from Taiwan, did not shake hands at the end.

When match point was won, Ostapenko screamed towards Chan's coaching box before celebrating with her teammate. Despite Ostapenko's boisterous and vocal act following the victory, Chan had no issue shaking her hand at the net.

But once that was done, Chan walked off the court without looking at Hsieh.

The pair reportedly have a decade-long feud that stems from Hsieh claiming the Chinese Taipei Tennis Association gave greater resources and funding to Chan.

The loss brings an end to an eventful grand slam for Joint.

She advanced to the second round of the women's singles draw after defeating Liudmila Samsonova in the first round, but fell to ninth-seeded Ukrainian Elina Svitolina in a competitive three-set match.

In the women's doubles, Joint and Chan staged a huge comeback in a 10-point tiebreaker to defeat the Williams sisters in front of a packed crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Joint and Chan would then defeat the team of Tamara Korpatsch and Nicole Fossa Huergo in the second round.

Mixed emotions as Andreeva embraces injured idol after US Open win

US Open fans have witnessed a display of sportsmanship as Mirra Andreeva tended to and consoled an injured Anastasia Potapova as the fifth seed won their fourth-round match.

Potapova jarred her knee as she lost the first point of what turned out to be their final game on Louis Armstrong Stadium, prompting Andreeva to rush to the other end of the court to check on her.

She helped the 24th seed up and Potapova was able to limp to her bench, where Andreeva asked if someone could bring her ice.

The French Open champion finished off the next three points for a 5-7, 6-4, 6-3 victory that sent her to the quarterfinals in Flushing Meadows for the first time, jogging around the net again for a warm embrace.

"It's not the perfect end to the match," 19-year-old Andreeva said.

Potapova appeared to be tearing up as Andreeva came around the net for a long embrace after the final point.

Potapova represents Austria but was born in Russia and still played under that flag when she won the junior Wimbledon championship in 2016.

"For me, Nastya, she was always like a prodigy," Andreeva said of her 25-year-old opponent.

"She came on tour early. She also had a lot of wins. I also remember we were all watching and cheering for her when she won juniors Wimbledon title. I remember watching that match.

"For me, she was always, like, a little star that I was kind of always looking at."

Potapova (right) appeared to be tearing up as the pair embraced after match point. (Getty Images: Pete Staples/USTA)

Potapova won their first meeting on tour in 2022 but Andreeva has won the past four, preventing Potapova from reaching her first grand slam quarterfinal.

"First, she just beat me. So after, I just kind of knew that she's a tough player to play, but at the same time, she was so nice," Andreeva said.

"Then since then we would practice together, and just like that, the more you see each other, the more you spend time together, then you just talk about everything, discuss everything. Then, just like that, I feel like we have a good connection off the court."

Elsewhere, Qinwen Zheng mounted another extraordinary fightback to upset six-time major winner Iga Świątek and reach the quarterfinals.

Qinwen Zheng is the first qualifier since 2021 to make it this far in the women's draw. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

Zheng has become Flushing ‌Meadows' most entertaining escape artist this year, coming back from a 0-5 deficit in the deciding set against third-round foe Madison Keys.

She let the first five games slip through her fingers in 20 minutes against 2022 champion Świątek before digging in, and she collapsed to the court with her hands ⁠in her face after sealing the win on the fourth match ‌point.

China's Olympic champion is the first qualifier ​since Emma Raducanu in 2021 ‌to reach the quarterfinals of the women's draw, as she battles back from a chronic elbow injury that had stunted her career.

Two-time winner Naomi Osaka was summarily swept aside by second seed Elena Rybakina, who won 6-1, 6-4 in just over an hour.

Coco Gauff, the 2023 champion, beat 18-year-old Iva Jovic 6-1, 6-4 in an ​all-American clash to decide the final women's quarterfinalist.

Gauff will face Andreeva, and Rybakina will take on Zheng. On the other side of the draw, third seed Jessica Pegula faces Emma Navarro, while world number one Aryna Sabalenka is up against Wimbledon champions Linda Noskova.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Everything you need to know ahead of NFL Melbourne
World.content:
American Football will roll into the MCG for a regular-season NFL match for the first time on Friday.

The San Francisco 49ers will take on the Los Angeles Rams, who are the nominal home team for the game.

This will be the first regular-season NFL game ever hosted in Australia, although American Football matches have taken place in the country before.

Here's everything you need to know about the game.

When is the game?

Davante Adams (left) will look to continue his excellent form into the new year. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The game takes place on Friday morning AEST, with kick-off at 10:35am.

That is what time kick-off will be in Victoria, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, that is a 10:05am kick-off. In Western Australia, kick-off will be 8:35am.

This is to cater for the Thursday night television audience in the United States, with a New York kick-off time of 8:35pm, while in LA the game will get underway at 5:35pm.

If you are going to the game, the gates open at 7am local time, with access to the Yarra Park precinct, which the NFL has dubbed the NFL Stadium Campus.

There will be food, entertainment, sponsor activations and fan activities to keep punters busy once they get inside.

Who is playing?

The 49ers and the Rams will meet in their season opener. (Getty Images: Brooke Sutton)

The Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers are the two teams who are set to play in this historic clash.

The Rams are the home team and come into the season as one of the favourites for this year's Super Bowl, with a stacked offence and miserly defence.

If you think the Rams sound familiar but the LA bit is confusing you, that's because the team has moved around a bit.

The team was formed in 1936 as the Cleveland Rams, moved to LA in 1946, but then shifted to St Louis in 1995, where they stayed for 20 years.

In 2015, the Rams moved back to Los Angeles.

You don't need a hat like this, but I'm sure it will help. (Getty Images: MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Keith Birmingham)

They are two-time Super Bowl Champions, winning their most recent in 2021. They play at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood.

The 49ers have always expected to reach the play-offs at an absolute minimum and will think they can do so again, despite a season beset by injuries last year.

Formed in 1944, the 49ers have always been based in the Bay area, although they currently play outside San Francisco at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara.

They have won five Super Bowls, but have not won one since 1994, despite appearing in three Super Bowls since then, most recently in 2023.

How can I watch?

The game will be available to watch in Australia on Fox Sports/Kayo or on free-to-air on Channel Seven or 7Plus.

Coverage starts from 10am AEST.

Are tickets still available?

Want to join the Rams fans? There's still time. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/Greg Fiore)

If you'd rather watch the game live, as of Monday, there are still tickets available, both standing and seated, for the game at the MCG.

You can purchase the tickets via Ticketmaster.

Why is the NFL playing in Australia?

Heading into the 2026 season, there have been 62 regular-season NFL games played away from the USA.

Starting in 2005 with Mexico City, the NFL has gradually expanded its global reach, with games in nine different cities so far, with two more added in 2026.

Melbourne, Paris and Rio de Janeiro join London, Mexico City, Toronto, Berlin, Frankfurt, Munich, São Paulo and Madrid in hosting regular-season matches.

The idea is to spread the gospel and increase the global presence of a league that has no international competition outside of America.

MCG joins illustrious list

The MCG adds itself to an exclusive list of stadiums. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Morgan Hancock)

Here's a pub quiz stat for you — the MCG will become the fifth stadium to host an NFL game and the opening/closing ceremony of an Olympic Games.

The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum (1932, 1984), Berlin's Olympiastadion (1936), London's Wembley (1940) and the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro (2016) have all hosted an Olympic Games opening ceremony, as did the MCG in 1956.

The Stade de France (closing ceremony at Paris 2024) will join it on that list when it hosts its first game later in the season.

Given the Rams are the home team, they will now have hosted matches at two different Olympic stadiums, having played at the Coliseum between 1946-1979 and 2016-2019.

Perhaps less surprisingly, the MCG is the first stadium to have hosted a Cricket World Cup final and an NFL regular-season game, so there is that.

At 100,022, the stadium has the largest capacity of any that will be used by the league this season.

Players to watch: Rams

Matthew Stafford had a career-best year in 2025. (Getty Images: Kevin Sabitus)

Quarterback Matt Stafford led the league with 4,707 passing yards and 46 passing touchdowns last season, with just eight interceptions.

That was one reason why the Rams' offence was the best in the entire league, averaging 30.5 points per game last season.

He has two elite wide receivers in his armory in Davante Adams and Puka Nacua, who was rated as the fourth-best player in the entire league by the NFL cohort.

The potential issue is that Stafford is now 38 years old and has historically struggled to back up productive passing seasons in the past.

Defensively, Myles Garrett was recently polled as the number one player in the NFL by his peers, and it's easy to see why.

According to the NFL players, Myles Garrett is the best player around. (Getty Images: Ric Tapia)

The 30-year-old defensive end led the league in sacks (23) and tackles for loss (33) last season for the Browns and his acquisition fills a gaping hole that was ruthlessly exposed as the Rams struggled down the stretch in 2025.

It's not just Garrett who has come in, though. The Rams have recruited two elite cornerbacks in Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson.

They will also welcome back Super Bowl-winning defensive tackle Aaron Donald, who has come out of retirement to lead the defensive line one last time.

Players to watch: 49ers

Two of the 49ers best players either side of the ball; defensive end Nick Bosa and tight end George Kittle, are coming off serious injuries from last season, so all eyes will be on how they front up when they suit back up this year.

Brock Purdy will want to iron out his interceptions this season. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

On the defensive side, the 49ers pass rush is a genuine concern, especially if Bosa can't return from the ACL injury that ended his season, which means former Dallas Cowboy Osa Odighizuwa may need to really up his game from defensive tackle

Offensively, Brock Purdy will be desperate to stay fit for long enough to really get into a rhythm this season.

Last year the young quarterback started just nine games and managed a TD/INT ratio of 20/10. That's too many interceptions for an elite quarterback and, given the addition of quality wide receivers Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, the Niners fans will hope he can find his accuracy.

Given all those new toys for Purdy to play with, running back Christian McCaffrey shouldn't need to be thrown to as many times as he was last year.

Christian McCaffrey got through a mountain of work in 2025. (Getty Images: Ezra Shaw)

The running back had an astonishing 102 receptions — the sixth most of any player in the league — for 924 yards and seven touchdowns last season.

That's in addition to his day job of running with the ball, where he had 1,202 yards from 311 rushes for 10 touchdowns, the eighth most rushing yards of anyone in the league.

His backup is likely to be Kaelon Black, so keep an eye on him as to whether he can carry some of that running load this season.

World.title: Cricket Australia green lights BBL privatisation, defying power states
World.content:
The Big Bash League will be partially privatised, in what looms as one of the most significant shake-ups of Australian cricket in decades.

Cricket Australia will defy heavyweight states New South Wales and Queensland to forge ahead with plans to allow states to explore sell-offs of 49 per cent stakes in their BBL franchises.

The decision to proceed was effectively made at a Cricket Australia board meeting last week, and will be officially green lit on Monday night.

BBL privatisation 'inevitable': CA Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg says private investment in the Big Bash League is "inevitable" and waiting for too long could mean "we've missed the boat" as more competitions pop up around the world.

It is understood a formal announcement will be made by Cricket Australia on Tuesday, in concert with several superstars of Australian cricket — a coup, given some initial pushback from the Australian Cricketers' Association.

However, there remains several details to be ironed out between the ACA and the CA, which has argued, amongst other things, for a greater share of revenue for its players.

The ACA insists it's supportive of privatisation as long as the long-term interests of the game are protected.

The players' union will continue to negotiate with Cricket Australia over, among other things, just how big a slice of the pie the players will receive.

This will form part of a new memorandum of understanding between the two parties.

Tasmania, Victoria and Western Australia are in support of the decision, that will allow states to undertake a market sounding process for the sale of 49 per cent stakes in their teams.

BBL privatisation became more of a reality when Cricket Victoria made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades franchise earlier this year. (AAP Image: James Ross)

But power states New South Wales and Queensland remain opposed to the plan and will undoubtedly be rankled by Cricket Australia's decision to press ahead without them fully on board.

South Australia remains lukewarm on the concept but is more open to the idea than New South Wales or Queensland.

New South Wales has long believed an injection of private equity would largely amount to a sugar hit, and broader structural reform is needed to ensure Cricket Australia's financial viability into the future.

Cricket New South Wales has been contacted for comment.

Cricket Australia believes the privatisation will allow the BBL to keep up with other domestic T20 competitions around the world, such as India's IPL. (AP)

In contrast, Cricket Australia believe that privatisation of the BBL will allow the league to keep pace with rival competitions around the world, with proceeds to be spread throughout the broader Australian cricket ecosystem.

Transactions could be complete before the start of next season.

It is likely that prospective international team owners will be courted across the upcoming summer, with potential buyers expected to be in Australia to cast their eye over this year's BBL tournament.

In June, the privatisation process was accelerated when Cricket Victoria pre-emptively made plans to sell the Melbourne Renegades, while retaining the Melbourne Stars licence.

Several state CEOs recently travelled to India and the UK to connect with prospective buyers, ahead of being given formal approval to commence a sell-off process by Cricket Australia.

Tech.title: Tesla Cybercab doesn’t have any manual controls — but it does have a virtual joystick
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

The Tesla Cybercab is notable for what it lacks, namely a steering wheel and pedal. By design, there is no way for this vehicle to be manually controlled — or so we thought. Less than a week after the Cybercab was officially launched in Austin, Texas, some riders have discovered the Cybercab’s secret manual controls that appears to be intended only for Tesla employees.

In at least two videos posted on X, Cybercab riders are encountering a virtual joystick that appears intended to control the vehicle’s movements. A square-shaped screen appears in the lower left corner of the central display, with a toggle in the middle for manual driving. It says “forward” at the top and “reverse” on the bottom. There are also buttons to “stop” the vehicle, sound the horn, and manually open the doors. To the right are views of the live camera displays, though in one rider’s video the image appears to be frozen on a Tesla Supercharger from a previous location.

Clearly these controls are intended for Tesla employees and depot workers who may need to nudge the Cybercab into a tight space at low speeds. Since the Cybercab lacks traditional controls, Tesla needed a work-around for fleet workers who may need to rearrange the vehicles in a parking lot, for example. This display would allow them to do that without having to call in a request to Tesla’s Cybercab control center or use a remote operator.

Theoretically these could also be used by law enforcement or emergency responders who may need to move a Cybercab off the road. Tesla has briefed Austin’s police department on the Cybercab service, though its unclear whether these manual controls were part of the conversation.

The customers who noticed the virtual joysticks tried unsuccessfully to use them to control the vehicle. Thankfully, they didn’t seem to work — or perhaps they weren’t using the controls accurately. Why these controls were on the display during customer rides is anyone’s guess. Chalk it up to an early bug that Tesla can hopefully fix before the Cybercabs gets any wider release.

Tesla built the Cybercab as a fully autonomous vehicle without manual controls. The purpose was to send the message that these controls are relics of the past, and the Cybercab is the vehicle of the future. But even the vehicle of the future may need some manual help every now and then.

Tech.title: The White House pulls its racist Tetris clone
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The White House has taken down its racist Tetris ripoff days after launching a website dedicated to “arcade games,” as spotted earlier by Kotaku. The Tetris clone, called “Build the Wall,” involved stacking different-sized blocks to prevent a “zombie border siege.”

It’s not clear why the White House removed the title, though the Tetris Company previously said that it’s looking into the situation. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy,” Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca told The Verge last week. “The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible. We are currently reviewing the matter.”

The Verge reached out to the Tetris Company with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

Other “games” that align with President Donald Trump’s agenda are still available on the White House’s website, including the Flappy Bird ripoff “Flappy Bill,” a Tapper-like game called “Supply Line,” “Trump Savings Tycoon,” and “Rio Run.”

Tech.title: JBL’s soundbar with detachable rear speakers is over $300 off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A lot of people are split between getting a nice all-in-one soundbar or spending more for an option that includes rear satellites for immersive surround sound. JBL’s Bar 700 Mark 2 system is one of the most unique options available, shipping with two modular speakers that charge when docked to the soundbar. When detached, the battery-powered (and mountable) speakers can be placed anywhere, lasting for up to ten hours before needing to recharge. If you’re seeking this kind of versatility, you might be pleased to know that the system has been steeply discounted at Amazon, costing $549.99 (originally $899.99).

The Bar 700 Mark 2 seems impressive on multiple fronts. The main soundbar component offers 7.1 channels, including two tweeters that fire to the side to bounce around audio with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X content. It offers vastly superior connectivity compared to some similarly-priced options, with HDMI in (with HDR 10 Plus and Dolby Vision passthrough), HDMI out with ARC and eARC support, plus optical audio. The set includes a wireless subwoofer, plus mounts.

One of the most appealing use cases for the Bar 700 Mark 2 is bringing one of its satellites with you around your house or apartment so you don’t totally miss out on the action. If the speaker’s battery is running low before you’re ready to return it to the soundbar, you can easily recharge it just by plugging in a USB-C power source.
